021爻 Case ID: XCASE-H04-L3 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-04-04 | Event ID: E12 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 勿用取女，行不順也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「不宜娶這樣的女子：她見到有財勢的男子便失去自持，沒有利益。」《象傳》解釋：行不順。

Historical event | Short narrative

After the founding of the Republic of China, Yuan Shikai occupied a central position in national government. His formal authority did not settle relations with provincial leaders, military commanders and political groups. The republican framework created expectations about the form of government, while regional forces retained resources and influence of their own. Any attempt to change that framework would require acceptance beyond the offices closest to Yuan. In 1915 Yuan moved toward a restoration of monarchy and the assumption of an imperial title. Supporters promoted the change, but public advocacy from his circle did not mean that provincial authorities and armed forces had agreed to the new political arrangement. The proposal directly altered the republican structure under which Yuan had acquired power. Opposition developed across political and regional networks. The movement commonly called the National Protection campaign challenged the imperial project, and military resistance followed the political break. As resistance widened, some figures and forces that had previously cooperated with Yuan ceased to support his plans. Opposition was not merely a disagreement about ceremonial names. It affected the ability of the central government to secure orders, retain regional allegiance and mobilize troops. What began as a proposed change in constitutional status turned into a conflict over who would exercise governing authority. Yuan cancelled the imperial system in 1916. That reversal was a concrete political outcome, but it did not immediately resolve the fragmentation of national power or the disagreements that had emerged during the crisis. The sequence is thus a republic with unresolved regional tensions, an attempted imperial change, resistance that included armed conflict, and the abandonment of the new monarchy. The surviving record supports those public developments. It does not require invented statements of private ambition from participants or a claim that every supporter changed position for the same reason. The case illustrates a political reversal whose consequences continued beyond the formal cancellation of the imperial title.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Meng's third line uses an ancient marriage image to question a course that cannot proceed properly. Yuan Shikai's attempt to establish an empire after a republic had been founded provides one possible political comparison. His 1915 initiative produced opposition and armed resistance, and the imperial system was cancelled in 1916. Public acclaim from supporters did not establish agreement among the authorities whose cooperation was needed. Before accepting a powerful role or announcing a major organizational change, ask whose consent is necessary and which existing commitments the change would disturb. A proposal may look complete within a leadership circle while its implementation depends on people outside that circle. Their ability to object is a material condition, not merely a public-relations problem. This is a retrospective analogy; no source shows Yuan using this Small Image as a guide. The gendered marriage wording belongs to the ancient passage and should not be repurposed to criticize women. Nor should a complex political collapse be explained through a single moral flaw. The relevant question is whether a decision has an adequate, openly tested basis for support.

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「困蒙的吝」《象傳》解釋：獨自遠離實際情況。

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1900, the Qing court confronted a rapidly changing crisis involving the Boxer movement, foreign powers and disputes within its own government. Armed intervention by foreign states combined with domestic mobilization to produce an increasingly dangerous situation around Beijing. The court had to decide how to respond to foreign forces and to the Boxers, while senior officials in different regions assessed the risks to their own populations and administrations. These assessments did not produce a single uniform policy. As the confrontation intensified, the Qing government issued an edict of war against foreign powers. Its declaration did not ensure that officials across the empire could carry out a common military plan. Some southeastern authorities pursued arrangements subsequently described as Southeastern Mutual Protection, reflecting their departure from the direction taken at the center. Foreign allied forces advanced on Beijing as fighting grew. The conflict cannot be reduced to an internal Chinese argument: armed foreign intervention was an integral part of its escalation. The allied forces entered Beijing, and the imperial court fled the capital. In 1901, the Qing government signed the Boxer Protocol, accepting major political and financial consequences. The crisis affected residents, local officials and national finances, not only decision makers at court. The sequence moved from competing responses to the Boxer movement and foreign military pressure, through a declaration of war and divergent provincial responses, to the occupation of Beijing and a treaty imposed after the fighting. Different actors made decisions at different moments, and the regional approaches did not all match central instructions. The record does not justify treating the Boxers as a single group with identical intentions or asserting that a particular private conversation determined every stage of the conflict. It also does not support attributing the war solely to the Qing court while omitting the actions of invading foreign armies. What can be traced is a failure to maintain a workable connection between central decisions, provincial assessments, actual military capabilities and rapidly changing conditions on the ground.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Meng's fourth line warns about ignorance sustained by distance from reality. The crisis of 1900 presents a political setting in which the Qing court, provincial officials and foreign military powers acted under sharply different assessments. The declaration of war, southeastern regional arrangements, the fall of Beijing and the subsequent Boxer Protocol show that decisions at the center did not create unified action across the country. In any difficult organization, a senior announcement should be tested against conditions at the places where it must be implemented. Which teams have the people and resources to act? What evidence contradicts the official assumptions? Who can safely report that a plan is failing? A decision becomes especially dangerous when disagreement is interpreted only as disloyalty. The historical analogy has limits. The event involved foreign armed intervention as well as internal Qing failures; its costs cannot be assigned to one actor alone. The source does not document a quotation of this Small Image by the Qing authorities. The passage is useful as a prompt to examine evidence, not as proof that a classical sentence explains the entire crisis.

Learning while employed is not the same as merely collecting qualifications. The source does not say Lü Meng learned through this Small Image; the comparison is retrospective. Historical event | Short narrative

During the Ming dynasty, communities along China's southeastern coast faced raids and unstable local security. Military officers had to respond with forces that could operate effectively in the field, not merely gather men carrying weapons. Qi Jiguang became associated with efforts to train troops against coastal raiders. Recruitment was only the first part of the task. A soldier who could use a weapon individually might still be unable to act effectively in a formation, particularly when several kinds of equipment had to be used together. Qi recruited men from Yiwu and organized training around selection, discipline and coordination. Soldiers were assigned roles and taught to work as a unit, taking account of spacing, movement and the different purposes of their weapons. Practising before an encounter was essential: a shouted order in combat could not substitute for earlier familiarity with the same movements. His military writings emphasized repeatable instruction and regulations that officers and men could put into practice rather than leaving discipline at the level of a general demand for bravery. The trained forces participated in campaigns against coastal raiding. The account of their development proceeds from insecurity in coastal regions to recruitment, organization and repeated drill, followed by operational use of the assembled force. Training did not remove every military uncertainty. Supply, terrain, the conduct of opponents and changing local circumstances also affected campaigns. Nor should the entire military record be assigned to the virtues of a single formation or commander. Other officers and ordinary soldiers carried out much of the labor of daily preparation and field service. The episode shows how a force was made usable through a sequence of administrative and practical steps. The source supports the importance Qi placed on coordinated action, but it does not establish exact words from every training session or guarantee that all units always performed as intended. The subsequent defensive work depended on maintaining instructions, discipline and cooperation after recruitment had ended. A military organization had to keep functioning beyond the moment when its members first assembled.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Meng's final line refers to defending against raiders through coordination between those above and below. Qi Jiguang's recruitment and training of troops in Yiwu provide a historical comparison: men had to learn compatible tasks, practise together and understand orders before they could operate as a unit against coastal threats. The organizational lesson is not that every group needs military discipline. It is that an agreed purpose must be supported by roles that people can actually carry out. In an emergency-response team, for example, assigning a coordinator without training participants in communication and handover procedures leaves the plan incomplete. Clear responsibilities and repeated practice make cooperation more reliable, while feedback from the people doing the work helps improve the system. This remains a retrospective interpretation. Qi's accounts do not establish that he designed his training around this passage of the Small Image. The military context also matters: ancient language about repelling raiders should not be used to endorse aggression. The historical story concerns organized defense and the practical demands of training, with outcomes still influenced by circumstances beyond the formation itself.

Historical event | Short narrative

In 154 BCE the Rebellion of the Seven States challenged the Western Han government. Rebel forces from Wu and Chu advanced, placing Liang under pressure. The Han court appointed Zhou Yafu to command an army. Liang urgently wanted relief, while Zhou had to consider the enemy’s supplies and the position of his own troops. Zhou Yafu held his position and worked to interrupt the Wu–Chu forces’ supply route rather than seeking an immediate frontal decision on terms set by the rebels. Liang continued to suffer pressure, and the decision not to rush directly to its aid provoked political dissatisfaction. Meanwhile, the rebels faced increasingly difficult provisioning. When they withdrew, Zhou took the opportunity to strike. The eventual defeat of the rebels came after a sequence of holding, disrupting supply, and attacking. The outcome did not cancel the danger faced by Liang. This account distinguishes a commander’s observable deployment from any unrecorded private feelings, and it should not turn a disputed strategic decision into a universally applicable formula. For Zhou Yafu, the pressure on Liang and the pressure on rebel provisions were connected but not identical problems. Protecting the broader campaign by targeting food supply could require patience even while an allied region requested immediate relief. Maintaining the Han position in the meantime was essential; leaving a supply route interrupted only briefly would not create the same conditions. The rebel withdrawal then offered a different military situation from the one at the start. This difference between the initial crisis and the later opportunity is necessary to understand his campaign. The historical sequence depends on several different kinds of action: an initial political or military problem, a response by people in positions to act, and an aftermath in which the arrangements still had to be implemented. Where a source summarizes a long period, it does not provide a day-by-day account or justify assigning motives to every participant.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Waiting for a workable moment. This line of the Small Image Commentary can be read beside the historical account without claiming that its actors were following the text. The episode began under constraints of authority, resources, and competing obligations. The action recorded in the sources was followed by consequences that people at the time could not simply treat as guaranteed. That order of events is important. For a present-day reader, the question is not how to predict the outcome from an ancient phrase, but how to make a responsible decision while evidence is incomplete. Start by separating verified facts from assumptions. Identify who can authorize the next step, who must carry it out, and who will bear any cost or delay. Ask whether the intended remedy has a practical route to the people affected. Set a review date, and state which evidence would require changing course. This is an editorial analogy, not proof of historical reliance on Xiaoxiang, and it does not endorse every decision made in the story. An effective comparison keeps its limits visible while leaving room to learn from the recorded sequence. What practical responsibility remains unresolved today?

In 1449, the Ming emperor Yingzong accompanied a military expedition northward against the Oirat forces. The presence of the ruler made the campaign more than a frontier operation: the movement of the army also exposed the central court to the fortunes of an expedition far from Beijing. A large military column depended on supplies, transport, reliable orders and coordination during its advance and return. The Ming forces encountered serious difficulties on the march. During the withdrawal, the army suffered a crushing defeat in the area known as Tumu, and the emperor was captured. The scale of the reverse cannot be explained by a single decision or an unverified figure for the numbers involved. Command, logistics, routes and the opposing army's actions all formed part of the conditions under which the disaster occurred. News of the defeat reached Beijing while the emperor was still in captivity. Civil and military officials then faced a linked set of urgent tasks. They had to arrange the city's defense, organize command and consider how government would operate without the sovereign present. The military defeat thus moved quickly from an expedition's route into the institutions of the capital. The measures taken in Beijing were a response to the crisis, not a sign that its outcome had been foreseen at the expedition's outset. The essential chronology is the decision to conduct the campaign, the emperor's participation, difficulties on the return, the defeat at Tumu, his capture, and the reorganization of defense and government at the capital. Historical accounts differ in their evaluation of individuals and in some numerical details. Those uncertainties should not be filled with invented scenes or reported speech. The event demonstrates that the consequences of military failure could extend beyond the battlefield, affecting political authority and daily administration while the immediate struggle remained unresolved.

As Cao Cao's armies moved south into Jing Province, Liu Bei could no longer remain in his existing position. His withdrawal involved soldiers, followers and civilians, not simply a force of troops able to march at a uniform speed. The route south placed these different groups under pressure as Cao Cao's pursuit approached. There was no guarantee that everyone who had set out together could stay together during the movement. The crisis became acute at Changban. Pursuing forces struck Liu Bei's column, and the retreat turned into a serious defeat and dispersal. People accompanying the army faced danger as the military position collapsed. The surviving troops and leaders could not treat the withdrawal as a completed plan; they had to find one another and identify where enough men could gather to continue. The record does not allow the experience of each civilian or soldier to be reconstructed, nor does it support inventing a single conversation that determined the outcome. Liu Bei continued moving after Changban and later rejoined forces associated with Guan Yu and Liu Qi. These reunions helped provide a basis for renewed military organization. Contact with Sun Quan then offered a possible route to cooperation against Cao Cao. The subsequent alliance did not erase the losses at Changban or mean that the retreat had been designed from the beginning as a route to a successful coalition. The historical sequence therefore runs from the loss of a position in Jing, through a hazardous withdrawal and defeat at Changban, to the gradual reassembly of surviving forces and attempts to find external support. The movement was shaped by a pursuing army and by the needs of people following Liu Bei. Its aftermath included both a retained political-military presence and the human cost of the retreat. It should not be rewritten as an effortless strategic escape.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Retreat and regroup before losses expand. This line of the Small Image Commentary can be read beside the historical account without claiming that its actors were following the text. The episode began under constraints of authority, resources, and competing obligations. The action recorded in the sources was followed by consequences that people at the time could not simply treat as guaranteed. That order of events is important. For a present-day reader, the question is not how to predict the outcome from an ancient phrase, but how to make a responsible decision while evidence is incomplete. Start by separating verified facts from assumptions. Identify who can authorize the next step, who must carry it out, and who will bear any cost or delay. Ask whether the intended remedy has a practical route to the people affected. Set a review date, and state which evidence would require changing course. This is an editorial analogy, not proof of historical reliance on Xiaoxiang, and it does not endorse every decision made in the story. An effective comparison keeps its limits visible while leaving room to learn from the recorded sequence. What practical responsibility remains unresolved today?

Population records, provisions, and the recruitment or replenishment of manpower formed part of the support reaching Liu Bang’s forces. These were not isolated tasks completed once at the beginning of the war. After troops consumed supplies and suffered losses, the rear organization had to replenish what could be provided and arrange onward transport. The story is about sustained support in the background of changing military events. An expedition’s field officers were visible in surviving accounts of battle, while the machinery that maintained food and reinforcements worked over much longer intervals. A shortage might originate far from a battlefield and still determine whether operations could continue. Because Xiao He had responsibility in Guanzhong, he was connected to that recurring problem of supply. His work occurred within a functioning community from which labor and food were gathered. Recognizing his role does not turn those social resources into an unlimited stock; it clarifies why continuing administration was part of the military story. The historical sequence depends on several different kinds of action: an initial political or military problem, a response by people in positions to act, and an aftermath in which the arrangements still had to be implemented. Historical event | Short narrative

The Qin dynasty's collapse left rival leaders competing over the Guanzhong region and the political order that would follow. Liu Bang entered the former Qin heartland ahead of some other forces. Xiang Yu, who commanded a powerful army, viewed the situation with suspicion. The two men had taken part in the opposition to Qin, but their positions after the dynasty's fall were no longer identical. A meeting at Hongmen took place against this unsettled background. Liu Bang went to the encampment associated with Xiang Yu for a meeting and banquet. The setting was not a gathering between parties with equal military power. Zhang Liang and other participants communicated with people on both sides, seeking to keep the encounter from turning into an immediate attack on Liu Bang. The Shiji presents an elaborate account of who entered, who spoke and how the participants responded. These reported conversations belong to an ancient historian's reconstructed narrative and must not be mistaken for a verbatim transcript. As the meeting continued, there were moves to take harsher action against Liu Bang. His position within Xiang Yu's camp remained vulnerable. Liu Bang eventually left the gathering, while Zhang Liang remained to deal with the gifts and formalities associated with his departure. The immediate encounter ended without Liu Bang being killed at the banquet. It did not end the dispute over command, territory and future authority. The episode has a clear progression: competition following Qin's fall prompted the meeting; Liu Bang entered a stronger rival's camp; intermediaries managed communication and departure; and he returned from the encounter while the broader struggle continued. The story illustrates what the Shiji says happened, not an invented account of private calculations. Neither later victory nor later defeat can turn the evening into a comprehensive settlement of the rivalry. The aftermath must be distinguished from the original decision and evaluated from the surviving record.

06.1 — Line 1

031爻 Case ID: XCASE-H06-L1 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-06-02 | Event ID: E06 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 不永所事，訟不可長也。雖小有言，其辯明也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「不要讓爭訟持續，雖有小議論，終究吉祥。」《象傳》解釋：訟這種狀態不能長久。「雖小有言」《象傳》解釋：其辯明。

Historical event | Short narrative

The Song–Liao Treaty of Chanyuan The Liao army moved south into territory contested with the Northern Song. At the Song court, military pressure forced a decision about whether to continue fighting or attempt a settlement. Emperor Zhenzong went to Chanzhou, closer to the military front. His presence placed the court's leaders in direct contact with the conditions under which an agreement would have to be negotiated. The two governments commanded their own forces, and neither could end the confrontation merely by announcing a preference for peace. Representatives of Song and Liao exchanged proposals while the armies remained a factor in the discussion. They needed to settle the immediate military confrontation and identify obligations that could be followed after troops stopped fighting. The negotiations produced the Treaty of Chanyuan in 1005. Song agreed to provide annual payments to Liao; both dynasties continued as separate governments within an agreed framework for their frontier relations. These were concrete terms, not a declaration that the two sides had ceased to have competing interests. Once the agreement was made, the immediate campaign came to an end. Soldiers and officials on the frontier still had to operate under the settlement. The Song treasury had to provide the promised annual payments, so ending the fighting also created a continuing fiscal obligation. Communications and border arrangements remained necessary. For a substantial period, the agreement reduced warfare on the scale of the preceding confrontation, although it did not eliminate every frontier dispute or diplomatic disagreement. The chronology shows three distinct stages: an armed advance and an urgent Song response; negotiations involving political and military calculations; and an agreement whose terms had to be implemented over time. The outcome cannot be reduced to a simple victory by either side. The source narrative supports the fact of negotiation, the date of the settlement, and the continuing obligations it created. It does not allow every cost of the arrangement to be calculated from this episode alone.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The first line of Song cautions against letting a dispute continue without limit. The Chanyuan settlement provides a historical comparison: Song and Liao moved from military confrontation to negotiated commitments, but peace carried obligations that neither side could ignore. The story is not about a quarrel disappearing because everyone suddenly agreed. When a workplace disagreement persists, identify the specific question that must be settled. What facts can all sides verify? Which commitments can each party actually carry out? Who has authority to approve an outcome, and when will its effects be reviewed? A negotiated end may cost money, time, or concessions. Those costs should be visible rather than disguised as effortless harmony. The Small Image is being applied retrospectively; there is no record that the treaty negotiators used this passage. Nor does ending one confrontation prove that all later disagreements were resolved. A useful settlement closes the immediate issue and leaves a workable procedure for the questions that remain.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

06.2 — Line 2

032爻 Case ID: XCASE-H06-L2 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-06-03 | Event ID: E33 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 不克訟，歸逋竄也。自下訟上，患至掇也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「訴訟不能取勝，回歸本分、改變心意，安守正道則吉。」《象傳》解釋：歸逋竄。「自下訟上」《象傳》解釋：患至掇。

Historical event | Short narrative

Liu Bei’s retreat and regrouping after Changban When Cao Cao advanced into Jing Province, Liu Bei could no longer maintain his previous position there. He moved south with troops and accompanying civilians. That movement took place under pressure from a stronger pursuing force. The people travelling with Liu Bei were not all soldiers able to march at the same speed, and the route did not offer the security of a settled base. Retreat was therefore both a military movement and a difficult effort to preserve those who remained with him. Cao Cao's forces caught up with Liu Bei near Changban. The encounter brought a serious defeat and scattered parts of the retreating group. The historical sequence does not support portraying the episode as an orderly withdrawal in which every participant reached safety. Troops and civilians faced danger, and Liu Bei could not simply reverse the battlefield result by insisting on holding his earlier ground. The immediate consequence was the loss of effective control over the situation at Changban. After the defeat, Liu Bei continued to move and made contact with other forces. He regrouped with elements associated with Guan Yu and Liu Qi. The surviving political and military organization then sought cooperation with Sun Quan against Cao Cao's advance. This later alliance was a new development requiring diplomacy and shared military arrangements. It should not be treated as proof that Liu Bei had predicted the later course of events before the setback. The account thus proceeds from the loss of an established position, through pursuit and defeat, to renewed organization and an attempt to gain outside support. Preserving some capacity for future action came at the same time as substantial immediate losses. The sources describe important stages of the retreat and subsequent regrouping, but do not supply a complete roll of everyone displaced or killed. The case remains a story of an unsuccessful stand, a costly withdrawal, and the work needed to rebuild afterward.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The second line of Song describes the danger of persisting in a dispute when the balance of power is unfavorable. Liu Bei's experience at Changban offers a comparison: he suffered defeat during a southward retreat, then gathered surviving forces and pursued an alliance. The later cooperation did not erase the losses already incurred. At work, an unwinnable confrontation may call for a change of method rather than a louder argument. Identify what can still be protected: essential records, people affected by the dispute, contractual responsibilities, and a safe channel for future discussions. Withdrawing from one meeting or proposal need not mean abandoning a legitimate concern. It can create space to seek another procedure or obtain assistance. This is a modern analogy, not a statement that Liu Bei followed the Small Image. The ancient text's language of rank does not determine anyone's present-day legal rights. Where a dispute involves safety, discrimination, or a duty to report wrongdoing, withdrawal should include appropriate protection and formal support—not silence.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

06.3 — Line 3

033爻 Case ID: XCASE-H06-L3 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-06-04 | Event ID: E15 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 食舊德，從上吉也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「承受舊有德業，守正仍有危險，終究吉祥；若從事王事，不以成功自居。」《象傳》解釋：順從上位者吉。

Historical event | Short narrative

Feng Yi and the name “General of the Great Tree” In the early Eastern Han period, Liu Xiu and the generals supporting him fought to establish control amid competing armed groups. Commanders took part in campaigns and accumulated military achievements. Their work also placed them in a political environment in which credit and recognition mattered. When military leaders assembled, discussions of their exploits could become occasions for comparison with one another. Feng Yi was one of the commanders serving in that setting, not a detached observer of the fighting. The Book of the Later Han records a small but distinctive scene. When other generals gathered to discuss their accomplishments, Feng Yi would withdraw beneath a tree rather than join their competition for credit. The conduct became associated with the name “General of the Great Tree.” The anecdote is presented within a biography of an active military figure. It does not say that he ceased to undertake assignments, refused all recognition, or stopped contributing to the campaigns underway. Feng Yi continued to perform military duties. His preference not to join these particular exchanges was one feature of his public reputation; it was not a substitute for command or service. The biography preserves the nickname and the behavior linked to it, allowing later readers to recognize how chroniclers represented relations among successful commanders. The account does not provide a complete comparison of all officers' battlefield contributions, nor a record of what every person in the gathering said. The story begins with service in a struggle to establish a new dynasty. It moves to gatherings where military accomplishments were discussed and to Feng Yi's repeated withdrawal from those exchanges. Its later trace is the reputation preserved by the historian's account. Because the source is a biographical portrait, the praise attached to the anecdote should be distinguished from independently measurable performance. Feng Yi's refusal to compete verbally for honor is historically recorded as a characteristic action, not evidence that recognition or military authority became irrelevant.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The third line of Song can be read as a reminder to carry out a responsibility without turning every difference into a struggle over status. Feng Yi's biography describes a commander who stepped away when other generals compared their achievements. He remained a serving officer; avoiding those exchanges did not remove his duties. In a team review, distinguish three things: what you personally delivered, what colleagues contributed, and what remains unfinished. Recognition should be accurate, but it need not become a contest in which another person's work is diminished. A quiet response is useful only when the underlying facts are still recorded. Silence should not conceal an unfair evaluation or leave essential responsibilities unassigned. The link to Song is a retrospective reading. No surviving account says that Feng Yi acted according to this Small Image passage. The historical anecdote also comes from a biography shaped by the writer's judgment. Use it to consider how a team discusses credit, not as a rule that conscientious workers must never speak on their own behalf.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

06.4 — Line 4

034爻 Case ID: XCASE-H06-L4 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-06-05 | Event ID: E40 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 復即命渝，安貞，不失也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「訴訟不能取勝，回歸本分、改變心意，安守正道則吉。」《象傳》解釋：不失。

Historical event | Short narrative

The Xi’an Incident and the release of Chiang Kai-shek In 1936, pressure from Japan's expansion continued to shape Chinese politics, while military conflict between the Nationalist government and the Communists remained unresolved. Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng disagreed with Chiang Kai-shek's existing priorities. In Xi'an, they detained Chiang, changing an ongoing political dispute into an immediate crisis concerning the safety and authority of the national leader. Military commanders and political organizations beyond the city also had to consider how they would respond. The detention did not settle the disagreements that had produced it. Different parties became involved in negotiations over Chiang's release and the political course that might follow. Discussions addressed the urgent danger that a further military response could broaden the conflict. The participants were not acting with identical goals, and the circumstances did not provide a simple guarantee that all parties would accept the same long-term arrangement. Negotiation became the process through which the immediate crisis was addressed. Chiang was eventually released. The incident brought the issues of ending internal warfare and resisting Japanese aggression into sharper political focus. Yet the release did not amount to a detailed, automatically enforceable agreement on every future relationship among the parties. Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng also experienced different political consequences after the event. The outcome of the detention and the subsequent careers of its participants belong to related but distinct parts of the record. The historical sequence runs from competing wartime priorities, through the detention and negotiations, to release and unresolved questions about cooperation. Its significance is not exhausted by the fact that one person returned from Xi'an. The source supports the broad course of the event, including the move from force to discussion, but it does not establish that detention itself was a justified way to settle political conflict. It also does not provide a single complete account of every understanding reached in the negotiations.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The fourth line of Song points to a change in the course of a dispute without necessarily surrendering every underlying commitment. The Xi'an Incident is a difficult historical comparison: a detention created an acute political and personal-security crisis, negotiations followed, and Chiang Kai-shek was released. The broader question of cooperation remained unsettled. In a serious organizational conflict, separating the urgent safety problem from the long-term disagreement may be the first workable step. Confirm who can speak for each side, what must happen immediately, and which matters require later discussion. Record agreements precisely. Ending a crisis meeting does not ensure that every structural cause of conflict has been addressed. This analogy neither approves the use of detention nor suggests that coercion is a useful management tool. The historical actors are not documented as applying the Small Image. Its modern value is limited to examining the sequence: an existing dispute, an escalation, negotiations, a specific immediate outcome, and questions that still require responsible attention.

Small Image original: 訟，元吉，以中正也。

Historical event | Short narrative

Bao Zheng’s objections to Zhang Yaozuo’s appointments During the reign of Emperor Renzong in the Northern Song, Zhang Yaozuo received official appointments while also having family connections to the imperial household. Those connections became part of a controversy over who should hold important posts. Court officials charged with offering criticism of government decisions had a recognized role in presenting objections to the ruler. For them, the issue was not simply whether one man possessed a title, but whether appointments were being made under standards that others could scrutinize. Bao Zheng and other remonstrance officials raised objections through memorials and court discussion. They questioned the appointments and pressed the emperor to reconsider. Their arguments therefore entered the formal machinery of government rather than remaining private remarks about Zhang. The disagreement concerned the exercise of imperial appointment power, while the remonstrance officials' power was to present objections and continue pressing their case. The emperor retained the authority to decide on appointments. The surviving materials refer to repeated criticism and discussion, showing that the controversy was not resolved by a single dramatic confrontation. Different appointments and moments in the dispute must be distinguished. Bao Zheng was not presiding over a criminal trial in which he could pronounce Zhang guilty. Popular tales about a magistrate's courtroom should not replace the historical setting of memorials, personnel decisions, and court debate. The case begins with appointments that provoked concern about family influence. It continues through formal objections by Bao Zheng and others, followed by further deliberation within the court. Its lasting record is that officials challenged the exercise of appointment authority in a documented institutional setting. The sources do not reveal every participant's private motives, and they do not justify equating kinship with criminal wrongdoing. The historical point is the existence of a public procedural challenge to the use of power, not the invention of a single courtroom verdict.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The fifth line of Song connects the resolution of disputes with a centered, appropriate standard. Bao Zheng's objections to Zhang Yaozuo's appointments offer a historical example of how concerns about political favoritism entered official discussion. Bao and his colleagues could submit memorials, but they did not control every appointment or sit as criminal judges over the person they criticized. When an organization disputes a promotion or contract award, move beyond personal accusations. Identify the post, published criteria, decision maker, relevant relationships, and the procedure for reconsideration. Record the reasons for an objection and give affected people an opportunity to answer. A fair process is not the same as presuming that a person with influential relatives has committed an offense. This is a modern analogy rather than evidence that Bao Zheng used the Small Image line. The record concerns imperial personnel authority and remonstrance; it should not be recast as a contemporary court proceeding. The practical question is whether a decision can be explained by consistent standards.

036爻 Case ID: XCASE-H06-L6 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-06-07 | Event ID: E43 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 以訟受服，亦不足敬也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「以訟受服」《象傳》解釋：亦不足敬。

Historical event | Short narrative

The Xuanwu Gate Incident and the Tang succession Under Tang Gaozu, the imperial succession had already placed Li Jiancheng in the position of crown prince. Li Shimin, another son of the emperor, had substantial military achievements and his own support among commanders and officials. The royal family's competing centers of power created an increasingly dangerous struggle over who would control the court. Both men possessed political standing, but the established line of succession and the influence gained in military campaigns did not lead to an agreed division of authority. In 626, Li Shimin used armed force at Xuanwu Gate, an important entrance to the palace complex. Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji were killed. The incident immediately changed the balance of power within the imperial family and the court. It was not a normal administrative appointment or a peaceful resolution of a disagreement. The deaths of members of the ruling family were an integral part of the way control was transferred. Following the incident, Li Shimin obtained the political and military advantage and subsequently became emperor, remembered as Tang Taizong. The earlier succession arrangements could no longer proceed as planned. Later accounts of Taizong's reign address policies and achievements from a different period. Whatever conclusions historians reach about his later government, they do not erase the violence through which the succession struggle was settled in 626. The narrative moves from unresolved royal competition, to the action at Xuanwu Gate, and then to a changed succession and government. The surviving histories were compiled within political traditions shaped by later rule, so their explanations of motives and responsibility require careful reading. The record supports the essential acts and sequence, but does not allow reconstructed private conversations to be presented as verified transcripts. This was a contest over state power in which the victorious side secured office through lethal force. The political result and its human cost must remain visible together.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The final line of Song questions whether a distinction gained through contention is worthy of respect simply because it was won. The Xuanwu Gate Incident provides a severe historical comparison: Li Shimin emerged in control and later became emperor, but the change in succession involved the deaths of Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji. In everyday life, winning an argument, election, promotion, or contract is not enough to evaluate how the result was achieved. Review the method, the rules, and the people harmed along the way. A formal title can establish authority, but it does not automatically establish that every action used to obtain it was appropriate. Later achievements may deserve separate assessment without erasing earlier conduct. This is a retrospective ethical analogy. The sources do not say that Li Shimin consulted or quoted this Small Image line, and ancient dynastic competition cannot be equated directly with modern workplaces. The central distinction remains useful: an outcome can be effective while the means by which it was obtained still require scrutiny.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

07.1 — Line 1

037爻 Case ID: XCASE-H07-L1 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-07-02 | Event ID: E07 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 師出以律；失律，凶也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「師出以律；失律」《象傳》解釋：凶。

Historical event | Short narrative

The Battle of Bi and divided Jin command In 597 BCE, Jin and Chu armies faced one another near Bi. Commanders in the Jin camp disagreed about crossing the river and engaging the opposing force. The decision was not a minor question of timing. Crossing would place soldiers on the far bank and could oblige the remaining units to alter their positions in response. A coordinated decision was therefore essential to the army’s deployment. The Jin officer Xian Hu crossed with his troops despite the position taken by his commander. Other officers now faced a situation different from the one for which the army had been preparing. The force already across the river could not simply be treated as though it had remained in camp. During the ensuing discussion, Zhi Zhuangzi cited the Book of Changes on the need for an army to march under discipline. His point concerned the immediate chain of command: when a force has an appointed commander but subordinate leaders act independently, orders can cease to govern the army as a whole. The warning did not reverse the crossing or restore the original deployment. Jin continued toward confrontation and was defeated by Chu at Bi. The surviving account links a disputed order, an officer’s unilateral action, a warning drawn from the Changes, and the subsequent defeat. It does not establish that the warning was accepted, or that the outcome resulted from one violation alone. Command decisions, deployment and the opponent’s actions all belonged to the course of the battle. The Zuo Tradition records an actual reference to a Changes line about military discipline. That is not proof that Zhi Zhuangzi quoted this particular Small Image commentary, or that anyone conducted a new divination at the scene. The historical sequence remains clear without either claim. The episode consequently distinguishes the conduct of a council from the later course of an army in battle.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The first line of Shi connects military action with discipline. At Bi, a Jin officer crossed a river before the army had settled on a common course. Zhi Zhuangzi used a Changes line to challenge the problem of divided command. The army continued into battle and was defeated. The account is useful because it separates a warning from the question of whether leaders acted on it. In a modern organization, conflicting instructions can arise when several managers change a shared plan without notifying the people who must deliver it. Before work begins, identify who makes the final decision, who can raise objections, and how a change reaches everyone affected. Record exceptions rather than relying on personal understandings. Discipline should enable concerns to be heard and decisions to be executed, not suppress information from the people closest to a problem. This is a retrospective application of the Small Image. The ancient source quotes a related Changes line, but does not establish direct use of this commentary. Nor should a battlefield defeat be reduced to one person’s disobedience. The practical question is whether a team can still act from the same agreed instructions.

Evidence B — retrospective editorial comparison.

Small Image original: 在師中吉，承天寵也。王三錫命，懷萬邦也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「身居軍中統率得當，吉而無咎；君王多次授命嘉獎。」《象傳》解釋：承天寵。「身居軍中統率得當，吉而無咎；君王多次授命嘉獎。」《象傳》解釋：懷萬邦。

Historical event | Short narrative

Zhou Yafu and the Rebellion of the Seven States In 154 BCE, a coalition of regional kingdoms rose against the Western Han court. Forces from Wu and Chu advanced against Liang, putting its rulers under direct pressure. The imperial government appointed Zhou Yafu to command the response. He had to consider two demands at once: Liang needed immediate relief, while the opposing army relied on supply lines that could become vulnerable if the Han force chose its position carefully. Zhou did not make an immediate frontal rescue his principal method. He held his own position and sent forces to interrupt the Wu–Chu supply route. This decision meant that Liang remained under pressure while the main imperial force waited. That was a political difficulty as well as a military one. Those suffering the attack could see that relief was not arriving by the most direct route, and Zhou’s choice attracted criticism. The imperial army still had to defend its position while the interruption of enemy supplies took effect. As the rebels’ provision became increasingly difficult, their ability to maintain the offensive weakened. Zhou then moved against them as they withdrew, helping bring the rebellion to an end. The sequence involved an appointment to command, pressure for rapid assistance, a sustained position, action against supply lines and an eventual attack under changed circumstances. Victory did not mean that each decision had been risk-free, and a commander’s authority did not remove the consequences borne by another territory. His campaign instead offers a recorded occasion for examining what a military mandate permits, and what an appointed commander must actually deliver.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Shi’s second line concerns a commander operating under an acknowledged mandate. Zhou Yafu’s response to the Seven States rebellion illustrates why a mandate matters in practice. Although Liang needed help, Zhou held his position, cut enemy supplies and moved when the opposing force weakened. The decision produced military results, but it also left Liang exposed and attracted criticism. A manager who is asked to lead a difficult project needs more than a title. The sponsor should clarify the objective, authority, resources and circumstances in which the plan must be reconsidered. People carrying the immediate burden also need a channel to raise objections. Giving responsibility without decision rights creates confusion; granting authority without accountability can create a different problem. The ancient phrase about favor from Heaven is part of the classical language. It should not be used to claim supernatural approval for a historical victory. No evidence connects Zhou Yafu’s strategy directly to this Small Image passage. As an analogy, the lesson is narrower: a workable mandate allows a leader to coordinate action, while the effects on others still require examination.

The Tumu Crisis and the capture of the Ming emperor In 1449, the Ming emperor Yingzong accompanied a large army on a campaign against the Oirat forces. The presence of the emperor changed the stakes of the expedition. Soldiers, officials and commanders had to move a substantial force across long distances, with food, transport and orders coordinated through the journey. Any breakdown could affect not only the troops on the road but also the central government in Beijing. The campaign did not achieve the outcome its organizers sought. During the return, Ming forces suffered a major defeat in the Tumu area, and the emperor was captured. The incident was therefore more than a battlefield reverse. The political head of the dynasty was in enemy hands, survivors had to be accounted for, and news of the defeat had to reach officials responsible for defending the capital. The combination of movement, provision and command problems formed part of the crisis, although the precise weight of each factor cannot be established from a short narrative. When the news arrived in Beijing, the court confronted an emergency while the emperor was still a prisoner. Officials had to arrange the city’s defense and address the exercise of political authority. The defense of the capital could not await the emperor’s return. Soldiers needed orders, administrators needed a functioning chain of command, and decisions about the state had to proceed under extraordinary conditions. These were direct consequences of the earlier expedition and defeat. Accounts of Tumu differ on some numbers and on responsibility assigned to individual figures. The essential chronology is more securely stated: an imperial expedition, difficulties in the course of the campaign, defeat during the return, the emperor’s capture, and urgent action in Beijing. The record does not indicate that commanders followed or invoked this Small Image text. Keeping the documented sequence intact allows the military and civilian costs to remain visible without constructing invented battlefield speeches or assigning every loss to a single person.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Shi’s third line speaks about soldiers carried home dead and an undertaking that fails to achieve its purpose. The Tumu Crisis gives that image a grave historical counterpart. In 1449, the Ming emperor joined an expedition against Oirat forces; the army suffered a major defeat, and the emperor was captured. Beijing then had to organize its defense while the ruler remained a prisoner. When evaluating a high-risk mission, consider more than whether its stated objective sounds worthwhile. Can the organization move the necessary resources? Is authority clear if the plan changes? Who takes over if the leader becomes unavailable? These questions matter because a failure can reach people who never took part in the original decision. This comparison does not treat the Small Image as a prediction or recommend military action. Historical sources differ about troop totals and individual culpability, so numerical claims should not be repeated without checking their scope. Nor does the case prove that one planning error explains every casualty. It shows that large operations can produce consequences far beyond the immediate point of defeat.

Early Song reorganization of military command After the Song dynasty was established, its first emperor faced a problem inherited from the political and military circumstances of his rise. Senior commanders controlled important forces, and the new government needed the army to keep functioning while it reduced the danger that a general might exercise military power independently of the court. Simply dismissing commanders without replacing the chain of command could disrupt the forces on which the dynasty depended. Under Emperor Taizu, the court gradually changed the responsibilities and positions of high-ranking military officers. Some generals left active commands, and military authority was brought into arrangements more closely controlled by the center. For the units involved, a change in command meant more than a new name on an official register. Orders still had to reach troops, officers had to know whom to answer, and the government had to manage the position of men whose earlier service had helped establish the regime. Later generations often compress these changes into the well-known story called 'releasing military power over cups of wine.' That expression is associated with an account of a banquet and conversations between the ruler and commanders. The dating and exact words of those scenes are disputed. The defensible historical sequence does not require supposing that every reorganization was agreed upon during one evening. What matters for this account is that responsibilities changed and new structures of military control had to operate afterward. The immediate political outcome was a redistribution of command. Its long-term effects belong to the wider history of Song civil and military institutions and cannot be captured by a single anecdote. Officers who relinquished commands still had positions and obligations to be arranged, while the state continued to rely on soldiers and administrators to enforce its decisions. There is no evidence that Emperor Taizu applied this particular Small Image commentary in his reforms. As a historical narrative, the episode shows a newly established government reorganizing power after gaining control. The disputed banquet dialogue is not reproduced as if it were a verbatim record, and the changes are not presented as an automatic or universally successful model of governance.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The last line of Shi moves from military action to the arrangement of authority and rewards afterward. Rewarding achievement and defining future authority are related but different tasks. This is a retrospective Small Image analogy. The term 'unsuitable people' in the classical passage does not justify judging individuals by birth, faction or status. Modern suitability must be assessed through responsibilities, competence and fair procedure. Nor should a later banquet legend replace the longer institutional history that the available sources actually describe.

Historical event | Short narrative

Shang Yang rewards the movement of a wooden pole In the state of Qin during the Warring States period, Shang Yang was preparing to introduce a series of new regulations. A government could issue an order, but the order would have little immediate credibility if residents doubted that officials would carry it out. The court needed people to recognize a new set of rules while existing habits and expectations remained in place. The historical account places a small, highly visible test before the formal publication of the laws. According to Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian, Shang Yang had a wooden pole set up near a city gate. A public announcement offered a reward to anyone who moved it to a specified location. The task was simple enough for bystanders to understand and check. At first, people did not trust the announcement. The reward was then raised. When one person finally moved the pole, the promised payment was actually made. The account presents both the announced condition and the completed payment as acts that people could observe, rather than a private agreement between officials. The new laws were subsequently made public. Their implementation involved much more than the single test at the gate: households, officials and soldiers now faced regulations with consequences extending across Qin society. The reward episode establishes that one public promise was fulfilled. It cannot establish that every later order was fair, that every affected resident approved, or that harsh punishments used in the reforms were justified. Those questions belong to the wider history of the new legal and administrative system. The sequence preserved by the historian runs from uncertainty about official promises, through the announcement and completion of a small task, to the publication of larger reforms. No verified transcript records the thoughts of the person who moved the pole or those watching. The anecdote has a strong exemplary purpose in the source, and that purpose should not be mistaken for an independently documented survey of public trust.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

The first line of Bi concerns the beginning of a dependable connection. In the historical account, Shang Yang offered a public reward for moving a wooden pole. People initially hesitated, but a participant eventually performed the task and received the payment. That sequence gave residents something specific to compare: the government’s announcement and its observable action. When launching a team or a new service, a similarly modest test can be more informative than a grand declaration. State one deliverable, name who is responsible, and publish the condition for success. Then complete it and let others verify the result. A fulfilled promise can establish a basis for further cooperation, but it cannot substitute for fair rules or sound decisions over time. Trust requires later conduct as well as the first demonstration. This is a retrospective comparison with the Small Image, not evidence that Shang Yang consulted it. The ancient narrative was selected to illustrate political credibility; it does not prove that all the subsequent reforms were beneficial. The question for a modern reader is straightforward: what small promise can your organization fulfill in a way that other people can check?

The Qing court and the crisis of 1900 In 1900, the Qing court faced overlapping crises involving the Boxer movement, foreign military intervention and disputes among officials over how to respond. The movement spread amid tensions within Chinese society and hostility toward foreign influence. At the same time, outside powers had their own armed forces and political aims. Choices made in Beijing therefore affected relations beyond the capital, while governors in other regions had to consider the danger to the areas under their administration. As the crisis intensified, the Qing government issued an edict declaring war against foreign powers. The decision did not create uniform agreement throughout the empire. Some provincial authorities in the southeast followed an arrangement later known as the Southeast Mutual Protection, rather than conducting their affairs in the same way as the court. The contrast showed that central announcements and regional action could diverge even during a major international emergency. Meanwhile foreign forces advanced, and the military confrontation widened. The allied foreign armies entered Beijing. The imperial court fled, and negotiations subsequently led to the Boxer Protocol in 1901. The agreement imposed heavy obligations and became one of the lasting political and financial consequences of the conflict. These events followed a sequence of unrest, changing official policies, military escalation, the fall of the capital and a settlement made under coercive circumstances. They affected residents and officials in different ways and cannot be reduced to the choices of one court faction alone. It would also be inaccurate to discuss the Qing government’s misjudgments while omitting the armed invasion by foreign powers. The sources document different actors, varying regional responses and severe consequences. They do not establish a single motive shared by everyone associated with the Boxer movement, and they provide no evidence that officials selected allies by applying the Small Image of Bi. The historical course can be told without assigning collective blame to ordinary residents or inventing private conversations in the palace.

When choosing allies today, ask what each party can actually do, which commitments are verifiable and who may suffer if the relationship fails. Decisions should be reviewed as circumstances develop. This interpretation is retrospective. The useful question is how to test the consequences of cooperation before depending on it under pressure.

Different leaders and organizations acted at different times, and their decisions had consequences for local members as well as the central parties. The collapse involved widespread political violence. People who had operated under the earlier alliance confronted new risks of arrest, displacement and death. Organizations had to redefine their positions, and the two parties moved toward prolonged armed confrontation. The Northern Expedition had created opportunities for joint activity, but military progress did not by itself settle disagreements over power or social mobilization. The relationship therefore ended without a shared institutional arrangement capable of carrying its divisions forward. The subsequent conflicts were part of the longer political history of twentieth-century China, not an immediate or inevitable result of a single meeting. The source material allows readers to identify a cooperative phase, accumulating disagreements, the distinct Shanghai and Wuhan breaks, and the transition toward armed hostility. It does not establish that every participant shared an identical motive, or that a line of the Small Image was cited to determine any of these choices. Treating the breakdown as a historical sequence keeps the affected people and different centers of action visible instead of reducing the events to the abstract claim that an alliance simply lacked a leader.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

Bi’s last line speaks of an alliance that cannot reach a lasting conclusion. The First United Front offers an historical comparison. The Kuomintang and Chinese Communist Party cooperated during the Northern Expedition, but disagreements over political direction, military control and social movements intensified. The 1927 breaks in Shanghai and Wuhan occurred through different decisions and brought serious political violence. Long military confrontation followed. Partnerships need more than a common banner. They require a way to make decisions when objectives diverge, a process for protecting participants and terms for revising or ending cooperation. If one group controls all the practical levers while another bears the costs, formal unity may conceal conflict. A difficult disagreement should be identified and addressed before it becomes a crisis for the people doing the work. After prolonged fighting on the Korean peninsula, the opposing forces negotiated over how military hostilities could be halted. The agreement specified arrangements for halting hostilities and maintaining a military dividing line. Its terms had to be communicated to units still facing each other. That implementation, rather than the signature alone, gave the military agreement its immediate practical effect. The armistice interrupted large-scale fighting but did not constitute a comprehensive peace treaty. The peninsula’s underlying political disagreements remained. A ceasefire and a final political settlement are therefore different outcomes, and the achievement of the first should not be mistaken for the completion of the second. The parties had to agree on a point at which firing would stop while forces remained positioned across from each other. They also had to distinguish a military mechanism from the political disputes that had brought armies into the war. Once the terms were announced, units needed to recognize the same ceasefire obligations. The unresolved political issues did not vanish when the shooting declined. The ceasefire arrangement needed all involved military organizations to understand the relevant dividing lines and timing. That posed a different challenge from reaching broad political agreement about the peninsula. A military order could halt specified hostile actions while leaving disagreements on sovereignty and the peninsula’s future untouched. The existence of prisoners and previously sustained fighting further made implementation a process with practical steps. These points belong within the aftermath, since without them the account might mistakenly imply that an armistice concluded every dispute that the war had generated.

10.4 Fourth line — Proceed cautiously before a stronger party

10.4 — Line 4

058爻 Case ID: XCASE-H10-L4 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-10-05 | Event ID: E10 | Evidence: B

Historical event | Short narrative

During the Warring States period, Qin offered cities in exchange for the prized He Shi jade belonging to Zhao. The Zhao court feared that sending the object might result in its loss without the promised territory, while rejecting the request risked confrontation with a stronger state. Lin Xiangru was chosen to carry the jade to Qin and negotiate. At the Qin court, the exchange did not move directly toward the delivery of cities. Lin arranged to regain possession of the jade and used ceremonial procedures to preserve room for negotiation. He then made arrangements for the object to be returned to Zhao while he remained to face Qin’s ruler. The two sides did not complete the proposed exchange on the terms initially presented. The narrative in the Records of the Grand Historian includes developed speeches, which are ancient literary representations rather than verifiable stenographic transcripts. The central actions—dispatch, negotiation, return of the jade, and Lin’s continued presence—form the historical story. Qin and Zhao did not suddenly become equal powers because this particular negotiation ended without the loss of the jade. The jade was the physical object at the center of negotiations, but the promised cities were the political condition attached to its transfer. Returning the object separated possession from further bargaining. Lin’s continued presence in Qin after its removal meant that the immediate task and the safety of the envoy were no longer the same issue. Ancient reported speeches can illuminate the narrative structure without being repeated as authenticated words. Zhao’s original predicament involved two unequal risks, because losing the jade and provoking Qin were both possible. The court’s decision to send an envoy allowed negotiation rather than immediate refusal, but gave Lin a responsibility to safeguard the object. 069爻 Case ID: XCASE-H12-L3 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-12-04 | Event ID: E12 | Evidence: B

Historical event | Short narrative

After the founding of the republic, Yuan Shikai occupied a commanding position in the central government, but his relationship with provincial and political interests remained complicated. In 1915 he moved to replace the republican form of government with a monarchy, changing the political framework under which existing offices had operated. Support for the imperial project was not universal. Opposition appeared in public politics and then in the National Protection War. Provincial leaders and forces that had previously cooperated with Yuan did not necessarily accept the new constitutional claim. Political disagreement thus had military as well as institutional consequences. In 1916 Yuan abandoned the monarchical project. That reversal did not remove the political conflicts surrounding the distribution of power. The surviving sequence is a proposed imperial restoration, widening opposition, war, and cancellation. It is not evidence that every supporter or opponent held the same motives. The change in regime title required not just central announcement but acceptance by officials and armed forces across the country. Provinces responded under circumstances that did not always match the central government’s expectations. As armed opposition expanded, the effectiveness of proclamations depended on military control and local cooperation. Ending the imperial claim was an identifiable reversal, but not the end of the political crisis. The attempt to create a monarchy altered the stated basis on which offices operated after the founding of the republic. That change required recognition from provinces, officers, and political groupings whose cooperation was not guaranteed. Opposition during the National Protection War made the weakness of that recognition visible. Cancellation of the project in 1916 was a direct response to a changed political situation, not an announcement that restored every previous relationship. The affair therefore traces a move from a proposed institutional transformation to resistance, fighting, withdrawal of the claim, and continuing instability.

12.4 Fourth line — New duties require institutional authority

Historical event | Short narrative

The 1911 Revolution created a need for government institutions capable of representing the republican movement and conducting ordinary administration. Several provinces had broken with the Qing court, but their declarations did not automatically establish a unified national budget, bureaucracy, or chain of military command. On 1 January 1912, Sun Yat-sen took office as provisional president in Nanjing. The provisional government organized offices and issued documents intended to translate political change into administration. Officials began operating under new institutional names while negotiations with the Qing side and other powers continued. The provisional government’s direct control remained geographically and financially limited. Appointing officers, communicating instructions, and sustaining institutions required support beyond the ceremony of inauguration. The case therefore extends from revolutionary declarations through institutional formation into continuing struggles over practical authority. The new government needed departments capable of exchanging documents, receiving information, and carrying out orders. The fact that provinces endorsed a republican direction did not mean they had surrendered their tax income or control of troops to one office. The provisional government’s early actions must therefore be understood alongside the limits of its resources and the continuing negotiations with northern authorities. The installation of a provisional president provided a recognizable formal start to government in Nanjing, but it did not mean every part of the country was administered from that office. Ministries and civil officers needed resources and procedures to turn documents into action. Provinces that had separated from Qing rule still exercised influence over their own forces and revenues. Negotiation with northern leaders continued while the new government undertook daily business. That overlap between institutional founding and contested authority is central to the chronology and explains why inauguration alone could not complete the revolution’s work. Every institution still had to secure cooperation and resources in order to operate beyond its founding announcements.

The subsequent question was how officials, armies, and budgets would operate under republican institutions. This is why the story continues beyond the best-known date of the imperial abdication. Early Western Han rulers governed a population that depended heavily on agricultural production while the state also needed resources to support administration. A land tax reduced the part of a harvest that a household could keep. Any decision to remit that revenue therefore affected both the farmers and the treasury, and the government had to consider how other obligations would continue. The Records of the Grand Historian reports that in the thirteenth year of Emperor Wen’s reign he ordered the removal of the land tax. The change addressed a specific fiscal burden rather than abolishing every tax or form of labor service. For the policy to affect actual households, local administrators had to apply the order to the relevant assessments. A decree at court and the amount collected in a rural district were connected but not identical steps. The record establishes the order and its stated policy context, not a complete account of gains received by every household. Other fiscal obligations remained. The episode consequently runs from concern over agriculture and the demands made upon cultivators, through an imperial tax decision, to its implementation as one part of a broader system of government finance. Maintaining that distinction is necessary to preserve the chronology without treating a later outcome as inevitable.

17.1 — Line 1

097爻 Case ID: XCASE-H17-L1 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-17-02 | Event ID: E04 | Evidence: B

小象傳 original: 官有渝，從正吉也。出門交有功，不失也。

Small Image | English rendering: Changes in office can be favorable when the right course is followed; dealings outside one’s immediate circle can accomplish useful work.

Historical event | Short narrative

In the early years of the Three Kingdoms era, Lü Meng was already serving Sun Quan as a military officer in the lower Yangtze region. His duties involved troops and campaigns, yet these responsibilities did not eliminate the need to understand earlier wars, institutions, and political decisions. Sun Quan urged him to undertake regular reading. According to an account quoted by Pei Songzhi in his commentary on the Records of the Three Kingdoms, the ruler did not expect Lü Meng to abandon military service and become a professional classical scholar. He wanted an officer with practical responsibilities to gain broader historical knowledge. Lü Meng first pointed to his demanding schedule. Sun Quan replied by referring to the burdens of his own position and argued that work need not make study impossible. The surviving narrative conveys the substance of that exchange; the polished dialogue familiar from later teaching materials should not be mistaken for a verbatim record. Lü Meng accepted the advice and began to read while continuing his existing duties. He was not reassigned from his post simply to become a student, and the change was not completed in a single meeting. Learning had to fit around work already under way. The later part of the account introduces Lu Su, another important officer. When the two discussed affairs, Lu Su recognized that Lü Meng had acquired knowledge and judgment beyond his earlier reputation. The resulting reassessment by a colleague marks the recorded outcome of the educational episode. It does not establish that every subsequent campaign succeeded because of reading or that any particular text supplied a military plan. The sequence in the surviving source is nevertheless clear: Sun Quan noticed a gap between experience and knowledge, recommended study, Lü Meng followed that recommendation while remaining at work, and Lu Su later acknowledged a change in his ability to discuss public affairs. The account describes a professional development process, not a miraculous transformation or evidence that anyone used the Small Image commentary to direct it.

Interpretive analogy | Social post

A new role needs more than an old reputation. Lü Meng continued serving as an officer while learning from historical texts. Sun Quan recommended study because military responsibilities called for more than practical experience alone. Later, Lu Su noticed the change in their discussions. When your work changes, identify the knowledge you can no longer afford to leave unexamined. Choose a regular reading or practice commitment while still meeting existing obligations. This is a comparison made by today’s reader, not a statement that the people in the event consulted this passage of the Small Image. Centralization therefore involved administration as well as individual appointments. A decision recorded in a history is not necessarily the same as the practical result it was intended to produce. 18 — Gu (Repairing Corruption)

18.1 First six — Correcting inherited policies need not reject the past

18.1 — Line 1

103爻 Case ID: XCASE-H18-L1 | Unit ID: XIANG-U-18-02 | Event ID: E65 | Evidence: A
