Historical event | Short narrative

During the opening stage of the Long March, the Central Red Army moved toward the Xiang River region under severe military pressure. Forces opposing its withdrawal sought to block the route, while pursuing units threatened the rear. The movement of a large army was not simply a matter of finding a ford. Troops, equipment, supplies and people accompanying the force had to move through a limited area while other formations maintained a passage. The river and the surrounding positions became a decisive obstacle in an already difficult withdrawal. Fighting developed as the Red Army tried to cross. The forces assigned to protect the movement came under heavy pressure, and the troops attempting to reach and pass the crossing suffered considerable casualties and organizational losses. Some units continued onward after the passage, but this did not restore the people and material lost during the operation. Accounts of the Xiang River campaign emphasize the cost of the fighting and the difficulties created by the route, marching arrangements and command decisions. The immediate military outcome was that surviving elements continued the withdrawal at a markedly reduced strength. The army's subsequent movement involved further reconsideration of earlier choices about command and direction. Historical discussions report different figures for losses because they do not always count the same period, units or kinds of attrition. It would therefore be misleading to present one disputed total as though it were a universally accepted count of battlefield deaths. The documentary sequence is clear enough without embellishment: an army under pursuit approached a defended river, fought to complete the crossing, sustained grievous losses, and continued with fewer people and less equipment. The event was not a triumphant passage without cost. No invented dying words, private emotions or unrecorded scenes are needed to convey the scale of what happened. The record also does not establish one identical experience for all formations taking part in the withdrawal. The crossings and fighting occurred amid a wider movement.

Historical event | Short narrative

The 1911 Revolution created a need for government institutions capable of representing the republican movement and conducting ordinary administration. Several provinces had broken with the Qing court, but their declarations did not automatically establish a unified national budget, bureaucracy, or chain of military command. On 1 January 1912, Sun Yat-sen took office as provisional president in Nanjing. The provisional government organized offices and issued documents intended to translate political change into administration. Officials began operating under new institutional names while negotiations with the Qing side and other powers continued. The provisional government’s direct control remained geographically and financially limited. Appointing officers, communicating instructions, and sustaining institutions required support beyond the ceremony of inauguration. The case therefore extends from revolutionary declarations through institutional formation into continuing struggles over practical authority. The new government needed departments capable of exchanging documents, receiving information, and carrying out orders. The fact that provinces endorsed a republican direction did not mean they had surrendered their tax income or control of troops to one office. The provisional government’s early actions must therefore be understood alongside the limits of its resources and the continuing negotiations with northern authorities. The installation of a provisional president provided a recognizable formal start to government in Nanjing, but it did not mean every part of the country was administered from that office. Ministries and civil officers needed resources and procedures to turn documents into action. Provinces that had separated from Qing rule still exercised influence over their own forces and revenues. Negotiation with northern leaders continued while the new government undertook daily business. That overlap between institutional founding and contested authority is central to the chronology and explains why inauguration alone could not complete the revolution’s work. Every institution still had to secure cooperation and resources in order to operate beyond its founding announcements.

Early Western Han rulers governed a population that depended heavily on agricultural production while the state also needed resources to support administration. A land tax reduced the part of a harvest that a household could keep. Any decision to remit that revenue therefore affected both the farmers and the treasury, and the government had to consider how other obligations would continue. The Records of the Grand Historian reports that in the thirteenth year of Emperor Wen’s reign he ordered the removal of the land tax. The change addressed a specific fiscal burden rather than abolishing every tax or form of labor service. For the policy to affect actual households, local administrators had to apply the order to the relevant assessments. A decree at court and the amount collected in a rural district were connected but not identical steps. The record establishes the order and its stated policy context, not a complete account of gains received by every household. Other fiscal obligations remained. The episode consequently runs from concern over agriculture and the demands made upon cultivators, through an imperial tax decision, to its implementation as one part of a broader system of government finance. In the Sui dynasty, the court undertook construction of Renshou Palace outside the principal capital. Work proceeded under officials responsible for carrying out the ruler's building program. The visible result could be assessed only after construction, whereas the burdens of procurement and labor began much earlier. 43.1 — Not forcing a confrontation before conditions allow it

43.1 — Line 1

253爻 Case ID: XCASE-H43-L1 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-43-02 | Event ID: E64 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 不勝而往，咎也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「不勝而往」《象傳》解釋：咎。

English editorial reading focus: Not forcing a confrontation before conditions allow it (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

After the collapse of the Qing dynasty, republican institutions in China were announced before a stable nationwide settlement of political authority had been achieved. The revolution of 1911 had displaced the old dynastic framework, but the distribution of military forces, provincial resources, and central government power remained disputed. In 1912, the new republic began to organize its presidency, legislature, and administrative offices. The formal adoption of republican titles did not by itself establish an agreed procedure for every conflict among political actors. Yuan Shikai held the presidency and commanded important political and military resources. At the same time, political parties and representatives contested how the republic should be governed and how the executive should be limited. Competition within the new order sharpened during the following years, as disputes over parliamentary authority, armed power, and constitutional arrangements accumulated. In 1913, political conflict moved beyond debate into military confrontation in the struggle commonly called the Second Revolution. The government defeated opposing forces, and the balance between central authority and constitutional institutions changed further. These events did not end the underlying disagreement about the form of the state. Yuan subsequently sought to replace the republic with a monarchy. The campaign for imperial restoration in 1915 generated another wave of opposition and armed conflict; the imperial project was abandoned in 1916. These developments should not be collapsed into one continuous plan with a predetermined outcome. Different participants entered the disputes at different stages, and events such as the 1913 conflict and the later imperial project require their own dates and actors. The record supports a sequence of constitutional promises, contested institutions, military confrontation, and renewed disputes about sovereignty. It does not support invented speeches or private motives. The early republic's experience illustrates that a new political name was not equivalent to a settled distribution of authority. Institutional design, military command, regional participation, and the treatment of opponents remained unresolved tasks after the dynasty had ended.

43.2 — Preparation is what makes an unexpected crisis manageable

43.2 — Line 2

254爻 Case ID: XCASE-H43-L2 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-43-03 | Event ID: E19 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 莫夜有戎，得中道也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「警惕呼號；夜間即使有兵事，也不必憂慮。」《象傳》解釋：居於中位道。

English editorial reading focus: Preparation is what makes an unexpected crisis manageable (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

In 158 BCE, Emperor Wen of the Western Han visited military camps while the empire faced security concerns on its northern frontier. At camps he had inspected earlier, the imperial procession had been allowed relatively easy entry. His visit to the camp at Xiliu, commanded by Zhou Yafu, unfolded differently. Soldiers guarding the gates refused to open them merely because the emperor's carriage had arrived. They explained that the camp operated under military commands and that entry required the appropriate authorization. The emperor's attendants could not make their status a substitute for the camp's established procedure. Only after the relevant message had been conveyed and permission secured did the procession pass through the gate. The differences continued inside. Military rules prohibited rapid driving within the camp, and the imperial party slowed its carriages accordingly. Zhou Yafu then received the visitor according to military etiquette rather than treating the encounter as a routine court appearance. The emperor eventually departed and expressed approval of the discipline he had observed. The Records of the Grand Historian presents these actions as a connected series of scenes: the initial refusal at the gate, the request for authorization, the restriction on movement, the meeting with the commander, and the emperor's later assessment. They illustrate what a military command system looked like when it operated even in the presence of the monarch. The gate guards did not prevent entry permanently, and Zhou Yafu did not reject the emperor's authority. The entry was completed through the procedure the camp already used. The later praise is also important to its chronology: those serving at the gate did not know at the beginning how the emperor would judge the experience. As with other ancient narrative histories, the account was composed after the events and cannot establish that every conversation was preserved word for word. Nor can a single inspection show that Emperor Wen always respected regulations elsewhere. What this episode records is one visit in which orders were enforced, permission was obtained, and the commander received the emperor without suspending the camp's discipline. The story is not evidence that either man consulted Hexagram 19 or its Small Image commentary.

By 383 CE, Former Qin under Fu Jian controlled extensive territory in northern China. The government assembled forces for a major campaign against Eastern Jin. Jin forces opposed the southern advance. In fighting near the Fei River, Former Qin suffered defeat and its army broke apart. The visible scale of Fu Jian’s resources had not guaranteed that the various contingents would act as a coherent force under stress. An offensive organized with substantial forces ended without its intended political result. After the defeat, political divisions within the territories previously ruled by Former Qin became more pronounced. Ancient accounts include dramatic battlefield details and large troop numbers that cannot all be treated as precise measurements. The supportable sequence is mobilization, defeat near the Fei River, and a decline in the regime’s ability to hold its political coalition together. A state’s ability to summon soldiers was only one part of its ability to conduct an extended campaign. The assembled forces needed to march together and receive orders when circumstances changed. The engagement at the river tested these arrangements under combat pressure. After the defeat, the government also faced political consequences among groups whose earlier cooperation had held its northern territories together. The defeat also altered the political balance far from the site of combat. Former Qin had assembled an extensive political structure, and military authority had held together groups whose interests were not always identical. A major reverse could therefore undermine confidence in that central control. The resulting changes were not confined to the men who fought near the river. This historical sequence helps explain why the aftermath must include political fragmentation as well as battlefield failure, while uncertainty about exact numerical estimates should remain visible to the reader.

English editorial reading focus: Establishing limits before disorder grows (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

As Qin authority collapsed, rival armies advanced toward the Guanzhong region, where the former imperial capital and its surrounding communities faced a change of rulers. Liu Bang entered the area with armed followers. For residents who had experienced Qin administration and the disruption of war, the immediate questions were practical: which laws would remain, how soldiers would behave, and who could enforce the new promises. Military arrival alone could not settle those uncertainties. According to the historical account in the Records of the Grand Historian, Liu Bang assembled local elders and announced a simplified set of three legal provisions. The measure is conventionally remembered as the Three-Article Covenant. It addressed serious offenses while abandoning many burdens associated in the account with the former regime. The announcement was also a public undertaking by an advancing commander. Its credibility depended on the conduct of the occupying forces after the announcement, not merely on the wording of the proclamation. The immediate sequence was therefore the collapse of Qin control, the entry of Liu Bang's forces, a meeting with local representatives, and the presentation of rules that residents could understand. Soldiers still had to maintain order under those rules. Local families continued living amid political uncertainty, because other contenders had not disappeared. Xiang Yu remained a powerful military rival, and decisions about who would ultimately control Guanzhong were not concluded by the covenant. The declaration became an important element in later accounts of Liu Bang's ability to obtain local cooperation. Yet the larger struggle continued beyond this episode, eventually developing into competition among the forces that had helped destroy Qin rule. Neither the announcement nor its favorable portrayal in historical writing proves that all inhabitants approved, or that every subsequent action followed the same standard. The documented episode is a change of authority accompanied by a publicly stated legal commitment; what happened afterward depended on continued military and political developments.

In other parts of his career he still had to accept assignments, supervise troops, and respond to conditions of war. These activities gave meaning to the title of general independently of the nickname. The historian’s selection of an unusual social gesture made it memorable, but a single kind of behavior cannot explain the whole career. The sequence is service, a repeated reaction in gatherings, and the survival of the nickname in the written tradition.

In 1927, violent political action in Shanghai and a separate break in Wuhan destroyed the cooperative arrangement. These developments involved different dates, participants, and victims. Political differences were no longer only disputes inside a working coalition; repression and armed conflict affected members and affiliated organizations. People who had operated within the same political framework encountered drastically altered conditions. The breakdown led toward prolonged military confrontation. Rival approaches to workers’ and peasants’ movements and city authority became practical disputes, not just differences in party documents. When separation and repression occurred, the implications extended to people connected with both organizations. The sequence of Shanghai and Wuhan events needs to be preserved because the two locations were not merely alternative names for one decision. Their aftermath contributed to sustained confrontation beyond the first rupture.

Historical event | Short narrative

The 1911 Revolution created a need for government institutions capable of representing the republican movement and conducting ordinary administration. Several provinces had broken with the Qing court, but their declarations did not automatically establish a unified national budget, bureaucracy, or chain of military command. On 1 January 1912, Sun Yat-sen took office as provisional president in Nanjing. The provisional government organized offices and issued documents intended to translate political change into administration. Officials began operating under new institutional names while negotiations with the Qing side and other powers continued. The provisional government’s direct control remained geographically and financially limited. Appointing officers, communicating instructions, and sustaining institutions required support beyond the ceremony of inauguration. The case therefore extends from revolutionary declarations through institutional formation into continuing struggles over practical authority. The new government needed departments capable of exchanging documents, receiving information, and carrying out orders. The fact that provinces endorsed a republican direction did not mean they had surrendered their tax income or control of troops to one office. The provisional government’s early actions must therefore be understood alongside the limits of its resources and the continuing negotiations with northern authorities. The installation of a provisional president provided a recognizable formal start to government in Nanjing, but it did not mean every part of the country was administered from that office. Ministries and civil officers needed resources and procedures to turn documents into action. Provinces that had separated from Qing rule still exercised influence over their own forces and revenues. Negotiation with northern leaders continued while the new government undertook daily business. That overlap between institutional founding and contested authority is central to the chronology and explains why inauguration alone could not complete the revolution’s work. Every institution still had to secure cooperation and resources in order to operate beyond its founding announcements.

45.6 — A common victory can leave unresolved anxieties

In 1945, the end of the war against Japan left China with enormous questions about the reception of territory, the control of armed forces, and the formation of a postwar political order. Nationalist and Communist organizations retained different political structures and troops. Victory over an external enemy did not answer how all of these institutions would coexist. Negotiations, including those at Chongqing, attempted to establish common principles. Meanwhile the disposition of troops and the administration of local areas remained contentious. Signed statements and instructions from political leaders did not automatically produce an identical result wherever units were stationed. Armed incidents and disagreements continued after the initial celebrations of victory. During 1946 the fighting escalated into full-scale civil war. The sequence runs from wartime victory through attempted postwar agreements to renewed fighting. The existence of negotiations remains important, but neither victory nor diplomatic declarations should be misrepresented as a durable settlement already achieved. The end of the international conflict changed the immediate military context while leaving rival forces with their own organization and areas of influence. Reception of towns, stations, and administrative offices was not merely a matter of announcing victory. Negotiators could settle language in a document more quickly than political or military authorities could settle competing commands on the ground. That gap became visible as renewed clashes spread. In the months after Japan’s surrender, administering places formerly held by the Japanese was a practical problem for governments with rival forces. Each side also had its own claims about future national arrangements. Agreements at a negotiating table could propose a shared political framework, but local command structures did not automatically change. This mismatch made the period following victory uncertain for both military units and residents of contested areas. The escalation during 1946 thus belongs to the aftermath of unresolved arrangements rather than to the original wartime victory itself.

Historical event | Short narrative

In the early years of the Three Kingdoms era, Lü Meng was already serving Sun Quan as a military officer in the lower Yangtze region. His duties involved troops and campaigns, yet these responsibilities did not eliminate the need to understand earlier wars, institutions, and political decisions. Sun Quan urged him to undertake regular reading. According to an account quoted by Pei Songzhi in his commentary on the Records of the Three Kingdoms, the ruler did not expect Lü Meng to abandon military service and become a professional classical scholar. He wanted an officer with practical responsibilities to gain broader historical knowledge. Lü Meng first pointed to his demanding schedule. Sun Quan replied by referring to the burdens of his own position and argued that work need not make study impossible. The surviving narrative conveys the substance of that exchange; the polished dialogue familiar from later teaching materials should not be mistaken for a verbatim record. Lü Meng accepted the advice and began to read while continuing his existing duties. He was not reassigned from his post simply to become a student, and the change was not completed in a single meeting. Learning had to fit around work already under way. The later part of the account introduces Lu Su, another important officer. When the two discussed affairs, Lu Su recognized that Lü Meng had acquired knowledge and judgment beyond his earlier reputation. The resulting reassessment by a colleague marks the recorded outcome of the educational episode. It does not establish that every subsequent campaign succeeded because of reading or that any particular text supplied a military plan. The sequence in the surviving source is nevertheless clear: Sun Quan noticed a gap between experience and knowledge, recommended study, Lü Meng followed that recommendation while remaining at work, and Lu Su later acknowledged a change in his ability to discuss public affairs. The account describes a professional development process, not a miraculous transformation or evidence that anyone used the Small Image commentary to direct it.

46.3 — Easing resistance does not remove the need for order

46.3 — Line 3

273爻 Case ID: XCASE-H46-L3 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-46-04 | Event ID: E35 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 升虛邑，无所疑也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「上升進入空城，暢行無阻。」《象傳》解釋：無所疑。

English editorial reading focus: Easing resistance does not remove the need for order (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1926 the Northern Expedition advanced toward Wuchang, a major city on the Yangtze. Defenders controlled the city and its approaches. An early assault failed to achieve the attackers’ objective, requiring the campaign to continue under conditions that demanded troops, supplies, and a maintained encirclement. The attackers kept pressure on the defenses after the initial setback. The struggle continued until October 1926, when the Northern Expedition forces took Wuchang. The result expanded their military and political reach, but the elapsed time and fighting imposed costs on the defenders, the attacking troops, and civilians within the besieged city. The capture of Wuchang was a stage of the wider Northern Expedition, not the end of political disagreements among those associated with it. A retrospective account should preserve both the failed early assault and the later success. The city’s inhabitants also lived through the consequences of the siege, whether or not they were involved in command decisions. An early assault and a later siege are different phases of an offensive. During the intervening weeks, attackers had to maintain pressure and defenders continued to occupy the city. Neither side could assume the other would cease resistance after the first engagement. The October result thus followed a sustained campaign, and later political events followed the occupation of the city. The time between the unsuccessful attack and the eventual capture matters because combat did not simply pause until an inevitable victory. Armies on both sides remained engaged in the effort to control access to Wuchang. Civilians inside the city were subject to the restrictions of the siege while outside troops maintained their positions. When the city fell in October, that result ended one phase of the campaign but did not settle later political differences among those who had advanced under the wider Northern Expedition banner. Those outcomes belong to separate stages of the account.

46.5 — Creating a step-by-step route into public service

46.5 — Line 5

275爻 Case ID: XCASE-H46-L5 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-46-06 | Event ID: E46 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 貞吉升階，大得志也。

Historical event | Short narrative

Between the Sui and Tang periods, the Chinese state gradually gave examinations a larger part in selecting some officials. Earlier appointment practices and family connections continued to matter, but subjects such as the jinshi examination opened an additional route through which educated men might seek public office. The change was gradual and was not implemented everywhere or for everyone in an identical form. Studying for an examination required books, instruction and time; travel to a place of assessment could impose further expense. As the examination route developed, candidates prepared written work and sought to meet requirements established by the government. Those who passed still faced the separate process of appointment, and not every successful candidate received an office immediately. The system also existed alongside other avenues to public service. It did not eliminate the importance of family wealth, social networks or access to education. For individuals without a powerful lineage the examinations could provide opportunities, yet differences in resources continued to shape who could realistically participate. Over subsequent generations the role and organization of civil examinations expanded and changed. Historians debate details of when particular subjects began and at what point the system acquired its later institutional form. Consequently, it would be inaccurate to assign the mature imperial examination system to a single founding day. The documented sequence instead moves from adjustments in recruitment, through the establishment and use of examination subjects, to further development under later dynasties. Passing a test was one stage in that process rather than automatic entry into government. The surviving history supports an account of changing pathways to office, not a fictional account of a particular candidate's private struggles or a claim that effort guaranteed promotion. This distinction is necessary when adapting institutional history into a short narrative. What can be described is the evolving institution rather than the thoughts or fortunes of an invented examination candidate. The difference matters for readers.

46.6 — Pursuing rank alone can weaken public standing

46.6 — Line 6

276爻 Case ID: XCASE-H46-L6 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-46-07 | Event ID: E12 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 冥升在上，消不富也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「冥升在上」《象傳》解釋：消不富。

English editorial reading focus: Pursuing rank alone can weaken public standing (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

After the founding of the republic, Yuan Shikai occupied a commanding position in the central government, but his relationship with provincial and political interests remained complicated. In 1915 he moved to replace the republican form of government with a monarchy, changing the political framework under which existing offices had operated. Support for the imperial project was not universal. Opposition appeared in public politics and then in the National Protection War. Provincial leaders and forces that had previously cooperated with Yuan did not necessarily accept the new constitutional claim. Political disagreement thus had military as well as institutional consequences. In 1916 Yuan abandoned the monarchical project. That reversal did not remove the political conflicts surrounding the distribution of power. The surviving sequence is a proposed imperial restoration, widening opposition, war, and cancellation. It is not evidence that every supporter or opponent held the same motives. The change in regime title required not just central announcement but acceptance by officials and armed forces across the country. Provinces responded under circumstances that did not always match the central government’s expectations. As armed opposition expanded, the effectiveness of proclamations depended on military control and local cooperation. Ending the imperial claim was an identifiable reversal, but not the end of the political crisis. The attempt to create a monarchy altered the stated basis on which offices operated after the founding of the republic. That change required recognition from provinces, officers, and political groupings whose cooperation was not guaranteed. Opposition during the National Protection War made the weakness of that recognition visible. Cancellation of the project in 1916 was a direct response to a changed political situation, not an announcement that restored every previous relationship. Small Image original: 入于幽谷，幽不明也。

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1900 the Boxer movement, foreign intervention and divisions within the Qing leadership converged in a rapidly worsening political and military crisis. Officials at court and in the provinces did not all assess the available options in the same way. Foreign armed forces were already part of the conflict, and decisions taken in Beijing had consequences beyond the capital. The Qing court issued an edict of war against foreign powers as the crisis deepened. Allied foreign forces advanced and entered Beijing, while the court fled the city. Some officials in the southeast pursued arrangements commonly called the Mutual Protection of Southeast China, which reflected a divergence from the central response. The chronology includes domestic mobilization, armed intervention, the war edict, military defeat and separate provincial actions. In 1901 the Boxer Protocol imposed severe obligations on the Qing government and people. The episode should not be reduced to an error by one person, nor should criticism of the court’s choices obscure the role of foreign military intervention. The source supports a complex chain of decisions and consequences, not a claim that every province acted alike or that the Xiaoxiang text informed those decisions. The historical sequence depends on several different kinds of action: an initial political or military problem, a response by people in positions to act, and an aftermath in which the arrangements still had to be implemented. Where a source summarizes a long period, it does not provide a day-by-day account or justify assigning motives to every participant. A decision recorded in a history is not necessarily the same as the practical result it was intended to produce. Orders, discussions and appointments are identifiable moments; their implementation affects officials, troops or residents afterward. Maintaining that distinction is necessary to preserve the chronology without treating a later outcome as inevitable. The surviving sources allow the episode to be told in this order without recreating conversations or inner thoughts. They do not establish that everyone affected welcomed the decision, nor do they allow a single person or one written announcement to stand for all the later events.

Small Image original: 據于蒺藜，乘剛也。入于其宮，不見其妻，不祥也。

Historical event | Short narrative

In the Spring and Autumn period, the Qi official Cui Wuzi considered marrying Tang Jiang. The marriage was a political and personal matter involving a powerful man, a woman whose own wishes are not preserved in the surviving account, and advisers whose views appear in the historical record. Before the marriage, Cui sought a divination. The result was described as Kun changing to Da Guo. Chen Wenzi responded by referring to the third line of Kun, a line whose image includes being trapped among stones and thorns and failing to see one's wife upon returning home. He treated the result as an adverse warning about the proposed union. Cui rejected that interpretation and proceeded with the marriage. The narrative therefore preserves both an unfavorable reading and a decision not to follow it. The later history of Qi brought a separate political crisis. The state's ruler, Duke Zhuang, became involved with Tang Jiang, and the conflict around Cui's household entered the larger contest between ruler and minister. Duke Zhuang was eventually killed in the violent political upheaval recorded by the Zuozhuan. The account places the earlier marriage divination alongside these later developments, inviting comparison across events separated by time. The sequence nonetheless involves several decisions, people, and political relationships. A warning did not by itself prevent the marriage; nor did the divination create the subsequent killing. The historical record does not record Tang Jiang's own account of her choices or consent, and assigning responsibility for the violence to her would misstate what can be established. Cui and the ruling house operated within an unequal political system in which domestic relationships could become matters of state. What survives is a chain of reported actions: the marriage proposal, the divination, Chen's objection, Cui's decision to marry, and the later conflict involving the ruler. The episodes can be narrated in order without inventing private conversations or claiming that the omen predicted an inevitable result.

A succession conflict in the state of Jin forced Chong'er to leave the political position he had once occupied. With companions who remained alongside him, he spent years moving among other states. As an exile, he did not command the administrative and military resources of Jin. His situation depended on whether other rulers received him, offered provisions or chose to become involved in Jin's affairs. The treatment he received was not uniform. Some hosts offered assistance, while other encounters brought less favorable treatment. Throughout these travels, Chong'er and his followers had to maintain their association without a secure timetable for returning home. The record presents a succession of contacts and shifting circumstances, rather than a single, uninterrupted plan that carried him straight to the throne. There is no sound basis for assigning private thoughts to every host or for creating conversations missing from the surviving accounts. Eventually the state of Qin provided support that helped Chong'er return to Jin. He became ruler, later known as Duke Wen of Jin. His accession followed both the long period abroad and changes within Jin that made a return possible. Assistance from Qin mattered, but external backing alone would not explain every development within the state he was returning to. The order is important. First came the succession struggle and departure; then many years of movement, dependency and changing receptions; finally a political opening and Qin's assistance enabled a return and accession. His subsequent rule belongs to the aftermath, not to a destiny established on the day of his exile. Looking back from the eventual result can obscure how uncertain his position was during those years. The history supports a story of political displacement, enduring relationships and a later restoration, not a guarantee that every exile who waits will gain power. The aftermath must be distinguished from the original decision and evaluated from the surviving record.

Late accounts of the Shang period describe increasing tension between the Shang ruler and Xibo Chang, later remembered as King Wen of Zhou. According to this traditional narrative, people serving Xibo Chang undertook efforts to obtain his release while Zhou affairs still required attention. He eventually left confinement. The record is a later historical account rather than a collection of contemporary transcripts, and the exact dialogue or daily circumstances cannot be reconstructed from it. After his release, the growth of Zhou power continued through further events. Later knowledge of the Zhou dynasty’s eventual rise should not be projected backward as certainty during imprisonment. Stories about composing the Changes while confined belong to a separate evidentiary question and should not be added without support. The historical report does not provide a daily chronology of confinement, but it does distinguish detention from release. The associates seeking his freedom acted while relations between Zhou and Shang remained politically unequal. His eventual release restored the possibility of further political activity; it did not mean that the Zhou state had already achieved its later dynastic position. The surviving story is a traditional narrative transmitted through texts written much later than the events they purport to describe. Its clear phases are the confinement of Xibo Chang, efforts by his associates, and release. They do not yield a complete inventory of his activities during imprisonment. Likewise, political developments after he returned cannot be attributed to a known private plan formed at Youli. The gaps in the record matter: the account can be a connected short narrative without supplying invented meetings, detailed conversations, or explanations of what he secretly expected would happen.

47.6 — Changing methods when the original route cannot work

English editorial reading focus: Changing methods when the original route cannot work (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1936, mounting pressure from Japan existed alongside armed conflict within China. Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng opposed Chiang Kai-shek’s prevailing approach to these conflicts. In Xi’an they detained Chiang, transforming a serious political dispute into an immediate crisis over the security of the national leader and the conduct of military forces. Different political and military parties became involved in negotiations. The aim of the exchanges was to end the detention without allowing the crisis to expand into further fighting. Chiang was eventually released. The questions of suspending internal conflict and resisting Japan were brought more prominently into national politics, but agreement about every future obligation did not follow automatically. The subsequent positions of Zhang and Yang were not identical, and the larger political relationships remained disputed. Detention, negotiation, release, and later cooperation must therefore be kept in their proper order. Recalling the negotiated release does not by itself establish that the original detention was justified or that all later promises were implemented. The detention affected more than the person held: military units and political representatives beyond Xi’an had to consider the danger that further armed action might follow. Negotiators worked while the detention itself remained an unresolved fact. Even after release, statements about resistance to Japan, control of forces, and cooperation required action by separate organizations. Those later questions cannot be compressed into the moment Chiang left detention. The political landscape in which talks took place did not have a single unified chain of command. Representatives of several positions had to react to the seizure and to proposals for ending it. The immediate issue was whether the captive would be released; the broader dispute concerned military priorities and political relations under the pressure of Japanese expansion. The passage from detention to negotiation and release did not settle every one of those wider questions. Subsequent history therefore cannot be written as though an exchange of assurances erased the tensions present before the crisis.

48 — Jing — The Well

48.1 — Outdated infrastructure can no longer meet new needs

48.1 — Line 1

283爻 Case ID: XCASE-H48-L1 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-48-02 | Event ID: E09 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 井泥不食，下也。舊井无禽，時舍也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「井底淤泥，水不能飲；廢井連禽獸也不來。」《象傳》解釋：下。「井底淤泥，水不能飲；廢井連禽獸也不來。」《象傳》解釋：時舍。

English editorial reading focus: Outdated infrastructure can no longer meet new needs (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

After military defeats and encounters with industrial powers in the nineteenth century, Qing officials faced increasingly visible gaps in the manufacture of weapons, the operation of ships and the training of specialized personnel. Some officials responded by establishing arsenals, shipbuilding institutions and schools. These were not components of a single project completed on one date; they developed under different provincial and central authorities, with varying sources of funding. New workshops required imported or newly acquired equipment, raw materials and workers capable of operating unfamiliar machinery. Maritime institutions needed shipbuilding expertise and instruction, while military training had to adapt to equipment that could not be maintained through older arrangements alone. Establishing a facility was an institutional decision; producing useful goods and trained personnel required subsequent management. Officials therefore had to provide wages, supplies, administrative authority and continuity beyond the opening of a factory or school. During the movement, some installations began manufacturing and training students. Skills and industrial equipment accumulated, creating a basis for additional activity. But equipment did not automatically solve differences among regional commands. Naval and military resources also depended on coordination, maintenance, transport and decisions about deployment. A weapon manufactured in one place still had to reach the people assigned to use it, while trainees needed working positions within functioning organizations. By the end of the nineteenth century, the Qing state had more modern installations and trained personnel than before, while major financial and organizational weaknesses remained. Later defeats demonstrated limits in the whole military system; they did not mean the earlier machinery or education had never existed. The documented sequence runs from recognition of technical problems, through institutional investment and practical training, to the persistence of coordination challenges. This was a long process involving multiple officials and establishments, not the personal accomplishment or failure of one leader. Its effects must be assessed across equipment, administration and wartime operations separately.

48.2 — Isolated equipment cannot substitute for a working system

48.2 — Line 2

284爻 Case ID: XCASE-H48-L2 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-48-03 | Event ID: E28 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 井谷射鮒，无與也。

Historical event | Short narrative

By the late nineteenth century, the Qing government and regional officials had already invested in modern naval vessels, weapons production, and technical education. These initiatives created equipment and trained personnel, but possessing modern ships did not settle questions of strategy, logistics, maintenance, or coordination between different commands. In 1894, war between Qing China and Japan put the existing military system under the pressure of major operations on land and at sea. Forces that had developed through separate institutions now had to confront an opponent in a connected conflict. Naval vessels needed supplies and repairs, land forces depended on transport and reliable command, and information had to move among officials responsible for different parts of the war. The Qing armies and fleets suffered defeats during the campaign. The failure of particular operations exposed difficulties in organization and military cooperation that equipment purchases alone had not resolved. These results should not erase the technical work achieved before the war, but they do show that tools and institutions are not interchangeable. Military defeat was followed by diplomatic negotiations. In 1895 the Qing government signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki, under which Taiwan and the Penghu Islands were ceded to Japan. That agreement carried the consequences of the fighting beyond the battlefield and changed the political circumstances of people living in the territories transferred. The sequence ran from earlier acquisition of modern weapons and infrastructure, through wartime performance, to a settlement imposing territorial and financial obligations. The impact of the treaty on local populations outlasted the immediate military campaign. An account focused entirely on the equipment available before 1894 would miss the command problems that arose during the war; an account concerned only with defeat would ignore the substantial effort already devoted to military modernization. The source text therefore uses the conflict to distinguish partial advances from the functioning of an entire system. Its historical discussion is retrospective and does not demonstrate that Qing officials drew on the Small Image commentary when planning ships, campaigns, or negotiations.

48.3 — Ability needs an institution that can recognize it

English editorial reading focus: Ability needs an institution that can recognize it (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

Between the Sui and Tang periods, the Chinese state gradually gave examinations a larger part in selecting some officials. Earlier appointment practices and family connections continued to matter, but subjects such as the jinshi examination opened an additional route through which educated men might seek public office. The change was gradual and was not implemented everywhere or for everyone in an identical form. Studying for an examination required books, instruction and time; travel to a place of assessment could impose further expense. As the examination route developed, candidates prepared written work and sought to meet requirements established by the government. Those who passed still faced the separate process of appointment, and not every successful candidate received an office immediately. The system also existed alongside other avenues to public service. It did not eliminate the importance of family wealth, social networks or access to education. For individuals without a powerful lineage the examinations could provide opportunities, yet differences in resources continued to shape who could realistically participate. Over subsequent generations the role and organization of civil examinations expanded and changed. Historians debate details of when particular subjects began and at what point the system acquired its later institutional form. Consequently, it would be inaccurate to assign the mature imperial examination system to a single founding day. The documented sequence instead moves from adjustments in recruitment, through the establishment and use of examination subjects, to further development under later dynasties. Passing a test was one stage in that process rather than automatic entry into government. The surviving history supports an account of changing pathways to office, not a fictional account of a particular candidate's private struggles or a claim that effort guaranteed promotion. This distinction is necessary when adapting institutional history into a short narrative. What can be described is the evolving institution rather than the thoughts or fortunes of an invented examination candidate. The difference matters for readers.

48.4 — Common facilities require continued maintenance

48.4 — Line 4

286爻 Case ID: XCASE-H48-L4 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-48-05 | Event ID: E48 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 井甃无咎，修井也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「井壁修砌完整，無咎。」《象傳》解釋：水井已經修整完成。

English editorial reading focus: Common facilities require continued maintenance (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

In the Warring States period, the Chengdu Plain faced the practical problems of supplying fields with water while managing the changing flow and sediment of the rivers. The irrigation works associated with Dujiangyan developed in this setting. Traditional accounts connect major work in the region with the Qin administration of Shu. Their significance lies in how water could be diverted and distributed, not merely in the construction of a single monumental structure. The system made use of the local terrain and moving water. Dividing the river's flow and handling sediment were connected operations: a scheme that delivered water to farms also had to prevent material from making channels unusable. Construction established a working arrangement, but it did not eliminate seasonal differences. Residents and officials needed to manage the system as weather, river levels and agricultural demands changed. The available summary does not supply a daily work diary or allow detailed speech to be attributed to individual engineers. Over time, the irrigation network supported cultivation and settlement in the plain. Its continued usefulness depended on maintenance, removal of sediment and the adjustment of channels and distribution. The responsibilities were spread across generations, rather than completed by one group at one moment. Not all fields or settlements necessarily had identical access to water, and a brief account cannot substitute for technical studies of every part of the network. The narrative therefore begins with the need to manage an important river, proceeds through the establishment of works that guided and allocated its waters, and extends into repeated repair and management after initial construction. The long history of Dujiangyan is one of continued operation as well as initial engineering. The classical image of the well is a later analogy applied in this collection; it is not evidence that the designers consulted this passage or used it as a set of engineering instructions.

49.2 — Political transitions depend on workable timing and cooperation

49.2 — Line 2

290爻 Case ID: XCASE-H49-L2 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-49-03 | Event ID: E49 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 巳日革之，行有嘉也。

English editorial reading focus: Political transitions depend on workable timing and cooperation (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1911 the Wuchang uprising triggered a widening challenge to Qing authority. Provinces successively announced separation from the Qing government, although the participants did not all agree on the future political settlement. Military conflict and negotiations between northern and southern leaders proceeded in parallel. In 1912 the Qing emperor abdicated and a republican political form replaced the dynasty’s monarchy. The abdication represented a specific institutional break, but it followed multiple provincial decisions, military actions, and political exchanges. The change cannot be assigned exclusively to one individual or one day of armed uprising. After the abdication, military forces, officials, and local governments still had to determine how they related to the new central institutions. The establishment of a republic did not resolve every question of finance and authority. The historical outcome involved the end of an old regime and the beginning of another period of negotiation. A province declaring separation from the Qing did not by itself determine the legal position of other provinces or the national government. Military advances and conversations over an acceptable settlement occurred side by side. After the emperor’s abdication, offices and armed organizations still required new chains of responsibility. That practical aftermath was part of the revolution’s political transformation. The revolutionary sequence included armed resistance and negotiated institutional settlement. Provincial defections weakened the Qing administration, while those negotiating in the north and south still faced the issue of how military forces would fit into a new order. The emperor’s abdication ended the dynasty’s formal monarchy; it did not instantly give every locality an agreed set of administrative procedures. The subsequent question was how officials, armies, and budgets would operate under republican institutions. This is why the story continues beyond the best-known date of the imperial abdication. The formal constitutional change and the practical transfer of authority did not happen simultaneously across the whole territory.

49.3 — Major institutional change requires public explanation and evidence

49.3 — Line 3

291爻 Case ID: XCASE-H49-L3 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-49-04 | Event ID: E18 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 革言三就，又何之矣。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「冒進凶，固守也危；變革主張經多次審議成熟，才會取信。」《象傳》解釋：又何之。

English editorial reading focus: Major institutional change requires public explanation and evidence (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

During the reign of Duke Xiao of Qin, the state faced political and military competition from neighboring powers. Its leaders sought to organize land, households, taxation, and military service more effectively. Shang Yang entered the duke's service and became closely associated with a series of reforms that changed the administration of Qin. The reforms were not one isolated proclamation. They revised the registration of households, the organization of local authority, obligations owed to the state, and rewards for military achievements. Changes to the rules of service and rank altered the ways individuals could advance, while new administrative expectations affected communities already accustomed to other practices. Officials then had to enforce the laws across villages, farms, and military units. The regulations brought previously established interests into conflict with the state, and their severe penalties placed substantial burdens on individuals. These effects should be described alongside the stronger mobilization capacity that the reforms helped Qin acquire. New registration systems could make people and resources more visible to government, but the same visibility also made demands and punishments easier to enforce. Military rewards offered recognized incentives, although their existence did not remove the costs of war. The changes continued to shape Qin after their sponsor's political position deteriorated. When Duke Xiao died, Shang Yang lost the protection on which his career had depended. He was eventually executed, while important components of the institutional changes remained in use. The fate of the reformer and that of the institutions therefore followed different paths. Surviving historical narratives discuss both increasing state capacity and harsh treatment under the new arrangements. They do not provide a complete accounting of how every household experienced the reforms. The chronological outline is clear: competition created pressure for reorganization, Duke Xiao employed Shang Yang, rules changed and were enforced, Qin's institutions gained new means of mobilization, and Shang Yang himself fell after a change at court. The account does not show that he planned the reforms by consulting the Small Image commentary.

49.5 — Reform becomes visible through functioning public institutions

Historical event | Short narrative

The 1911 Revolution created a need for government institutions capable of representing the republican movement and conducting ordinary administration. Several provinces had broken with the Qing court, but their declarations did not automatically establish a unified national budget, bureaucracy, or chain of military command. On 1 January 1912, Sun Yat-sen took office as provisional president in Nanjing. The provisional government organized offices and issued documents intended to translate political change into administration. Officials began operating under new institutional names while negotiations with the Qing side and other powers continued. The provisional government’s direct control remained geographically and financially limited. Appointing officers, communicating instructions, and sustaining institutions required support beyond the ceremony of inauguration. The case therefore extends from revolutionary declarations through institutional formation into continuing struggles over practical authority. The new government needed departments capable of exchanging documents, receiving information, and carrying out orders. The fact that provinces endorsed a republican direction did not mean they had surrendered their tax income or control of troops to one office. The provisional government’s early actions must therefore be understood alongside the limits of its resources and the continuing negotiations with northern authorities. The installation of a provisional president provided a recognizable formal start to government in Nanjing, but it did not mean every part of the country was administered from that office. Ministries and civil officers needed resources and procedures to turn documents into action. Provinces that had separated from Qing rule still exercised influence over their own forces and revenues. Negotiation with northern leaders continued while the new government undertook daily business. That overlap between institutional founding and contested authority is central to the chronology and explains why inauguration alone could not complete the revolution’s work. Every institution still had to secure cooperation and resources in order to operate beyond its founding announcements.

50.1 — Removing inherited obstacles is part of establishing a new order

50.1 — Line 1

295爻 Case ID: XCASE-H50-L1 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-50-02 | Event ID: E18 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 鼎顛趾，未悖也。利出否，以從貴也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「鼎足顛倒，適宜倒出污物；娶妾因其子而得正，無咎。」《象傳》解釋：未悖。「鼎足顛倒，適宜倒出污物；娶妾因其子而得正，無咎。」《象傳》解釋：以從貴。

English editorial reading focus: Removing inherited obstacles is part of establishing a new order (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

During the reign of Duke Xiao of Qin, the state faced political and military competition from neighboring powers. Its leaders sought to organize land, households, taxation, and military service more effectively. Shang Yang entered the duke's service and became closely associated with a series of reforms that changed the administration of Qin. The reforms were not one isolated proclamation. They revised the registration of households, the organization of local authority, obligations owed to the state, and rewards for military achievements. Changes to the rules of service and rank altered the ways individuals could advance, while new administrative expectations affected communities already accustomed to other practices. Officials then had to enforce the laws across villages, farms, and military units. The regulations brought previously established interests into conflict with the state, and their severe penalties placed substantial burdens on individuals. These effects should be described alongside the stronger mobilization capacity that the reforms helped Qin acquire. New registration systems could make people and resources more visible to government, but the same visibility also made demands and punishments easier to enforce. Military rewards offered recognized incentives, although their existence did not remove the costs of war. The changes continued to shape Qin after their sponsor's political position deteriorated. When Duke Xiao died, Shang Yang lost the protection on which his career had depended. He was eventually executed, while important components of the institutional changes remained in use. The fate of the reformer and that of the institutions therefore followed different paths. Surviving historical narratives discuss both increasing state capacity and harsh treatment under the new arrangements. They do not provide a complete accounting of how every household experienced the reforms. The chronological outline is clear: competition created pressure for reorganization, Duke Xiao employed Shang Yang, rules changed and were enforced, Qin's institutions gained new means of mobilization, and Shang Yang himself fell after a change at court. During the struggle between Liu Bang and Xiang Yu, field armies repeatedly needed soldiers, food, and other supplies. Liu Bang’s access to the Guanzhong region provided an administrative and agricultural base, but that base would have contributed little if its civil government had ceased functioning. Frontline demands changed as campaigns continued. Xiao He remained primarily in Guanzhong and maintained administrative work. Population records, provisions, and the recruitment or replenishment of manpower formed part of the support reaching Liu Bang’s forces. These were not isolated tasks completed once at the beginning of the war. After troops consumed supplies and suffered losses, the rear organization had to replenish what could be provided and arrange onward transport. Registers mattered when manpower had to be identified; stored provisions mattered when supplies had to be prepared and moved. These connected activities took place before and after particular battles. Xiao He’s work cannot be described as a single dramatic encounter, since the essential feature was the regularity of repeated administrative tasks. An expedition’s field officers were visible in surviving accounts of battle, while the machinery that maintained food and reinforcements worked over much longer intervals. A shortage might originate far from a battlefield and still determine whether operations could continue. Because Xiao He had responsibility in Guanzhong, he was connected to that recurring problem of supply. His work occurred within a functioning community from which labor and food were gathered. Recognizing his role does not turn those social resources into an unlimited stock; it clarifies why continuing administration was part of the military story.

After military defeats and encounters with industrial powers in the nineteenth century, Qing officials faced increasingly visible gaps in the manufacture of weapons, the operation of ships and the training of specialized personnel. Some officials responded by establishing arsenals, shipbuilding institutions and schools. These were not components of a single project completed on one date; they developed under different provincial and central authorities, with varying sources of funding. New workshops required imported or newly acquired equipment, raw materials and workers capable of operating unfamiliar machinery. Maritime institutions needed shipbuilding expertise and instruction, while military training had to adapt to equipment that could not be maintained through older arrangements alone. Establishing a facility was an institutional decision; producing useful goods and trained personnel required subsequent management. Officials therefore had to provide wages, supplies, administrative authority and continuity beyond the opening of a factory or school. During the movement, some installations began manufacturing and training students. Skills and industrial equipment accumulated, creating a basis for additional activity. But equipment did not automatically solve differences among regional commands. Naval and military resources also depended on coordination, maintenance, transport and decisions about deployment. A weapon manufactured in one place still had to reach the people assigned to use it, while trainees needed working positions within functioning organizations. By the end of the nineteenth century, the Qing state had more modern installations and trained personnel than before, while major financial and organizational weaknesses remained. Later defeats demonstrated limits in the whole military system; they did not mean the earlier machinery or education had never existed. The documented sequence runs from recognition of technical problems, through institutional investment and practical training, to the persistence of coordination challenges. This was a long process involving multiple officials and establishments, not the personal accomplishment or failure of one leader. Its effects must be assessed across equipment, administration and wartime operations separately.

50.4 — When leadership capacity fails, the public bears the consequences

50.4 — Line 4

Small Image original: 覆公餗，信如何也。

Historical event | Short narrative

In 1449, the Ming emperor Yingzong accompanied a military expedition northward against the Oirat forces. The presence of the ruler made the campaign more than a frontier operation: the movement of the army also exposed the central court to the fortunes of an expedition far from Beijing. A large military column depended on supplies, transport, reliable orders and coordination during its advance and return. The Ming forces encountered serious difficulties on the march. During the withdrawal, the army suffered a crushing defeat in the area known as Tumu, and the emperor was captured. The scale of the reverse cannot be explained by a single decision or an unverified figure for the numbers involved. Command, logistics, routes and the opposing army's actions all formed part of the conditions under which the disaster occurred. News of the defeat reached Beijing while the emperor was still in captivity. Civil and military officials then faced a linked set of urgent tasks. They had to arrange the city's defense, organize command and consider how government would operate without the sovereign present. The military defeat thus moved quickly from an expedition's route into the institutions of the capital. The measures taken in Beijing were a response to the crisis, not a sign that its outcome had been foreseen at the expedition's outset. The essential chronology is the decision to conduct the campaign, the emperor's participation, difficulties on the return, the defeat at Tumu, his capture, and the reorganization of defense and government at the capital. Historical accounts differ in their evaluation of individuals and in some numerical details. Those uncertainties should not be filled with invented scenes or reported speech. The event demonstrates that the consequences of military failure could extend beyond the battlefield, affecting political authority and daily administration while the immediate struggle remained unresolved.

50.5 — A central institution needs actual powers and working procedures

50.5 — Line 5

299爻 Case ID: XCASE-H50-L5 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-50-06 | Event ID: E50 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 鼎黃耳，中以為實也。

Historical event | Short narrative

The 1911 Revolution created a need for government institutions capable of representing the republican movement and conducting ordinary administration. Several provinces had broken with the Qing court, but their declarations did not automatically establish a unified national budget, bureaucracy, or chain of military command. On 1 January 1912, Sun Yat-sen took office as provisional president in Nanjing. The provisional government organized offices and issued documents intended to translate political change into administration. Officials began operating under new institutional names while negotiations with the Qing side and other powers continued. The provisional government’s direct control remained geographically and financially limited. Appointing officers, communicating instructions, and sustaining institutions required support beyond the ceremony of inauguration. The case therefore extends from revolutionary declarations through institutional formation into continuing struggles over practical authority. The new government needed departments capable of exchanging documents, receiving information, and carrying out orders. The fact that provinces endorsed a republican direction did not mean they had surrendered their tax income or control of troops to one office. The provisional government’s early actions must therefore be understood alongside the limits of its resources and the continuing negotiations with northern authorities. The installation of a provisional president provided a recognizable formal start to government in Nanjing, but it did not mean every part of the country was administered from that office. Ministries and civil officers needed resources and procedures to turn documents into action. Provinces that had separated from Qing rule still exercised influence over their own forces and revenues. Negotiation with northern leaders continued while the new government undertook daily business. That overlap between institutional founding and contested authority is central to the chronology and explains why inauguration alone could not complete the revolution’s work. Every institution still had to secure cooperation and resources in order to operate beyond its founding announcements.

As the Liao army moved south, the Song court faced an immediate military challenge near its northern approaches. Envoys negotiated a settlement that became the Chanyuan Covenant in 1005. The Song government accepted recurring payments to Liao, and the two polities maintained a frontier relationship under agreed terms. The arrangement addressed the immediate military confrontation, although it imposed continuing financial obligations. An agreement on paper had to be followed by orders to troops, exchanges among officials and observance of the agreed border practices. Major war between these powers was reduced for a considerable period, but the frontier did not become free of political negotiation or tension. The costs of the settlement and the reduction of large-scale fighting must both appear in the narrative. Peace was not achieved by one side simply declaring that conflict was over; its practical operation depended on sustained arrangements after the negotiations. 51.1 — After the shock, organize a response grounded in evidence

51.1 — Line 1

301爻 Case ID: XCASE-H51-L1 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-51-02 | Event ID: E51 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 震來虩虩，恐致福也。笑言啞啞，后有則也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「震來先恐懼，後能談笑，吉。」《象傳》解釋：恐致福。「震來先恐懼，後能談笑，吉。」《象傳》解釋：后有則。

English editorial reading focus: After the shock, organize a response grounded in evidence (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

In July 1937, military tension around the Lugou Bridge area near Beiping drew Chinese and Japanese forces into an escalating confrontation. Japanese troops had been conducting exercises in the vicinity, while Chinese troops held positions connected with the city's approaches. A local clash occurred on the night of July 7. Accounts differ on certain immediate details, but the incident became a point of rapid political and military escalation. Officers and authorities on the scene faced decisions about troop positions and responses while larger governments received reports from the area. Negotiations and temporary arrangements did not produce a durable settlement. Additional fighting developed around Beiping and Tianjin, and the scale of the confrontation moved far beyond the initial encounter. Japanese forces advanced in North China, while Chinese forces attempted to organize resistance and protect their positions. As the situation widened, the consequences were no longer confined to a disputed bridge or a single garrison. Civilians were exposed to military action, disruption of daily work, displacement, and uncertainty about which authorities could maintain local order. In the following months, fighting expanded to other major regions, including the Shanghai area, and the conflict became a prolonged war. The incident is therefore best narrated in stages rather than as a single moment that automatically determined the entire later history: mounting military tension; the July 7 confrontation; efforts to negotiate and reinforce positions; renewed battles and wider troop movements; and the beginning of large-scale war. A short account cannot settle all disputed questions about who initiated every local action, nor can it assign the course of a multinational conflict to one officer's conduct. The accessible chronology nevertheless establishes that efforts to contain the initial violence failed and that subsequent operations greatly increased the human and political stakes. The event became known as the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, or the July Seventh Incident. Its importance lies in the transition from a localized armed confrontation to a much wider conflict. 51.3 — A setback should trigger a reassessment of deployment

51.3 — Line 3

303爻 Case ID: XCASE-H51-L3 | Unit ID: XIANG-L-51-04 | Event ID: E39 | Evidence: B

Small Image original: 震蘇蘇，位不當也。

Existing Traditional Chinese rendering: 「因震恐而不安；能因恐懼行動，便無災。」《象傳》解釋：所處位置不恰當。

English editorial reading focus: A setback should trigger a reassessment of deployment (thematic, not a literal translation).

Historical event | Short narrative

After the Shu campaign entered Longyou, the position at Jieting became critical to the continuation of Zhuge Liang’s first northern expedition. Ma Su was entrusted with local command. His deployment failed to hold the position, and the campaign could no longer proceed on its original assumptions. The importance of Jieting lay in its connection to the rest of the expedition, not simply in its name on a map. With Jieting lost, Zhuge Liang withdrew his forces. A withdrawal required soldiers and their officers to abandon the planned advance and return to a more defensible arrangement; the decision did not erase the costs already incurred. Zhuge Liang then submitted a memorial requesting a reduction of his own rank. The memorial acknowledged his responsibility for the choice of commander rather than assigning the entire failure to a subordinate. The military loss, the withdrawal, and the memorial were separate stages of the same episode. The surviving record supports this sequence, but it does not justify importing the fictional Empty Fort Stratagem into it. The episode also cannot establish that one appointment alone explained every aspect of the campaign’s failure. The site mattered because an advancing army could not move independently of its supporting positions. Once the approach became untenable, the remaining forces needed a withdrawal instead of continuing along the original route. The memorial is relevant precisely because it appears after the failure, when the commander was reviewing responsibility for decisions already made. Neither the act of retreating nor the statement of responsibility reverses the loss of the position. The command structure also mattered after the immediate battlefield reversal. The responsibility for appointing Ma Su was not identical to the responsibility for every action taken at Jieting, yet it was a decision Zhuge Liang could acknowledge in a formal document. The forces assigned to protect the movement came under heavy pressure, and the troops attempting to reach and pass the crossing suffered considerable casualties and organizational losses. In July 1937, military tension around the Lugou Bridge area near Beiping drew Chinese and Japanese forces into an escalating confrontation. Japanese troops had been conducting exercises in the vicinity, while Chinese troops held positions connected with the city's approaches. A local clash occurred on the night of July 7. Accounts differ on certain immediate details, but the incident became a point of rapid political and military escalation. Officers and authorities on the scene faced decisions about troop positions and responses while larger governments received reports from the area. Negotiations and temporary arrangements did not produce a durable settlement. Additional fighting developed around Beiping and Tianjin, and the scale of the confrontation moved far beyond the initial encounter. Japanese forces advanced in North China, while Chinese forces attempted to organize resistance and protect their positions. As the situation widened, the consequences were no longer confined to a disputed bridge or a single garrison. Civilians were exposed to military action, disruption of daily work, displacement, and uncertainty about which authorities could maintain local order. In the following months, fighting expanded to other major regions, including the Shanghai area, and the conflict became a prolonged war. The incident is therefore best narrated in stages rather than as a single moment that automatically determined the entire later history: mounting military tension; the July 7 confrontation; efforts to negotiate and reinforce positions; renewed battles and wider troop movements; and the beginning of large-scale war. A short account cannot settle all disputed questions about who initiated every local action, nor can it assign the course of a multinational conflict to one officer's conduct. The accessible chronology nevertheless establishes that efforts to contain the initial violence failed and that subsequent operations greatly increased the human and political stakes. The event became known as the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, or the July Seventh Incident. Its importance lies in the transition from a localized armed confrontation to a much wider conflict.
