64 Hexagram Cases

01 乾 | Hexagram 01

EUUS-PM-H01 · Rome, Europe · 800 CE · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Charlemagne crowned emperor. By the late eighth century, Charlemagne ruled a Frankish kingdom enlarged through successive campaigns and alliances. He had crossed the Alps more than once to support the papacy, while Rome itself was troubled by a dispute over Pope Leo III. After opponents attacked Leo in 799, the pope sought Charlemagne's protection. The Frankish ruler came to Rome in 800, where an inquiry addressed accusations against Leo and the pope publicly asserted his innocence. On Christmas Day, during worship at St Peter's, Leo placed a crown on Charlemagne's head and the assembled people acclaimed him emperor. The ceremony gave a new title to a ruler who already commanded extensive territory and armies. It also linked the Frankish court and the Roman church more closely, while raising questions about the meaning of imperial authority in a world that also had an emperor at Constantinople. Charlemagne returned to the work of ruling from his own court. Officials carried instructions into different parts of the realm, bishops and counts took part in governance, and campaigns continued along contested frontiers. The imperial title thus entered a political landscape that had already been assembled through years of Frankish rule. The crown did not create those institutions overnight. It marked a public claim that had to operate through the people and structures already available. Relations with Byzantium remained a diplomatic issue after the ceremony; recognition of Charlemagne's imperial title was negotiated in the years that followed. When he died in 814, succession passed to his son Louis, and the political order he had assembled faced the ordinary problems of inheritance and regional power. The story begins with a ruler summoned into a Roman crisis, reaches its visible turning point at a Christmas coronation, and continues through the less ceremonial work of governing an empire whose components did not become uniform simply because one title had changed.

Interpretive analogy The judgment of Qian describes forceful beginnings and sustained movement. Charlemagne's coronation offers a retrospective way to ask what happens after a powerful leader acquires a larger public title. The Frankish ruler did not begin to govern in 800; armies, officials, church connections, and local obligations already formed the base of his rule. The crown made a claim visible to Rome and to other powers, but it also created further questions about recognition, succession, and the reach of command. A modern reader can separate the moment of announcement from the work needed to carry an announcement into daily institutions. The historical comparison concerns continuity after a visible beginning, not a prediction about the emperor's fortunes. The hexagram is not a source for Charlemagne's decisions, and no evidence here shows that he consulted the Zhouyi. The documented chronology supports the coronation and its political aftermath; the comparison is an editorial lens for examining the gap between initiating an order and sustaining it.

Evidence note: The source supports the event, not a claim that participants used the Zhouyi. Historical source ↗

02 坤 | Hexagram 02

EUUS-PM-H02 · Athens, Europe · c. 594 BCE · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Solon's reforms at Athens. In archaic Athens, debt and unequal access to land and political power had deepened conflict between poorer residents and established families. Some Athenians could lose their freedom through obligations secured on their own persons. Around 594 BCE, Solon was given authority to mediate and legislate amid this crisis. He cancelled existing debts of the kind that bound people, prohibited future loans secured on the debtor's person, and arranged for some who had been sold away to return. He did not redistribute all land, a demand that would have satisfied one side while sharply threatening another. His settlement also reorganized political participation by property classes, opening certain civic roles while reserving the highest offices for wealthier groups. A council and courts formed part of the revised arrangements, though the exact operation of early Athenian institutions is reconstructed from later accounts. Solon published laws that citizens would have to use after he left office. The constitutional changes also placed citizens into income groups that affected their eligibility for office and military obligations. Ancient authors do not agree on every detail of the reforms, and later Athenians reworked the political system. These limits matter when describing Solon's measures as a compromise rather than the completed birth of democracy. The measures changed the immediate terms of debt and public life, but they did not erase differences of wealth or end factional rivalry. Later Athens passed through further struggles, including tyranny, before another round of institutional reform. Ancient writers preserved Solon's legislation together with debates about what he meant to accomplish. Their accounts are written after the event and do not let us watch every assembly or negotiation. The sequence remains clear: a city facing social fracture empowered one lawgiver; he removed the most severe debt bonds and revised rules of participation; the city then had to live with a compromise that neither gave every poor household land nor left elite authority untouched.

Interpretive analogy Kun can be read as a reminder that political order must receive and accommodate the people who will live under it. Solon's settlement followed a conflict with more than one demand. Debt relief addressed a severe form of dependency, while his refusal to divide land left other inequalities in place. The result was a set of laws and institutions that different Athenians would have to use, contest, and revise. The analogy invites a reader to ask who bears the costs of compromise and whether new rules can remain workable after the mediator departs. The relief of debt bondage and the preservation of other inequalities should be considered together; neither feature alone describes the entire settlement. It does not turn Solon into a follower of the Zhouyi, and it does not declare his settlement fair to every group. Ancient sources record reforms and later struggles; connecting them to Kun is a present-day interpretive choice. A useful application is to examine whose voices and material needs a new political framework actually makes room for.

Evidence note: The source supports the event, not a claim that participants used the Zhouyi. Historical source ↗

03 屯 | Hexagram 03

EUUS-PM-H03 · Athens, Europe · c. 508 BCE · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Cleisthenes' tribal reforms. After the fall of the Peisistratid tyranny, Athens did not immediately settle on a stable civic order. Leading families competed, and Isagoras gained the archonship while Cleisthenes sought support among the broader citizen body. Isagoras called on the Spartan king Cleomenes. With Spartan backing, opponents of Cleisthenes expelled families and tried to replace existing political arrangements. Athenians resisted the intervention, besieged the occupying group on the Acropolis, and recalled Cleisthenes and other exiles. Cleisthenes then recast the basis of civic membership. Instead of relying on four older tribes tied to established affiliations, he formed ten tribes whose components drew on urban, inland, and coastal districts. Local demes became important units of identification and public registration. A council of five hundred, with members drawn from the new tribes, gave the reorganized citizen body a continuing institution for public business. These measures spread political connections across different parts of Attica, but they did not extend equal civic rights to every resident. The new tribes combined residents from different regions, making older local and familial alignments less decisive in the formal organization of civic life. Demes maintained their own registers, so the change reached beyond the central assembly and into the way citizens were identified in ordinary public business. Women, enslaved people, and many noncitizens remained outside the citizen framework. The reforms also came out of conflict, not a calm founding ceremony. They had to be enacted after an attempted intervention and then used in elections, councils, military organization, and local records. Later ancient accounts describe both the struggle with Isagoras and the new arrangements, though historians still scrutinize their details. The order of events matters: factional contest drew outside force into Athens; local resistance reopened politics; Cleisthenes' reforms supplied new units through which citizens could act. The resulting democracy developed further in later decades rather than arriving complete in a single year.

Interpretive analogy Zhun speaks to the difficulty of a beginning before its institutions can stand on their own. The Athenian reorganization followed a fight over who could govern and who counted as part of the political community. Cleisthenes did more than proclaim a new principle: the demes, mixed tribes, and council created procedures for repeated public action. Yet participation remained bounded by citizenship, and subsequent Athenians still had to work through the arrangements. The comparison asks what practical structures a reform needs when its first supporters face resistance. The later history of Athenian democracy should be traced separately from the first enactment of these reforms and their immediate conflict. It also asks who remains outside a newly enlarged political body. This is a retrospective reading of Zhun, not a historical claim that Cleisthenes used a Chinese text. Aristotle's later account and other ancient evidence concern Athenian politics; the hexagram supplies only a modern question about difficult beginnings and the need to build institutions before calling a crisis resolved.

04 蒙 | Hexagram 04

EUUS-PM-H04 · Aegean, Europe · c. 478 BCE · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Aristides and allied contributions. After the Persian invasions of Greece, many Aegean communities still feared renewed attacks and needed a way to maintain ships and campaigns. The leadership of the Greek coalition shifted toward Athens as dissatisfaction with Spartan commander Pausanias grew. Allied cities met in a new association whose treasury was placed on Delos. Members could provide ships or make monetary contributions for the common effort. Establishing what each city owed was a political as well as an accounting task: the members differed in size, resources, and capacity to maintain a navy. Ancient accounts assign an important role to Aristides in the initial assessment. His reputation for fairness made the distribution more acceptable to the allies, and the assessment created a working basis for collecting contributions. The new league could then fund continuing operations against Persian positions. It also required administrators, records, and decisions about when common forces would sail. In the years after its formation, the balance within the association changed. Thucydides later described the original assessment as a foundation for the league's tribute, while other ancient accounts emphasized Aristides' role. These sources were written with different interests and at different distances from the first assessment. A cautious account can say what the assessment was for without inventing exact conversations among the allied delegates. Athens increasingly directed its resources and military policy, and some allies resisted obligations they no longer regarded as freely shared. Contributions first presented as support for a common defense became part of a larger dispute about Athenian control. The ancient evidence provides the broad sequence—war against Persia, organization of allies, assessment of ships and money, and the league's later growth—but not a complete ledger for every first-year negotiation. Aristides' task belongs at the beginning of that sequence. Setting terms helped the coalition operate; it did not settle forever the question of who would control the coalition once the immediate fear of invasion diminished.

Interpretive analogy Meng can be used to ask how a new association learns its rules. The Aegean allies needed more than a general promise to resist Persia. They had to decide who would supply ships, who would pay money, and who would keep the records. Aristides' initial assessment gave the league an operating arrangement that members could understand and compare. Later Athenian dominance shows why a workable beginning is not a permanent guarantee of consent. A contribution may be accepted for a common emergency and contested when the purpose or power balance changes. This analogy does not suggest that Aristides read the Zhouyi or that the judgment predicted the league's future. The assessment created a shared starting point, but the power to revise and enforce it became as important as the original calculation. Ancient sources document the assessment and the association's subsequent history. The present comparison invites designers of alliances to make obligations explicit, review them as circumstances change, and listen when members no longer see their contributions serving the purpose that first brought them together.

05 需 | Hexagram 05

EUUS-PM-H05 · Italy, Europe · 217 BCE · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Fabius avoids pitched battle. In 218 BCE Hannibal crossed into Italy with a Carthaginian army, and Roman forces suffered major defeats. The disaster at Lake Trasimene in 217 left Rome looking for a way to resist an opponent who had repeatedly won open battles. The Romans appointed Quintus Fabius Maximus dictator. Rather than seek another decisive encounter, he followed Hannibal's movements, protected positions where he could, and tried to limit the invader's access to supplies. This approach could not prevent every raid or save every allied community. It also looked unsatisfactory to Romans who wanted a visible victory and feared that delay would appear weak. Fabius faced political criticism while maintaining a force that could continue the war. When his extraordinary appointment ended, other Roman commanders took a different path. In 216, a large Roman army met Hannibal at Cannae and suffered a catastrophic defeat. Rome nevertheless continued fighting. Fabius also had to keep Roman allies from losing confidence while Hannibal remained in Italy. His own troops expected leadership, yet he could not offer them the kind of decisive engagement many Romans imagined. This political burden was part of the strategy: preserving the army involved explaining why survival and continued pressure mattered while enemy raids remained visible. It raised new forces, defended its alliances, and gradually applied pressure on Carthaginian holdings beyond the immediate battlefield in Italy. Later writers made Fabius a symbol of delaying strategy, but the war's course was shaped by many commanders, communities, and campaigns. The relevant sequence begins with repeated Roman losses, moves through an attempt to avoid battle on Hannibal's preferred terms, and continues through disagreement about that attempt. His avoidance of a pitched battle did not itself win the war; it preserved an option to fight later and elsewhere while Roman leaders still had to manage the costs of an enemy army in Italy.

Interpretive analogy Xu, often rendered as waiting, can be considered alongside Fabius' conduct after Trasimene. His delay was not inactivity. It involved moving an army, limiting supplies, accepting criticism, and leaving some communities exposed while avoiding another battle on unfavorable terms. The subsequent Roman defeat at Cannae makes the risks of an immediate clash visible, but it does not prove that every decision by Fabius was correct. A present-day political or military reader can ask what an organization is preserving while it waits, who bears the costs, and what conditions would justify a different course. The time gained by delay has to be used. Preserving an army or alliance matters only if it enables an achievable next step under changing conditions. This is a later interpretive comparison, not an account of Roman commanders consulting the Zhouyi. Ancient histories document the war and the debate over strategy; the hexagram provides a question about timing. Waiting should have an aim, a means of sustaining people through the interval, and a point at which the choice can be reviewed.

06 訟 | Hexagram 06

EUUS-PM-H06 · Greece, Europe · 421 BCE · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Peace of Nicias. Athens and Sparta had fought for years when their leaders negotiated what became known as the Peace of Nicias in 421 BCE. The Peloponnesian War had cost both sides men, money, and positions. Earlier attempts to gain a decisive advantage had failed, and the deaths of important commanders changed the political setting for negotiation. The agreement was intended to last fifty years. Its terms provided for the return of prisoners and territories and sought to establish a basis for relations between the two powers. Writing the terms did not make every ally accept them. Some cities had interests that conflicted with what Athens and Sparta had promised each other, and questions about the return of particular places proved difficult. Prisoners could be exchanged, but control of towns and the loyalty of allies required separate action. Rival states continued to search for partners, and the diplomatic map shifted even while the agreement formally existed. The agreement's nominal duration of fifty years made its ambitions plain, but a long term on parchment could not substitute for mutual confidence. Contested places and reluctant allies made each provision a separate test. The ancient account follows attempts to carry out the terms alongside new alignments, showing why implementation was part of the peace rather than a minor detail after it. The war did not end permanently in 421. Athens later mounted its disastrous expedition to Sicily, and direct conflict with Sparta resumed on a larger scale. Thucydides' account allows readers to follow the negotiations and the disputes over implementation rather than treating the treaty as a single moment of peace. The sequence runs from exhaustion and changing leadership, through an agreement between major adversaries, to the continuing failure to settle obligations among all parties affected. The negotiators created a pause and a framework for exchange. They did not remove the causes of mistrust or command every allied city to treat the settlement as final.

Interpretive analogy Song describes contention and the difficulty of carrying a dispute to its end. The Peace of Nicias offers a concrete comparison: Athens and Sparta could sign terms while their allies, territorial claims, and competing strategies remained unsettled. Negotiation changed what the two principal governments said they would do. Implementation required other people to return prisoners, transfer control, and refrain from new alignments. A modern reader can distinguish the value of a pause from the stronger claim that an underlying conflict has been resolved. The analogy also asks whose interests are missing when two large parties define a settlement. A ceasefire and a durable settlement are different outcomes; the treaty's continuing disputes should not be hidden behind its formal date. It does not suggest that the negotiators knew the Zhouyi. Thucydides supplies evidence about the treaty and its troubled aftermath; the relationship to Song is a present-day reading. Where a dispute touches several communities, the terms for stopping must be testable, and the parties need ways to address the obligations that remain after the signatures.

07 師 | Hexagram 07

EUUS-PM-H07 · Greece, Europe · 480 BCE · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Themistocles and Salamis. In 480 BCE a Persian invasion forced the Greek city-states to make difficult choices about where to resist. After fighting at Thermopylae, Persian forces entered Attica and Athens was evacuated. The Athenians had invested in a fleet, and Themistocles pressed the case for continuing resistance at sea. The allied Greek commanders did not always agree about the location of the next battle. Some preferred to defend nearer the Peloponnese; others argued that the narrow waters around Salamis offered a better position against a larger fleet. Greek ships gathered near the island as Persian vessels approached. The battle that followed was fought in constricted water, where the size of the invading fleet could not be used in the same way as on open sea. Greek forces defeated the Persian fleet, while the wider invasion continued on land. Salamis did not end the war in one day. The ships were manned by communities that had already borne the cost of invasion and evacuation. Keeping a fleet assembled required allied cities to accept a common command at the moment of danger. After the battle, the Greeks still needed land forces and supply arrangements. Salamis altered the balance at sea without removing Persian armies from the wider campaign. Greek allies still had to maintain cooperation, defend their cities, and fight further campaigns, including those of the following year. Ancient sources differ in details of speeches and maneuvers, and dramatic stories about Themistocles need to be treated as part of those traditions rather than recorded dialogue. The broad course is clear: a city was evacuated, allied commanders debated a position, ships fought at Salamis, and the coalition continued the war after its naval success. The outcome depended on fleet preparation, command decisions, allies, geography, and the actions of the crews who rowed and fought the ships.

Interpretive analogy Shi, the hexagram of the army, invites a question about coordinated command. At Salamis, allied Greek fleets faced an invading force while their leaders disagreed about the place to fight. Evacuating Athens and assembling ships did not by themselves produce a victory. Crews needed to reach the chosen waters, commanders needed enough common purpose to hold the coalition, and the battle had to be fought under conditions their ships could use. A reader should also keep the aftermath in view: the naval result did not finish the war. The case also draws attention to the people rowing and maintaining ships, whose repeated work made any commander's plan physically possible. The comparison is retrospective; neither Themistocles nor the allies are documented here as users of the Zhouyi. Ancient evidence supports the invasion, evacuation, naval battle, and subsequent campaigns. The hexagram is a way to frame questions about shared plans, discipline, and the limits of a single success, rather than a claim that one ancient text explains the battle.

08 比 | Hexagram 08

EUUS-PM-H08 · Aegean, Europe · 478 BCE · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Creation of the Delian League. After the Persian invasions, Greek cities around the Aegean faced the prospect of further operations against Persian power. The earlier coalition had fought together in an emergency, but maintaining ships, crews, and supplies required a continuing arrangement. Around 478 BCE, several states joined an alliance under Athenian leadership. Its common treasury was placed on Delos, and members were expected to contribute ships or money. A shared defense could now be financed beyond a single campaign season. Athens provided leadership and naval strength, while smaller communities gained a place in a wider military organization. The members' contributions had to be assessed, collected, recorded, and used for operations. The alliance did not remain unchanged. As Athens directed more campaigns, some member cities became less willing to meet obligations or accept its decisions. Athens used force against resistance, and the treasury was later moved from Delos to Athens. The treasury at Delos gave the new association a visible center, but money collected there had to be translated into ships, crews, and campaigns. A city providing cash rather than vessels became dependent on others for naval action. Over time that difference affected its ability to refuse Athenian decisions, a change not settled at the first meeting. What began as a league organized against Persia became increasingly bound to Athenian power. The source record shows both the initial association and the later tensions, without letting every member's view be reduced to one motive. The sequence starts with a common external threat, proceeds to a funded and organized naval coalition, and continues into arguments over authority and consent. An alliance helped members act together, but the institution also created a durable mechanism for extracting resources. Its later direction depended on choices made after the first emergency had passed, not simply on the terms announced at its beginning.

Interpretive analogy Bi can suggest drawing together, which makes the Delian League an instructive retrospective comparison. The member cities initially needed ships, money, and a recognizable center for continuing operations. Acting together increased their reach. Yet the same arrangements that made cooperation possible gave Athens a way to direct contributions and punish resistance. The analogy asks whether an alliance's members retain a meaningful voice once they have made a common commitment. It also asks how often the purpose and cost of membership are reconsidered. This is not evidence that Athenian or other Greek leaders consulted the Zhouyi. The comparison is most useful when it follows an alliance beyond its founding ceremony and asks how members can question its evolving use. Ancient sources document the league's formation and subsequent transformation; the connection to Bi is editorial. For present-day readers, the case shows that unity is sustained by more than a shared enemy. Members need transparent obligations, credible procedures for disagreement, and a continuing reason to regard the institution as their own.

09 小畜 | Hexagram 09

EUUS-PM-H09 · North America / British empire · 1754 · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Albany Plan of Union. In 1754, competition between Britain and France in North America raised urgent questions about colonial defense and relations with Indigenous nations. Delegates from several British colonies met at Albany, where officials sought better coordination. Benjamin Franklin and others considered a plan for a general colonial government that could manage common defense and certain wider affairs. The proposed Albany Plan of Union would have created a president general appointed by the Crown and a grand council chosen through the colonial assemblies. It was an attempt to organize action across colonies that otherwise made many decisions separately. Delegates debated and approved a version of the proposal, but approval at the meeting did not make it law. Colonial assemblies worried about yielding authority, and officials in Britain had their own objections. The plan was not adopted by the governments whose support it needed. War with France nevertheless expanded, and the colonies continued to face shared military demands without the union the Albany delegates had proposed. The Albany meeting also concerned relations with the Haudenosaunee, whose interests were not identical to those of the colonial delegates. The union plan cannot stand in for their agreements or decisions. The proposed council's allocation of authority would have changed how colonial governments handled defense, which helps explain why approval by a conference was insufficient for adoption. The episode later became part of American discussions about intercolonial cooperation, but the later federal constitution was made under different circumstances and cannot be treated as the direct implementation of the 1754 design. The sequence begins with an imperial rivalry and a meeting about defense, moves to a concrete institutional proposal, and ends with that proposal's failure to win the necessary approvals. Its immediate result was not a new government. It left a record of how delegates had tried to turn a common danger into a standing arrangement before a much larger conflict fully shaped their choices.

Interpretive analogy Xiao Xu points to the accumulation of limited resources and the difficulty of holding them together. At Albany, delegates proposed a common structure before the colonies had accepted one. The plan was detailed enough to identify a council and an executive role, but its authors could not supply the consent of colonial assemblies or British authorities merely by agreeing among themselves. That gap matters more than an easy story about a successful founding. A retrospective reading asks what smaller acts of preparation can do when a larger crisis is approaching, and what approvals are still missing. The proposal's failure is part of the story, because it reveals where consent and authority actually resided in 1754. It does not claim Franklin or the delegates took guidance from the Zhouyi. The meeting and the rejected proposal are historical events; the hexagram is a modern interpretive frame. Coordinating early can reveal a shared problem, but a proposal becomes an institution only when the people and governments expected to use it accept its powers and costs.

EUUS-PM-H10 · British empire / America · 1763–1775 · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Parliamentary taxation and colonial protest. After the Seven Years' War, Britain faced debts and the cost of maintaining authority across a larger North American empire. Parliament adopted new taxes and trade measures, including the Stamp Act of 1765 and later duties on imported goods. Many colonists objected that they were being taxed by a legislature in which they had no elected representatives. Merchants organized boycotts, colonial assemblies issued protests, and British ministers sometimes withdrew a measure while keeping the claim that Parliament could legislate for the colonies. Each partial retreat left the larger constitutional disagreement in place. The Tea Act and the destruction of tea in Boston brought further punishment and resistance. In 1774, Parliament's coercive measures against Massachusetts helped prompt colonies to send delegates to the First Continental Congress. Colonial leaders did not all seek independence at the outset. They argued over rights within the empire, representation, obedience, and how to respond to enforcement. The conflict was shaped by enforcement as well as by statutes. Customs officials, merchants, printers, and colonial assemblies all became involved as legislation reached individual ports and towns. British ministers sought revenue and imperial control, while different colonial leaders argued over the constitutional meaning of representation. Those arguments changed with each episode and cannot be compressed into one unchanging complaint held by everyone throughout the decade. British authorities also faced choices about whether to compromise or use force. By 1775, armed confrontations at Lexington and Concord had changed the dispute. The line from taxation to war was not a single inevitable step. It ran through legislation, petition, boycott, repeal, renewed assertion of authority, punishment, collective colonial action, and fighting. Parliamentary records and colonial documents preserve the public measures and arguments, though they cannot give one motive to every participant. The crisis shows how repeated decisions on both sides narrowed the room for an agreed political relationship.

Interpretive analogy Lu, often associated with careful conduct under risk, can be read beside Britain's escalating dispute with its colonies. A duty or administrative rule could look manageable when considered alone, yet each measure interacted with a larger claim about who had authority. Colonial resistance also grew through successive choices rather than one unanimous decision. The analogy asks leaders to trace what a step will mean to the people subject to it and what options will remain after the response. It does not say Parliament or the Continental Congress followed the Zhouyi. Careful conduct includes listening to how a rule is received and whether the institutions applying it can still command legitimate cooperation. The legislation, protests, and outbreak of fighting have their own documentary history. The hexagram supplies an editorial question about proceeding with care when ordinary-looking moves carry constitutional consequences. A useful lesson from the sequence is to review the dispute that a policy embodies, the likely response to its enforcement, and the space left for negotiation after each side acts.

Historical event Continental Congress. In 1774, British measures following the Boston Tea Party sharpened the conflict between imperial authorities and the North American colonies. Delegates from twelve colonies met in Philadelphia as the First Continental Congress. They did not yet govern an independent country. They drafted petitions, coordinated a boycott, and tried to present a shared position while their colonies retained different interests and instructions. Fighting at Lexington and Concord in 1775 changed the setting for the Second Continental Congress. Delegates now had to support an army, appoint George Washington to command it, seek supplies, and debate the colonies' political future. In 1776, Congress declared independence, but a declaration did not equip soldiers or secure foreign recognition. Congress continued to issue resolutions, seek loans and allies, manage scarce resources, and argue over how the states should cooperate. The Articles of Confederation were drafted and eventually ratified in 1781, giving the association a formal framework while leaving significant powers with the states. The delegates also had to communicate decisions to communities separated by long distances and uneven wartime conditions. Congress could resolve to raise troops or issue paper money, but states and citizens had to provide the people and goods. This dependence made coordination a continuous task rather than an achievement completed with the first session. The wartime forum continued meeting even while its members changed and the conflict spread. Throughout the war, decisions made in Philadelphia had to be carried out by state governments, commanders, and local communities. The Continental Congress was therefore a continuing forum rather than a single meeting that settled every question. Its story runs from a common protest within the empire, through the need to coordinate armed resistance, to an independent union with unresolved problems of finance and authority. The delegates made shared decisions, but agreement on a goal did not erase disagreements about contributions, representation, and the powers of a common government.

Interpretive analogy Tai can suggest conditions in which communication and cooperation move more freely. The Continental Congress illustrates how delegates from different colonies built a channel for common decisions. Their first measures concerned protest and trade; war then forced them to address command, supplies, diplomacy, and the meaning of independence. The association gained strength when its members could state a shared aim, but its decisions still depended on states and communities for execution. A retrospective reading asks what makes cooperation workable after the initial agreement and how a common body deals with members who retain separate powers. Shared language can begin cooperation, yet the member communities must repeatedly decide whether to supply the means that common decisions require. No source shows that Congress used the Zhouyi in framing its actions. The documents establish its meetings and decisions; the link to Tai is a modern analogy. It should lead readers to examine channels of communication, public purpose, and the ordinary work needed to keep an alliance active when its members disagree.

Historical event Secret Committee of Correspondence. When fighting began between Britain and the colonies in 1775, the Continental Congress needed arms, supplies, and possible partners abroad. Open diplomatic recognition of an independent United States was not yet available, and European governments had their own calculations about entering a conflict with Britain. Congress created a Committee of Secret Correspondence to establish channels with people overseas. Its members contacted agents and intermediaries, sought information, and explored whether foreign support could be obtained without an immediate public alliance. Correspondence had to travel across the Atlantic, where messages could be delayed, intercepted, or overtaken by events. The secret planning made the public ultimatum especially controversial. Britain and France faced pressure not only from Washington but also from financial markets and debates at home. A ceasefire stopped their immediate advance, while the canal's operation and regional security still had to be addressed. Egypt's nationalization remained in place. The governments' different aims and the role of the United Nations shaped withdrawal over several stages rather than one simultaneous retreat. The sequence runs from nationalization, through a secretly coordinated plan and invasion, to an international response and retreat. The three attacking governments did not achieve a stable political settlement by gaining ground. Britain's and France's dependence on external financial and diplomatic conditions limited their room to continue. The crisis also changed how their power was seen in relation to the United States and to states seeking independence from older imperial influence. Historical sources record the plan, fighting, pressure, and withdrawal; none of those stages should be replaced by a simple tale of one side winning the canal.

Interpretive analogy Zhong Fu can be read as a question about trust between stated purpose and actual conduct. Britain and France publicly presented intervention as a way to separate forces, while the prior coordination with Israel became central to later understanding of the operation. U.S. opposition and UN action showed that military movement alone could not secure broad acceptance. A retrospective analogy asks how credibility is damaged when public reasons diverge from the sequence of decisions and how an ally responds when partners act without its support. Trust can be tested against the dated sequence of private agreements, public statements, and military moves. The comparison asks readers to keep these records alongside the official explanation rather than choosing one slogan as the whole story. It does not suggest that any participant used the Zhouyi. Diplomatic records, military events, and withdrawal orders provide the history. The hexagram is an editorial lens for examining whether words, commitments, and actions can be held together under scrutiny.

Evidence note: The source supports the event, not a claim that participants used the Zhouyi. Historical source ↗

62 小過 | Hexagram 62

EUUS-PM-H62 · United States / Europe security · 1972 · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event SALT I agreements. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, the United States and Soviet Union possessed large nuclear arsenals and continued developing strategic weapons. Leaders in both countries faced the danger that competitive deployments could grow without clear limits. Negotiators opened Strategic Arms Limitation Talks, known as SALT, in 1969. Technical discussions examined missiles, launchers, defensive systems, and the problem of verifying what each side possessed. In 1972, President Richard Nixon and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signed an Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty and an interim agreement limiting certain strategic offensive launchers. The accords did not eliminate nuclear weapons or stop every form of modernization. Some weapons and later technological changes remained outside the initial limits. Each side had to interpret the text, use available means to monitor compliance, and continue discussing unresolved issues. The ABM Treaty limited defensive missile systems in specified ways, while the interim agreement addressed certain launchers for a limited period. Negotiators had to distinguish existing weapons from new technologies and consider whether a restriction on one category might redirect competition into another. Later talks were necessary because the first accords could not freeze every strategic innovation. Their scope was deliberately narrower than the total nuclear danger. The talks did not put a single ceiling on all weapons held by either side. The agreements formed part of a broader period of détente, while rivalry and conflict through other regions persisted. The sequence begins with a dangerous accumulation of strategic arms, moves through prolonged talks over measurable categories, and reaches specific written limits that required continued observance. SALT I was an initial step, not the conclusion of the arms race. Its history is in the negotiated text and subsequent conduct rather than a claim that personal trust between two leaders made verification unnecessary. Narrow limits could matter even when the wider political relationship remained competitive.

Interpretive analogy Xiao Guo can suggest careful progress through limited acts. SALT I did not resolve the nuclear rivalry; it defined particular categories and constrained some of them. The negotiations required both sides to specify what could be counted and how compliance would be assessed. A retrospective analogy asks whether a modest, verifiable restriction can reduce one danger while larger disagreements remain, and whether leaders can resist presenting an initial step as a finished peace. A small agreement is worth examining for what it counts, what it leaves outside, and how both sides can observe performance without relying on private assurances. What is omitted matters as much as what is counted. It does not attribute the agreements to use of the Zhouyi. Negotiating records and treaty provisions establish the historical case. The hexagram is a modern editorial lens for proportion: a small measure can have real value if its scope is clear and its limits are honestly stated.

Evidence note: The source supports the event, not a claim that participants used the Zhouyi. Historical source ↗

63 既濟 | Hexagram 63

EUUS-PM-H63 · Europe / United States · 1975 · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Helsinki Final Act. In 1975, leaders of European states, the United States, Canada, and the Soviet Union concluded the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe with the Helsinki Final Act. The negotiations addressed borders, relations among states, economic and humanitarian contacts, and human rights principles. Participants did not all share the same political system or the same reasons for signing. Western governments emphasized rights and freer contact; Soviet leaders gave weight to security and recognition of postwar frontiers. The Final Act was a political commitment, not a treaty that could be enforced by a single international court. Its publication nevertheless provided language that governments and citizens could refer to. In later years, human rights groups in Eastern Europe invoked the commitments when documenting abuses, while governments met in follow-up conferences to review implementation. The Final Act included a commitment to respect existing frontiers alongside language about rights and contacts across borders. Those elements appealed to governments for different reasons. Monitoring groups later referred to the same public document when reporting restrictions on speech and movement. Governments could dispute interpretations, but they could not easily deny having endorsed the text. Follow-up meetings provided a place to raise the gap between written commitments and observed practice. The agreements remained available for public reference after the conference closed. That text endured. The text did not end repression or Cold War rivalry in 1975. It created an agreed standard that people could use to compare public promises with state behavior. The sequence runs from prolonged negotiation among adversaries, through signature, to monitoring and argument about what the signatories had undertaken. The participating countries accepted several baskets of commitments rather than one simple bargain. The aftermath matters because the act's political influence depended on people reading, citing, and contesting its words long after the leaders had left Helsinki.

Interpretive analogy Ji Ji can suggest something apparently brought to completion that still needs care. The Helsinki Final Act marked the end of negotiations and set out common language, but governments and citizens then disagreed about observance. Human rights groups used the signed commitments as a standard against which to measure conduct, while follow-up meetings kept the text in public circulation. A retrospective analogy asks what must be watched after an agreement is celebrated and who is able to call attention to noncompliance. Completion of negotiations creates a new obligation to compare conduct with text. The case warns against confusing a widely signed standard with immediate and uniform compliance in every state. It does not imply that the signatories read the Zhouyi. The signed document and later monitoring provide the history. The hexagram is an editorial frame for the danger of calling a political task finished at the moment of signature when the effects depend on continued scrutiny.

Evidence note: The source supports the event, not a claim that participants used the Zhouyi. Historical source ↗

64 未濟 | Hexagram 64

EUUS-PM-H64 · Eastern Europe / United States · 1989 · Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY

Historical event Fall of communist rule in Eastern Europe. In 1989, communist governments across Eastern Europe faced growing public demands for political change. The events did not follow one script. In Poland, negotiations helped bring partly free elections that produced a major victory for the opposition. In Hungary, reforms changed the political system and contributed to the opening of routes across its border. East Germans protested and left the country in large numbers; on November 9, confused announcements and public pressure led to the opening of crossings in the Berlin Wall. In Czechoslovakia, mass demonstrations and negotiations brought a transfer of power. Romania experienced violent conflict and the fall of Nicolae Ceaușescu. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev did not use the force that had supported earlier interventions in the region, though local decisions and conditions varied greatly. The sequence across the year runs from reform and protest, through elections, border openings, and negotiations, to the collapse or transformation of ruling parties in several states. The transformation was uneven even within a single year. Some ruling parties negotiated an exit; others lost control when crowds gathered and police or security forces could no longer impose the previous arrangements. New leaders then faced elections, constitutional revision, economic shortages, and the future of security alliances. The Soviet decision not to repeat earlier military interventions shaped the regional setting, but local organizations and citizens made distinct choices in each country. The next year's German reunification marked one further result, not the end of every transition. The end of one-party rule did not finish economic restructuring, constitutional design, or the question of Germany's future. German reunification followed in 1990, and other countries took different paths. The historical record is a collection of national stories connected by regional and Soviet change, not one coordinated American plan or a single night at the Berlin Wall. People in the countries concerned made the central decisions and bore their consequences.

Interpretive analogy Wei Ji can suggest a crossing still under way. The fall of communist rule in 1989 changed governments, opened borders, and brought elections, but it did not deliver one completed political or economic model across Eastern Europe. Poland's negotiations, East Germany's wall opening, and Romania's violence followed different courses. A retrospective analogy asks readers to distinguish an old order's end from the work of creating accountable institutions, and to keep local agency visible. The threshold is important because it opens choices without guaranteeing their outcomes. A retrospective comparison should follow the work of building institutions after the dramatic event, and should distinguish each country's path from the regional shorthand of 1989. It does not say the participants used the Zhouyi or that an American government directed every change. Elections, protests, official decisions, and later reforms form the historical record. The hexagram is an editorial lens for unfinished transitions: a dramatic threshold can be real while the outcomes beyond it remain uncertain and different from place to place.

Evidence note: The source supports the event, not a claim that participants used the Zhouyi. Historical source ↗

384 Line Cases

Line 1 | TW-PM-H01-L1 | XIANG-U-01-02

001爻 Historical event Charlemagne crowned emperor. By the late eighth century, Charlemagne ruled a Frankish kingdom enlarged through successive campaigns and alliances. He had crossed the Alps more than once to support the papacy, while Rome itself was troubled by a dispute over Pope Leo III. After opponents attacked Leo in 799, the pope sought Charlemagne's protection. The Frankish ruler came to Rome in 800, where an inquiry addressed accusations against Leo and the pope publicly asserted his innocence. On Christmas Day, during worship at St Peter's, Leo placed a crown on Charlemagne's head and the assembled people acclaimed him emperor. The ceremony gave a new title to a ruler who already commanded extensive territory and armies. It also linked the Frankish court and the Roman church more closely, while raising questions about the meaning of imperial authority in a world that also had an emperor at Constantinople. Charlemagne returned to the work of ruling from his own court. Officials carried instructions into different parts of the realm, bishops and counts took part in governance, and campaigns continued along contested frontiers. The crown did not create those institutions overnight. It marked a public claim that had to operate through the people and structures already available. Relations with Byzantium remained a diplomatic issue after the ceremony; recognition of Charlemagne's imperial title was negotiated in the years that followed. After the coronation, Charlemagne ordered a new oath of fidelity in 802. Royal envoys inspected local administration and carried instructions into regions governed through counts and ecclesiastical authorities. Members of the royal family also held responsibilities in different parts of the realm. In 812, an embassy from Constantinople recognized his imperial title following negotiations over the relationship between the two empires. In 813, Louis was associated with the imperial office at Aachen, before succeeding his father the following year. When he died in 814, succession passed to his son Louis, and the political order he had assembled faced the ordinary problems of inheritance and regional power.

Line-specific comparison The hidden dragon places capability below public authority. Before the coronation, Charlemagne already possessed a kingdom and military resources. Read this line through that earlier preparation, when a title had not yet publicly expressed the ruler's position. By the late eighth century, Charlemagne ruled a Frankish kingdom enlarged through successive campaigns and alliances. He had crossed the Alps more than once to support the papacy, while Rome itself was troubled by a dispute over Pope Leo III. After opponents attacked Leo in 799, the pope sought Charlemagne's protection. The Frankish ruler came to Rome in 800, where an inquiry addressed accusations against Leo and the pope publicly asserted his innocence. On Christmas Day, during worship at St Peter's, Leo placed a crown on Charlemagne's head and the assembled people acclaimed him emperor. What must exist before a public claim becomes credible? This is a present-day comparison. The historical source documents the event, not the participants’ use of this line or the Ten Wings.

Evidence: RETROSPECTIVE ANALOGY. Source confirms the event only. Historical reference ↗

Line 1 | TW-PM-H02-L1 | XIANG-U-02-02

007爻 Historical event Solon's reforms at Athens. In archaic Athens, debt and unequal access to land and political power had deepened conflict between poorer residents and established families. Some Athenians could lose their freedom through obligations secured on their own persons. Around 594 BCE, Solon was given authority to mediate and legislate amid this crisis. He cancelled existing debts of the kind that bound people, prohibited future loans secured on the debtor's person, and arranged for some who had been sold away to return. He did not redistribute all land, a demand that would have satisfied one side while sharply threatening another. His settlement also reorganized political participation by property classes, opening certain civic roles while reserving the highest offices for wealthier groups. A council and courts formed part of the revised arrangements, though the exact operation of early Athenian institutions is reconstructed from later accounts. Solon published laws that citizens would have to use after he left office. The measures changed the immediate terms of debt and public life, but they did not erase differences of wealth or end factional rivalry. Solon's measures also changed participation in public affairs. Property classes affected eligibility for offices, while citizens gained access to procedures for challenging judgments. The surviving traditions describe restrictions on debt bondage alongside these legal arrangements. Solon subsequently left Athens, and factions continued to contend for influence after his departure. Peisistratus later established a tyranny through repeated attempts to seize power. The city therefore continued under changing political leadership after the legislation, rather than settling immediately into the democracy familiar from its later history. Later Athens passed through further struggles, including tyranny, before another round of institutional reform. Their accounts are written after the event and do not let us watch every assembly or negotiation. Ancient authors do not agree on every detail of the reforms, and later Athenians reworked the political system.

Line-specific comparison Frost precedes hard ice through an accumulating process. Athenian debt bondage and social conflict can be read as mounting conditions that preceded Solon's appointment. Line 1 | TW-PM-H03-L1 | XIANG-U-03-02

013爻 Historical event Cleisthenes' tribal reforms. After the fall of the Peisistratid tyranny, Athens did not immediately settle on a stable civic order. Leading families competed, and Isagoras gained the archonship while Cleisthenes sought support among the broader citizen body. Isagoras called on the Spartan king Cleomenes. With Spartan backing, opponents of Cleisthenes expelled families and tried to replace existing political arrangements. Athenians resisted the intervention, besieged the occupying group on the Acropolis, and recalled Cleisthenes and other exiles. Cleisthenes then recast the basis of civic membership. Instead of relying on four older tribes tied to established affiliations, he formed ten tribes whose components drew on urban, inland, and coastal districts. Local demes became important units of identification and public registration. A council of five hundred, with members drawn from the new tribes, gave the reorganized citizen body a continuing institution for public business. These measures spread political connections across different parts of Attica, but they did not extend equal civic rights to every resident. Women, enslaved people, and many noncitizens remained outside the citizen framework. The reforms also came out of conflict, not a calm founding ceremony. They had to be enacted after an attempted intervention and then used in elections, councils, military organization, and local records. Later ancient accounts describe both the struggle with Isagoras and the new arrangements, though historians still scrutinize their details. The order of events matters: factional contest drew outside force into Athens; local resistance reopened politics; Cleisthenes' reforms supplied new units through which citizens could act. The resulting democracy developed further in later decades rather than arriving complete in a single year. The new tribes combined residents from different regions, making older local and familial alignments less decisive in the formal organization of civic life. Demes maintained their own registers, so the change reached beyond the central assembly and into the way citizens were identified in ordinary public business. The reorganized tribes also became the basis for a council of five hundred, with representation divided among the ten tribes. Citizens entered public life through their demes, which registered their membership. The institutions developed through later conflicts and reforms, including changes in the role of the assembly and other governing bodies. Women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners remained outside political citizenship. Political participation widened within the citizen body while these exclusions continued.

019爻 Historical event Aristides and allied contributions. After the Persian invasions of Greece, many Aegean communities still feared renewed attacks and needed a way to maintain ships and campaigns. The leadership of the Greek coalition shifted toward Athens as dissatisfaction with Spartan commander Pausanias grew. Allied cities met in a new association whose treasury was placed on Delos. Members could provide ships or make monetary contributions for the common effort. 025爻 Historical event Fabius avoids pitched battle. In 218 BCE Hannibal crossed into Italy with a Carthaginian army, and Roman forces suffered major defeats. The disaster at Lake Trasimene in 217 left Rome looking for a way to resist an opponent who had repeatedly won open battles. The Romans appointed Quintus Fabius Maximus dictator. Rather than seek another decisive encounter, he followed Hannibal's movements, protected positions where he could, and tried to limit the invader's access to supplies. This approach could not prevent every raid or save every allied community. It also looked unsatisfactory to Romans who wanted a visible victory and feared that delay would appear weak. Fabius faced political criticism while maintaining a force that could continue the war. When his extraordinary appointment ended, other Roman commanders took a different path. In 216, a large Roman army met Hannibal at Cannae and suffered a catastrophic defeat. Rome nevertheless continued fighting. It raised new forces, defended its alliances, and gradually applied pressure on Carthaginian holdings beyond the immediate battlefield in Italy. Fabius also had to keep Roman allies from losing confidence while Hannibal remained in Italy. His soldiers remained in the field while he followed Hannibal and avoided a decisive engagement against the Carthaginian army. Rome's effort later extended to operations in Spain and eventually to North Africa under Scipio. Hannibal remained in Italy for years while the Romans continued raising forces and holding or recovering allied communities. Fabius again served in high office and recovered Tarentum in 209 BCE. He died in 203 BCE, before the final Roman victory. Other commanders continued leading forces in Italy and overseas as the war approached its conclusion. The Carthaginians ultimately recalled Hannibal to defend North Africa. His defeat at Zama in 202 was followed by a peace that imposed substantial obligations on Carthage and ended the Second Punic War.

Line-specific comparison Waiting outside the danger preserves an ordinary course of action. Fabius' avoidance of Hannibal's preferred battlefield provides a close retrospective comparison: distance can keep an army available, even while raids and political criticism make waiting costly. 031爻 Historical event Peace of Nicias. Athens and Sparta had fought for years when their leaders negotiated what became known as the Peace of Nicias in 421 BCE. The Peloponnesian War had cost both sides men, money, and positions. Earlier attempts to gain a decisive advantage had failed, and the deaths of important commanders changed the political setting for negotiation. The agreement was intended to last fifty years. Its terms provided for the return of prisoners and territories and sought to establish a basis for relations between the two powers. Writing the terms did not make every ally accept them. Some cities had interests that conflicted with what Athens and Sparta had promised each other, and questions about the return of particular places proved difficult. Prisoners could be exchanged, but control of towns and the loyalty of allies required separate action. Rival states continued to search for partners, and the diplomatic map shifted even while the agreement formally existed. The war did not end permanently in 421. Athens later mounted its disastrous expedition to Sicily, and direct conflict with Sparta resumed on a larger scale. The negotiators created a pause and a framework for exchange. They did not remove the causes of mistrust or command every allied city to treat the settlement as final. Contested places and reluctant allies made each provision a separate test. The truce did not bring every allied city into agreement. Disputes over territory and the return of prisoners complicated relations, and new alignments linked Athens with other states hostile to Sparta. Fighting at Mantinea in 418 BCE altered those relationships. Athens subsequently undertook its expedition against Sicily, where Nicias became one of the commanders. That expedition ended in defeat in 413. The war between Athens and Sparta continued until the Athenian surrender in 404, long before the peace's announced fifty-year term could be completed.

037爻 Historical event Themistocles and Salamis. In 480 BCE a Persian invasion forced the Greek city-states to make difficult choices about where to resist. After fighting at Thermopylae, Persian forces entered Attica and Athens was evacuated. The Athenians had invested in a fleet, and Themistocles pressed the case for continuing resistance at sea. The allied Greek commanders did not always agree about the location of the next battle. Some preferred to defend nearer the Peloponnese; others argued that the narrow waters around Salamis offered a better position against a larger fleet. Greek ships gathered near the island as Persian vessels approached. The battle that followed was fought in constricted water, where the size of the invading fleet could not be used in the same way as on open sea. Greek forces defeated the Persian fleet, while the wider invasion continued on land. Salamis did not end the war in one day. Greek allies still had to maintain cooperation, defend their cities, and fight further campaigns, including those of the following year. The broad course is clear: a city was evacuated, allied commanders debated a position, ships fought at Salamis, and the coalition continued the war after its naval success. The outcome depended on fleet preparation, command decisions, allies, geography, and the actions of the crews who rowed and fought the ships. The ships were manned by communities that had already borne the cost of invasion and evacuation. Keeping a fleet assembled required allied cities to accept a common command at the moment of danger. After the battle, the Greeks still needed land forces and supply arrangements. Salamis altered the balance at sea without removing Persian armies from the wider campaign. After the naval defeat, Xerxes returned toward Asia with part of the Persian forces. Mardonius remained in Greece with an army and continued the campaign the following year. Greek forces defeated him at Plataea in 479 BCE, while another Greek victory followed at Mycale. Cities then faced questions about rebuilding and the organization of future defense. Athens restored its position and developed its naval role within the alliance that emerged after the invasions.

Line-specific comparison An army needs order before it moves; loss of discipline is dangerous. The Greek fleet at Salamis required cooperation among contingents with different leaders. This line directs attention to command and coordinated action before admiration for the eventual victory. 043爻 Historical event Creation of the Delian League. After the Persian invasions, Greek cities around the Aegean faced the prospect of further operations against Persian power. The earlier coalition had fought together in an emergency, but maintaining ships, crews, and supplies required a continuing arrangement. Around 478 BCE, several states joined an alliance under Athenian leadership. Its common treasury was placed on Delos, and members were expected to contribute ships or money. A shared defense could now be financed beyond a single campaign season. Athens provided leadership and naval strength, while smaller communities gained a place in a wider military organization. The members' contributions had to be assessed, collected, recorded, and used for operations. The alliance did not remain unchanged. As Athens directed more campaigns, some member cities became less willing to meet obligations or accept its decisions. Athens used force against resistance, and the treasury was later moved from Delos to Athens. What began as a league organized against Persia became increasingly bound to Athenian power. An alliance helped members act together, but the institution also created a durable mechanism for extracting resources. Its later direction depended on choices made after the first emergency had passed, not simply on the terms announced at its beginning. The treasury at Delos gave the new association a visible center, but money collected there had to be translated into ships, crews, and campaigns. A city providing cash rather than vessels became dependent on others for naval action. Over time that difference affected its ability to refuse Athenian decisions, a change not settled at the first meeting. In later decades, Athens suppressed revolts and required contributions from cities that sought to withdraw. Allied ships increasingly gave way to cash payments in many participating communities. The transfer of the treasury to Athens strengthened the connection between league resources and Athenian administration. Disputes over those resources and the obligations of membership continued as relations with Sparta deteriorated. The alliance remained a major instrument of Athenian power during the conflicts of the fifth century BCE.

Line-specific comparison The beginning of attachment can bring further favorable connections. The Delian League formed through cities joining a shared defense effort. Line 1 | TW-PM-H09-L1 | XIANG-U-09-02

049爻 Historical event Albany Plan of Union. In 1754, competition between Britain and France in North America raised urgent questions about colonial defense and relations with Indigenous nations. Delegates from several British colonies met at Albany, where officials sought better coordination. Benjamin Franklin and others considered a plan for a general colonial government that could manage common defense and certain wider affairs. The proposed Albany Plan of Union would have created a president general appointed by the Crown and a grand council chosen through the colonial assemblies. It was an attempt to organize action across colonies that otherwise made many decisions separately. Delegates debated and approved a version of the proposal, but approval at the meeting did not make it law. Colonial assemblies worried about yielding authority, and officials in Britain had their own objections. The plan was not adopted by the governments whose support it needed. War with France nevertheless expanded, and the colonies continued to face shared military demands without the union the Albany delegates had proposed. Its immediate result was not a new government. It left a record of how delegates had tried to turn a common danger into a standing arrangement before a much larger conflict fully shaped their choices. The Albany meeting also concerned relations with the Haudenosaunee, whose interests were not identical to those of the colonial delegates. After the meeting ended in July 1754, delegates returned to governments that retained their separate authority and had not transferred their governing powers to a continental body. No general president or grand council took office under the proposed plan, and the colonies continued to raise forces through their existing arrangements. Britain sent military forces to North America as the conflict expanded into the Seven Years' War. Later disputes over the costs of imperial defense emerged after that war. The colonies eventually coordinated resistance through congresses formed under circumstances different from those of the Albany meeting.

Line-specific comparison Returning along one's own proper path suggests recovering a sound basis for action. The Albany delegates could propose common defense, but adoption still required authority from colonial and imperial institutions. 055爻 Historical event Parliamentary taxation and colonial protest. After the Seven Years' War, Britain faced debts and the cost of maintaining authority across a larger North American empire. Parliament adopted new taxes and trade measures, including the Stamp Act of 1765 and later duties on imported goods. Many colonists objected that they were being taxed by a legislature in which they had no elected representatives. Merchants organized boycotts, colonial assemblies issued protests, and British ministers sometimes withdrew a measure while keeping the claim that Parliament could legislate for the colonies. Each partial retreat left the larger constitutional disagreement in place. The Tea Act and the destruction of tea in Boston brought further punishment and resistance. In 1774, Parliament's coercive measures against Massachusetts helped prompt colonies to send delegates to the First Continental Congress. Colonial leaders did not all seek independence at the outset. They argued over rights within the empire, representation, obedience, and how to respond to enforcement. British authorities also faced choices about whether to compromise or use force. By 1775, armed confrontations at Lexington and Concord had changed the dispute. The line from taxation to war was not a single inevitable step. It ran through legislation, petition, boycott, repeal, renewed assertion of authority, punishment, collective colonial action, and fighting. The conflict was shaped by enforcement as well as by statutes. Customs officials, merchants, printers, and colonial assemblies all became involved as legislation reached individual ports and towns. British ministers sought revenue and imperial control, while different colonial leaders argued over the constitutional meaning of representation. Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766 while asserting its authority through the Declaratory Act. Later duties and their enforcement produced further boycotts and confrontations. In 1773, Parliament's Tea Act was followed by the destruction of tea in Boston. Measures imposed in response closed the port and changed Massachusetts's governing arrangements. Colonial delegates then assembled in Philadelphia in 1774. The dispute moved from individual tax measures into organized intercolonial resistance and, in 1775, armed conflict.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H11-L1 | XIANG-U-11-02

061爻 Historical event Continental Congress. In 1774, British measures following the Boston Tea Party sharpened the conflict between imperial authorities and the North American colonies. Delegates from twelve colonies met in Philadelphia as the First Continental Congress. They did not yet govern an independent country. They drafted petitions, coordinated a boycott, and tried to present a shared position while their colonies retained different interests and instructions. Fighting at Lexington and Concord in 1775 changed the setting for the Second Continental Congress. Delegates now had to support an army, appoint George Washington to command it, seek supplies, and debate the colonies' political future. In 1776, Congress declared independence, but a declaration did not equip soldiers or secure foreign recognition. The Articles of Confederation were drafted and eventually ratified in 1781, giving the association a formal framework while leaving significant powers with the states. Throughout the war, decisions made in Philadelphia had to be carried out by state governments, commanders, and local communities. The delegates made shared decisions, but agreement on a goal did not erase disagreements about contributions, representation, and the powers of a common government. The delegates also had to communicate decisions to communities separated by long distances and uneven wartime conditions. Congress could resolve to raise troops or issue paper money, but states and citizens had to provide the people and goods. The wartime forum continued meeting even while its members changed and the conflict spread. Congress's diplomatic responsibilities expanded with independence and the pursuit of foreign assistance. Representatives negotiated with France, and Congress dealt with loans, military supply, and the terms of an eventual peace. Meanwhile, state governments continued administering many matters within their own territories. The Articles of Confederation took effect in March 1781, replacing the earlier congressional arrangement with a ratified framework. The Confederation Congress then continued the national work as the war approached its conclusion and peace negotiations followed.

Line-specific comparison Pulling one root draws connected roots with it. The Continental Congress grew from colonies coordinating their response to imperial measures. The comparison concerns linked participation: one community's action could invite others into a common undertaking. 067爻 Historical event Secret Committee of Correspondence. When fighting began between Britain and the colonies in 1775, the Continental Congress needed arms, supplies, and possible partners abroad. Open diplomatic recognition of an independent United States was not yet available, and European governments had their own calculations about entering a conflict with Britain. Congress created a Committee of Secret Correspondence to establish channels with people overseas. Its members contacted agents and intermediaries, sought information, and explored whether foreign support could be obtained without an immediate public alliance. Correspondence had to travel across the Atlantic, where messages could be delayed, intercepted, or overtaken by events. The committee's work developed alongside Congress's wider decisions about military command and independence. After the 1776 declaration, American representatives could make a clearer claim to act for a new state, but they still needed money, matériel, and recognition. France initially provided forms of assistance short of the open alliance concluded in 1778. Congress also reorganized its diplomatic work as the war continued, so the first committee was not a permanent foreign ministry. Historical records document committees, correspondence, and later agreements. They do not show a hidden, uninterrupted master plan or make every European contact an immediate success. The committee provided a practical means of keeping possibilities open while the status of the American cause remained contested. Contacts abroad involved uncertainty about whom an intermediary represented and what a foreign government was actually willing to supply. Letters and missions could explore possibilities without binding France or other states to a public commitment. The committee's work thus belonged to a period in which American leaders sought help while the legal and military future of their cause was still unresolved. In April 1777, Congress renamed the body the Committee for Foreign Affairs. Its responsibilities continued while commissioners negotiated in Europe and Congress dealt with the war in America. Disputes among representatives complicated the work, and the committee's members also had other congressional duties. In 1781, Congress established executive departments and selected Robert R. Livingston as secretary for foreign affairs. Diplomatic administration moved from the earlier committee into a more continuous departmental arrangement while representatives abroad continued negotiating.
