Line 1 | TW-PM-H13-L1 | XIANG-U-13-02

073爻 Historical event Declaration of Independence. By 1776, fighting between Britain and its North American colonies had lasted more than a year. The Continental Congress had created an army and sought supplies, but it still included delegates whose colonies had taken different paths toward independence. Local assemblies and conventions began authorizing a clearer break. Congress appointed a committee to prepare a public statement. Thomas Jefferson drafted the principal text, which other committee members and Congress revised. On July 2, Congress voted for independence; on July 4, it approved the Declaration's final wording. The document announced that the colonies regarded themselves as free and independent states. It set out claims about political authority and listed grievances against the British king, addressing audiences at home and abroad. Publication spread the decision, but signatures, printed copies, and public readings followed different schedules. The declaration did not end military danger. British forces continued their campaign, while the new states had to maintain an army, raise funds, and persuade other governments to recognize them. France entered a formal alliance in 1778, and Britain acknowledged independence only in the 1783 peace treaty. The Declaration expressed an aspiration to equality that coexisted with slavery and the exclusion of many people from political participation. Congress spoke for a political coalition whose future still depended on institutions, military survival, and further argument about whom the new order included. Printed copies reached places at different times, where readings and local responses gave the congressional text new audiences. The public statement helped representatives seek support abroad, but foreign governments still assessed the military prospects and their own strategic interests before deciding whether to recognize the new states. Congress appointed commissioners to pursue recognition and assistance in Europe. France signed treaties with the United States in 1778, and its participation widened the war. The American states continued under separate governments while Congress managed common military and diplomatic affairs. Britain did not recognize independence until the peace settlement of 1783. The Declaration therefore preceded both a formal alliance and the eventual recognition obtained through negotiations after years of fighting.

079爻 Historical event French alliance with the Americans. As the American war for independence continued, the Continental Congress looked for a European partner able to supply money, matériel, and naval power. France had its own reasons to weaken Britain, but it could not assume that the rebellion would endure. American envoys worked in Paris while French officials supplied assistance before a formal alliance. The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 strengthened the case for open cooperation. In February 1778, France and the United States concluded treaties of amity and commerce and alliance. The agreements recognized the United States and committed the parties to cooperation against Britain. Formal support changed the resources available to American commanders. French loans, supplies, soldiers, and especially naval forces became part of the wider war. The combined operations that culminated at Yorktown in 1781 depended on choices made years after the treaties were signed. France also carried substantial financial costs. Peace negotiations in 1783 ended the fighting with Britain but did not remove the debts and political strains accumulated during the war. The partnership brought power that had to be scheduled, paid for, and coordinated across the Atlantic, while each government continued to pursue interests of its own. French naval power changed the geography of the war by challenging British control at sea. At the same time, the French government had to fund its ships, soldiers, and credit to America. French and American forces cooperated in the campaign that trapped Cornwallis at Yorktown in 1781. The French fleet helped prevent British relief by sea, while land forces conducted the siege. Cornwallis's surrender was followed by continued diplomatic negotiation, not an immediate end to every theater of fighting. American and British representatives agreed preliminary peace terms in 1782, and the definitive treaty followed in 1783. France also negotiated its own settlement with Britain as the wider war ended.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H15-L1 | XIANG-U-15-02

085爻 Historical event Benjamin Franklin in France. Benjamin Franklin arrived in France in 1776 as an American representative while the war with Britain remained uncertain. France was already Britain's rival, yet open recognition of the rebellious colonies carried diplomatic and military risks. Franklin worked with other American commissioners to communicate the new state's needs and to cultivate support among French officials and the public. The envoys sought supplies, credit, and recognition, while also managing disagreements among themselves and receiving instructions that crossed the Atlantic slowly. French assistance preceded a formal treaty, but its extent and visibility changed as the war developed. News of the American victory at Saratoga made an open alliance more attractive to the French government. In 1778, France signed treaties with the United States. Franklin remained in Paris to help manage the alliance and later took part in the negotiations that led to the peace of 1783. His work was not a single persuasive speech or a social appearance. Letters, meetings, financial requests, naval planning, and the changing reports from America all shaped what France would do. The partnership also had limits: French and American interests overlapped without becoming identical. After the treaty, officials still had to turn promises into supplies and campaigns. Franklin's long stay connected the period before recognition to the years of alliance and peace making. Changing battlefield news could reach Paris only after an Atlantic crossing, so an envoy often had to work with incomplete information. Franklin's long tenure mattered partly because diplomatic relationships could be maintained between dramatic turning points. Franklin remained in France through the negotiations ending the war. He worked with John Adams and John Jay on the American peace commission, while relations with the French government continued alongside talks with Britain. The resulting settlement recognized independence and addressed boundaries, debts, and fishing rights. Franklin returned to the United States in 1785 after years representing American interests abroad. The tasks of financing a war, maintaining an alliance, and negotiating peace had occupied different stages of that service.

Franklin's work in France offers a comparison about representing a new state without letting personal distinction overshadow the mission. Line 1 | TW-PM-H16-L1 | XIANG-U-16-02

091爻 Historical event Articles of Confederation. During the American Revolution, the states needed a common structure to conduct war and diplomacy without surrendering the autonomy they had just defended against Britain. Congress drafted the Articles of Confederation in 1777, but all states had to ratify them, a process completed in 1781. The Articles called the union a league of friendship and left most powers with the states. Congress could conduct foreign affairs and request troops or money, yet it could not directly impose ordinary national taxes. In wartime, leaders had to obtain resources through state action and borrowing. After independence, the limits became more apparent. The government faced debts, disputes among states, and difficulty making collective decisions when interests differed. Some achievements still occurred under the Articles, including western land policy, so the period was not merely an absence of government. But calls for a stronger federal framework grew. A meeting initially concerned with interstate commerce led toward the Constitutional Convention of 1787, where delegates proposed replacing the Articles. The new Constitution went to the states for ratification and began operating in 1789. The Articles gave the states a working association, not a finished answer to every problem of governing together. Under the Articles, important measures required agreement among states, and amending the framework itself demanded unanimity. Those thresholds reflected caution about concentrated authority, but they also made adjustment difficult when urgent financial and commercial problems arose. The later Convention proposed a different ratification rule for the new Constitution, a controversial step in replacing the original framework. Ratification made the draft framework the states' operative common government. The Confederation Congress handled peace and western territory after the war, but continued to depend on the states for revenues. Interstate commercial disputes and the problems of national finance prompted calls for further meetings. A convention at Annapolis in 1786 sought a larger gathering, and delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787. Their proposed constitution was considered by state conventions. After the required ratifications, the new federal government began operating in 1789, replacing the confederation's central arrangements.

Line-specific comparison Proclaiming delight at the start can exhaust the purpose before work begins. The Articles of Confederation created a common framework, but public satisfaction could not supply revenue or effective implementation. Line 1 | TW-PM-H17-L1 | XIANG-U-17-02

097爻 Historical event Treaty of Paris. The American Revolutionary War involved fighting on land and sea long after Congress declared independence. In 1781, the surrender of a British army at Yorktown changed the prospects of continued large-scale operations, but the war and diplomacy were not finished. British, American, French, and other representatives entered complicated negotiations. American commissioners in Paris needed agreement on recognition, boundaries, and other terms while France remained an ally with interests of its own. Preliminary articles were signed in 1782. The definitive Treaty of Paris followed in September 1783. Britain recognized the independence of the United States, and the treaty drew boundaries for the new country. It also addressed debts, the treatment of Loyalists, and other matters that could not be settled merely by ending a battle. News and formal ratification crossed the Atlantic; armed forces and governments then had to put the terms into practice. British troops departed from New York later in 1783, while disputes over frontier posts and treaty obligations continued. Indigenous nations whose territories were affected had not been equal parties to the treaty, and its boundary clauses did not erase their claims. Peace was a negotiated change in relationships among governments, not a sudden disappearance of contested property and loyalties. The new United States obtained recognition but still had to govern its territory and deal with obligations it had accepted. The commissioners negotiated while the United States still faced financial strain and while British forces held positions in North America. Congress had to ratify the settlement, and the states had to confront treaty provisions touching private debts and property. The treaty's provisions thus needed attention on both sides of the Atlantic. British withdrawal from some frontier posts did not proceed as Americans expected, while disputes over debts and Loyalist property continued. American and British officials returned to negotiations over these unsettled matters in the following decade. Jay's Treaty in 1794 provided additional arrangements concerning posts, claims, and commerce. Meanwhile, the United States organized administration of western lands and pursued further agreements with Indigenous nations, whose interests had not been represented in the Paris negotiations between the states.

Line-specific comparison Changing an official position is favorable when it follows a proper course. Peace negotiations required Americans and Britons to move beyond wartime demands. The comparison concerns adjustment grounded in an attainable settlement rather than mere convenience. Line 1 | TW-PM-H18-L1 | XIANG-U-18-02

103爻 Historical event Constitutional Convention. By the mid-1780s, the United States had won independence but its government under the Articles of Confederation struggled to raise revenue and manage disputes among states. Congress could ask for contributions but lacked a reliable means of direct taxation. Representatives first considered changes to commercial arrangements; calls for a broader convention followed. In May 1787, delegates from most states assembled in Philadelphia. Rhode Island did not participate. The meeting went beyond a narrow revision of the Articles and debated a new federal structure. Delegates disagreed over representation, executive authority, taxation, and the relationship between national and state governments. Large and small states contested how they would vote in a legislature. The resulting compromises created two legislative chambers, an executive, and a judiciary, while also protecting slavery through provisions that had grave consequences. The Convention signed a proposed Constitution in September, but it could not put that text into force by itself. State ratifying conventions argued over its powers and demanded protections for individual rights. Enough states approved it for the new government to begin work in 1789; amendments later became the Bill of Rights. It begins with concrete weaknesses in the existing union, moves through contested drafting and compromise, and continues through public ratification and later amendment. The Convention replaced one framework through an agreed political process while leaving conflicts that later generations would have to confront. The Convention met behind closed doors, and its proposal became public only when the draft went to the states. Ratification arguments then reached wider audiences through newspapers, pamphlets, and conventions. After ratification, elections and appointments brought the new federal institutions into operation. George Washington became president in 1789, and Congress began organizing executive departments and the federal judiciary. The constitutional amendments that became the Bill of Rights were ratified in 1791. Foreign policy proceeded through the new division of responsibilities, with the executive conducting negotiations and the Senate considering treaties. Disputes over those powers continued as the country faced conflicts and commercial pressure from European states.

Line-specific comparison Repairing a father's disorder concerns taking responsibility for an inherited arrangement. The Constitutional Convention addressed weaknesses in the Articles. Line 1 | TW-PM-H19-L1 | XIANG-U-19-02

109爻 Historical event Jay Treaty. After Britain recognized American independence, several questions remained unsettled. British troops held frontier posts, the two countries disputed obligations involving debts and trade, and war in Europe complicated American shipping. President Washington sent John Jay to negotiate in London in 1794. Jay and British officials reached a treaty that arranged for evacuation of the western posts and addressed some claims through mixed commissions. The agreement did not settle every American complaint, including the continuing issue of impressment, and many Americans criticized it as too favorable to Britain. The Senate approved it with qualifications, and Washington decided to sign. Public protest continued, while Congress later debated funding needed to carry out the agreement. British withdrawal from the posts in 1796 gave one provision a concrete result. The treaty also maintained a path for commerce, even as tensions over maritime policy remained. Its sequence begins with unfinished terms after the Revolutionary War, proceeds through negotiation and bitter domestic argument, and continues into the actual handover of posts and work of the claims commissions. A diplomatic document did not settle the domestic question of who spoke for American interests. Jay's mission managed some disputes without ending all friction between the governments. The treaty became part of a continuing relationship in which both sides had to carry out particular provisions and deal with matters the agreement had left open. Some Americans saw the treaty as a necessary way to avoid war with Britain; others believed it conceded too much and endangered relations with France. Washington faced that domestic division while deciding whether to sign. The debate also tested the respective roles of president, Senate, and House in foreign policy, making implementation a constitutional issue as well as a diplomatic one. Political opposition persisted after the signature, and practical compliance required officials to carry out provisions over time. The Senate approved ratification with a condition concerning a commercial provision. Washington then endorsed the treaty, and debate continued over funding its implementation. British forces withdrew from the northern posts covered by the agreement. Commissions addressed specified claims and boundary matters. The treaty did not secure an end to impressment and left other maritime grievances unresolved. French hostility toward the agreement contributed to another period of tension in American foreign relations, including seizures of American shipping.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H20-L1 | XIANG-U-20-02

115爻 Historical event Washington's Farewell Address. As Washington's second presidential term drew to a close, the United States faced disputes over parties, foreign alliances, and its future place among European powers at war. Washington had decided not to seek another term. In 1796, a public farewell message appeared under his name after work on drafts with close advisers, including Alexander Hamilton. The address urged Americans to preserve the union, warned against forms of factional rivalry, and discussed the risks of permanent political attachments to foreign powers. It did not demand that the country cease all trade or diplomacy. Its arguments reflected a specific moment in which the young republic was trying to maintain independence while Britain and France fought. Washington left office in 1797 after an election placed John Adams in the presidency. The transfer gave the country an example of an elected leader relinquishing office, though party conflict and disagreement over foreign policy continued. The farewell became a widely read political text, interpreted differently by later generations. Its publication did not create national unity on command. Citizens and officials still had to decide how to handle treaties, parties, and future wars. The address was published ahead of an election in which organized parties had become increasingly visible. Washington's warning about faction therefore entered an active argument rather than a quiet national consensus. The address continued circulating after his departure, giving later Americans a text to cite and contest. Washington left the presidency when Adams took office in March 1797. The new administration faced deteriorating relations with France, and partisan argument over foreign policy continued. The address remained available in print as political leaders debated neutrality and overseas commitments. Different readers invoked different parts of it, including its discussion of constitutional government, union, faction, and international relations. Later changes in American foreign policy occurred through subsequent administrations and public debate rather than through a single binding provision of the address.

Washington's Farewell Address asks readers to consider political consequences beyond immediate factional appearances. Line 1 | TW-PM-H21-L1 | XIANG-U-21-02

121爻 Historical event The XYZ Affair. Relations between the United States and revolutionary France deteriorated in the 1790s. France objected to American dealings with Britain, and French privateers seized American merchant vessels. President John Adams sent envoys to seek a settlement in Paris in 1797. The representatives encountered intermediaries who discussed payments and other conditions before formal talks could proceed. The Americans declined the demands and the mission failed to reach the agreement it had sought. Adams informed Congress of the difficulties, then released dispatches with the names of some French intermediaries disguised as X, Y, and Z. Publication made the affair a domestic political crisis. Many Americans were angry at the apparent demands; parties also argued over Adams's policy, the release of documents, and the degree of military preparation. Congress supported naval defense and other measures while an undeclared naval conflict with France developed, especially in the Caribbean. Adams later pursued another diplomatic opening, and a convention signed in 1800 helped end the Quasi-War. The episode did not move directly from insult to a formal declaration of war. It ran from maritime disputes, through a failed negotiation and public disclosure, to limited fighting and a second attempt at settlement. The dispatches preserve what the American envoys reported, while French policy and American partisan reactions require separate attention. The underlying conflict concerned ships, treaties, money, and the terms on which two republics would speak to each other. The Quasi-War involved naval clashes rather than a congressional declaration of full-scale war. American policymakers therefore had to separate the immediate protection of merchant vessels from the question of a larger conflict with France. The later convention addressed outstanding treaty and claims issues, showing that the relationship could change again after the public anger surrounding the dispatches. The public dispute over the envoys' reports also shaped the administration's room for further talks with France. The conflict remained chiefly naval, with American ships protecting commerce and engaging French vessels. Adams eventually sent a new mission to seek agreement despite opposition within his own political camp. The Convention of 1800 ended the immediate conflict and terminated the earlier Franco-American alliance. Outstanding claims continued to require attention afterward. Relations thus passed from the failed Paris mission through undeclared maritime fighting into a negotiated settlement during the transition from the French Directory to Napoleon's government.

Line-specific comparison A restraint on the toes prevents further wrongful movement. Line 1 | TW-PM-H22-L1 | XIANG-U-22-02

127爻 Historical event The Barbary Wars. After the United States became independent, its merchant ships sailed into the Mediterranean without the same protection they had previously enjoyed under British arrangements. Rulers in North Africa demanded payments and seized vessels, and American administrations weighed tribute, negotiation, and naval force. In 1801, Tripoli's ruler declared war after a dispute over payments. The United States sent naval squadrons to the Mediterranean. Ships blockaded ports and fought engagements, but the campaign also suffered setbacks: the frigate Philadelphia ran aground and was captured in 1803, leaving its crew prisoners. American forces later destroyed the captured ship to keep it from serving Tripoli. A campaign across land toward Derna formed part of the pressure before an agreement in 1805 ended that war and secured the prisoners' release. Disputes over maritime demands did not stop permanently. During the War of 1812, American attention and naval resources were occupied elsewhere, and further conflict with Algiers followed in 1815. A new American squadron won engagements and obtained agreements. The events stretched across administrations and two wars rather than a single naval battle. Diplomacy, payments, shipbuilding, distant logistics, and combat all figured in what American officials called protection of commerce. North African states had their own political interests and were not one unified opponent. American administrations faced different North African governments at different moments, and agreements with one did not automatically bind another. Crews taken prisoner and merchants who risked their cargo experienced the costs before a broader strategy was settled. The naval campaigns had to be sustained far from American ports, with repairs and provisioning arranged across the Mediterranean. That distance made every deployment dependent on reliable communication and supplies. The 1805 agreement with Tripoli secured the release of American captives, while disputes elsewhere continued. After the War of 1812, the United States again sent naval forces to the Mediterranean. Negotiations with Algiers in 1815 followed American captures of Algerian vessels. Arrangements with other North African governments were also pursued. European powers conducted their own military and diplomatic operations in the region. The American campaigns ended particular tribute disputes without making every Mediterranean relationship subject to one common agreement.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H23-L1 | XIANG-U-23-02

133爻 Historical event Napoleonic Wars and U.S. neutrality. From 1803 onward, Napoleon's wars reshaped Europe and placed neutral trade under pressure. Britain and France each tried to limit commerce that might assist the other. British Orders in Council and French decrees affected ships carrying goods through Atlantic markets. The United States claimed neutral trading rights, but American vessels faced seizures, restrictions, and the seizure of sailors by British ships. Presidents and Congress tried different responses. Jefferson's embargo of 1807 sharply limited American overseas trade in an attempt to keep ships safe and use commercial pressure, but it imposed heavy costs on American ports and merchants. Congress replaced it with other trade measures. Meanwhile the European war and maritime disputes continued. The United States entered war with Britain in 1812; conflict with France's policies and the changing European situation remained part of the background to the earlier neutrality crisis. Napoleon's defeat in 1815 altered the European setting, but it did not undo the losses incurred by traders during the preceding years. There was no single instant at which neutrality disappeared. Laws, seizures, embargoes, reprisals, and war successively changed what neutral trade meant in practice. Official policy and merchant experience were not the same thing, and American decision makers disagreed over whether trade restrictions or armed resistance would better protect the country's position. Merchants had already committed capital to voyages before each new restriction or seizure changed the terms of trade. The embargo disrupted coastal and Atlantic business in the United States, prompting evasion and political protest. Policymakers had to weigh injury to domestic commerce against the hope that economic pressure would change European belligerents' behavior. The restrictions affected choices already made by traders. Congress replaced the embargo in 1809 with restrictions directed at Britain and France. Further legislation offered a return to trade if the belligerents changed their policies. Madison's administration dealt with competing reports and continuing maritime confrontations before asking for war with Britain in 1812. Peace negotiations later produced the Treaty of Ghent. Britain and the United States subsequently negotiated limits on lake armaments and boundary arrangements while European affairs changed following Napoleon's defeat.

Jefferson's embargo of 1807 sharply limited American overseas trade in an attempt to keep ships safe and use commercial pressure, but it imposed heavy costs on American ports and merchants. Line 1 | TW-PM-H24-L1 | XIANG-U-24-02

139爻 Historical event Louisiana Purchase. In 1803, the United States was concerned about access to New Orleans and the Mississippi River, routes important to farmers and merchants in the western states. France had regained Louisiana from Spain in an arrangement whose consequences for American navigation were uncertain. President Jefferson sent representatives to seek a way to secure American interests, initially focusing on New Orleans. Napoleon's government, facing renewed war in Europe and difficulties in its Caribbean plans, offered to sell the much larger Louisiana territory. American negotiators accepted, and a treaty was signed in April 1803. The purchase price and terms went to the United States government, where the Senate considered the agreement and Congress arranged the necessary funding. France transferred authority later that year. The new claim doubled the area over which the United States asserted sovereignty, but maps and treaty language did not settle every boundary. American officials then organized expeditions and administration in territory already inhabited by Indigenous nations, whose political rights were not determined by the two governments that signed the sale. Jefferson's administration also faced questions about the constitutional basis for acquiring territory. The treaty changed relations among states; it did not make the land empty or deliver a complete administrative system. The purchase's effects unfolded over decades through policies and conflicts far beyond the negotiations in Paris. France and the United States did not draw every western boundary with a shared, precise survey before the sale. Officials later faced questions about where the acquired claim ended and how it met Spanish and Indigenous territories. American representatives completed the purchase agreements in Paris, and the Senate approved ratification later in 1803. Authority was transferred at New Orleans in December. The government then organized the acquired territories and sent expeditions to gather information about the interior. American officials also continued negotiating with Spain about borders. Indigenous communities maintained their own lands, relationships, and political interests despite the transfer of France's claims. Later American settlement and federal policy extended the consequences of the purchase well beyond the diplomatic transaction.

Line-specific comparison An early return allows self-correction before the departure grows. The Louisiana negotiations began with a limited American objective and changed with France's offer. The line asks whether a government can recognize a workable course promptly without insisting on its first plan. Line 1 | TW-PM-H25-L1 | XIANG-U-25-02

145爻 Historical event War of 1812. Maritime conflict with Britain persisted after American independence. During Britain's war with Napoleonic France, British ships interfered with American commerce and impressed sailors, while American leaders disputed the scope of neutral rights. Diplomatic and trade restrictions had not produced a durable settlement. In June 1812, the United States declared war on Britain. American forces attempted invasions of Canada, and fighting occurred along the border, on the Great Lakes, at sea, and in the South. Both sides experienced successes and failures. In 1814 British troops entered Washington and burned public buildings, while Americans defended Baltimore. Negotiators met at Ghent as war continued. Their treaty, signed in December 1814, restored many prewar territorial arrangements but did not specifically resolve all the maritime practices that had helped bring on the conflict. Because news crossed the Atlantic slowly, the Battle of New Orleans was fought in January 1815 after the treaty had been signed but before the combatants there knew peace had been concluded. Ratification and implementation followed. Indigenous nations were also major actors and suffered lasting consequences, especially as American expansion continued after the war. Fighting on the Great Lakes depended on shipbuilding as well as field armies. Control of waterways affected supply and movement along the border, while campaigns in the South involved different communities and commanders. Treating the conflict as a single march from declaration to New Orleans would conceal these simultaneous theaters and the unequal consequences of the peace for Indigenous peoples. Peace came through several acts of ratification and communication, not just the date written on the treaty. The United States and Britain completed ratification of the Treaty of Ghent in early 1815. News traveled across the Atlantic and then to the forces still operating in different theaters. Prisoners and occupied places were addressed under the peace terms, while commissions were assigned boundary questions. The two governments negotiated further arrangements in 1817 and 1818. Trade and diplomacy resumed, although people displaced by fighting and Indigenous communities affected by the campaigns faced consequences that were not reversed by the restoration of peace.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H26-L1 | XIANG-U-26-02

151爻 Historical event Rush–Bagot Agreement. After the War of 1812, Britain and the United States still had armed vessels on the Great Lakes. Both governments had interests in maintaining access and security along a long, inhabited border, but a continued naval buildup could create fresh alarms. Negotiators Richard Rush and Charles Bagot exchanged notes in 1817 limiting the number and armament of vessels each side would keep on the lakes. The agreement did not erase all frontier disagreements or remove every military asset. It set a concrete ceiling for a particular kind of force in a particular region. Each government then had to translate the exchange of notes into practice and monitor the border relationship over time. Other questions, including boundaries and fishing rights, required further negotiation through separate agreements. The Great Lakes remained places of trade, settlement, and political change. The Rush–Bagot arrangement became an important element in reducing the risk that routine movements on the water would be read as preparations for another war. The negotiators chose to regulate what each side could visibly deploy rather than trying to solve every problem at once. The limitation endured because both governments continued to find it useful, not because the words written in 1817 could enforce themselves without later cooperation. The notes named small numbers of armed vessels allowed on specific lakes, making the limit easier to observe than a general promise of goodwill. The arrangement was later incorporated into the two countries' continuing diplomatic practice. Its durability reflected repeated decisions not to rebuild an unrestricted lake fleet as relations and border commerce changed. Its operation could be checked as ships were kept below the agreed level. The agreement developed through an exchange between Richard Rush and Charles Bagot in 1817. It specified limited armed vessels on the Great Lakes rather than imposing a prohibition on all boats or commercial navigation. The separate Convention of 1818 addressed parts of the northern boundary and other matters. Officials on both sides continued handling local disputes through diplomacy. The lake limitation remained part of Anglo-American relations as commercial traffic and settlements expanded around the waters.

Line-specific comparison Stopping in danger prevents entering disaster. The postwar naval rivalry on the Great Lakes offers a comparison about halting a competitive build-up before it becomes another confrontation. A pause can create room for a negotiated alternative. Line 1 | TW-PM-H27-L1 | XIANG-U-27-02

157爻 Historical event Monroe Doctrine. In 1823, European politics raised American questions about the future of colonies and newly independent states in the Western Hemisphere. Britain had commercial interests in Latin American independence, while the United States wanted to discourage renewed European colonization without entering an alliance under British leadership. President James Monroe, working with advisers including John Quincy Adams, set out the administration's position in his annual message to Congress. It opposed further European colonization in the Americas and distinguished political systems on the two sides of the Atlantic. The message was a unilateral American statement, not a treaty signed with the new Latin American republics. At the time, the United States had limited military capacity to enforce a hemisphere-wide rule. British naval strength and the choices of European and American governments also shaped what occurred. The statement became known later as the Monroe Doctrine, and its meaning was revised and invoked by subsequent administrations for different purposes. Its aftermath lies in later diplomatic interpretations, not an immediate change in every American border or government. Latin American states were political actors in their own right, not merely passive subjects of a U.S. announcement. The message established a claim about American policy; its practical reach had to be tested against events and capacities far beyond the moment Monroe delivered it. The message distinguished existing European colonies from attempts at new colonization, an important boundary within the American claim. U.S. leaders also promised not to intervene in European internal affairs. The statement formed part of Monroe's annual message to Congress in December 1823. It did not create an international organization or station new forces throughout the Americas. European powers retained existing colonies, and newly independent Latin American states pursued their own diplomacy. British maritime power and separate British interests remained important features of the setting. Later U.S. administrations referred to Monroe's position in further disputes, while the original passage continued to be cited as the basis of a named policy.

Line-specific comparison Abandoning one's own means while staring at another's nourishment is unworthy. The Monroe Doctrine invites discussion of matching a public position to national capabilities. Dependence on another power's fleet should be recognized rather than hidden by expansive language. Line 1 | TW-PM-H28-L1 | XIANG-U-28-02

163爻 Historical event Webster–Ashburton Treaty. By the early 1840s, Britain and the United States still disagreed about sections of the boundary between Maine and British North America. Earlier wording had left room for competing surveys and claims. Local incidents and militia mobilizations raised concern that a territorial quarrel could become an armed conflict. U.S. Secretary of State Daniel Webster and British envoy Lord Ashburton negotiated in Washington in 1842. Their treaty drew a compromise line in the northeast and addressed other border questions, including portions farther west. The agreement also contained provisions about naval cooperation against the Atlantic slave trade and extradition. Reaching terms required maps, legal arguments, and attention to local communities that would live with the new line. The negotiators could sign on behalf of their governments, but surveyors and officials still had to mark and administer the border. The compromise was criticized by people who believed their side had given up too much. Nevertheless, ratification allowed the two governments to manage several disputes through an agreed procedure rather than troops at the frontier. The agreement did not settle every future question between Britain and the United States. It gave a specific answer to a dangerous border dispute at a time when both governments had reason to prevent a larger war. Its impact was measured in the maps and administrative decisions that followed, not merely in the signing ceremony. The quarrel had already raised tensions along the Maine–New Brunswick region, where residents did not experience disputed lines as abstract lines on maps. Once the treaty was ratified, surveying and local administration translated a diplomatic compromise into places where people lived and worked. The treaty was signed in August 1842 and ratified by the two governments. Commissioners and officials then addressed the practical marking of agreed boundaries. The settlement also contained provisions concerning extradition and efforts against the Atlantic slave trade. Disputes over Oregon remained outside the completed northeastern boundary bargain and required a later treaty in 1846. Relations continued through those additional negotiations rather than ending with the agreement signed by Webster and Ashburton.

Line-specific comparison A soft protective layer beneath a heavy undertaking prevents damage. Boundary negotiations required preparatory knowledge and political support. This line asks what safeguards should be laid down before the larger settlement is placed on the negotiating table. Line 1 | TW-PM-H29-L1 | XIANG-U-29-02

169爻 Historical event Preventing recognition of the Confederacy. When the American Civil War began in 1861, Confederate leaders hoped that foreign governments might recognize their new state. Britain and France had commercial ties to cotton grown in the South, while the Union argued that secession was an internal rebellion and warned against external support. British and French governments declared neutrality and treated the Confederates as belligerents without recognizing Confederate independence. Union diplomats, including the American minister in London, worked to explain the federal position and to limit Confederate access to official backing. Events repeatedly threatened this balance. The Trent Affair of 1861, when a Union warship seized Confederate envoys from a British vessel, produced a crisis with Britain. Later, the construction of Confederate raiders in British ports led to further disputes. European governments followed military developments in North America. The Emancipation Proclamation, announced in 1862 and taking effect in 1863, also changed the public meaning of the Union war effort and complicated any British or French decision to favor a slaveholding Confederacy. European states did not grant the diplomatic recognition Confederate agents sought. Union representatives addressed the legal status of the war, defused particular incidents, and watched whether foreign policy might shift after battlefield news. Line 1 | TW-PM-H30-L1 | XIANG-U-30-02

175爻 Historical event Union blockade of Confederate ports. At the start of the American Civil War, the Union announced a naval blockade of ports controlled by the Confederacy. The policy was intended to restrict exports, especially cotton, and limit the entry of weapons and other supplies. Declaring a blockade was easier than stationing enough ships along a long coastline. Union naval forces had to acquire vessels, organize patrols, capture or deter blockade runners, and decide which coastal positions could be held. Early in the war many ships still passed through, but the blockade grew stronger as the navy expanded and Union forces captured major ports. Foreign governments had to consider the blockade's legal status because their merchants traded with both sides. The South continued to seek supplies through routes that remained open, and it also relied on inland resources. The policy's effects accumulated rather than appearing all at once. It combined with land campaigns, Confederate financial difficulties, and the loss of territory, none of which can be reduced to the blockade alone. By 1865, Union victory ended the war. Individual ships, crews, merchants, and coastal communities experienced the policy differently. A blockade is a continuing military and administrative undertaking: each attempted passage and each captured harbor changes its practical reach. The surviving records document the policy and its enforcement, while debates continue over its precise contribution relative to other causes of Confederate defeat. Union ships could not be present at every inlet at every hour. As the war went on, the capture of ports and the growth of patrol fleets narrowed the opportunities for blockade runners. These operational changes made a declared policy more effective, though goods still crossed where enforcement failed or alternative routes remained. As Union forces captured ports, the blockade's geography changed. Wilmington remained important to Confederate supply until operations against Fort Fisher in early 1865 closed that route. The navy continued intercepting vessels while armies advanced inland. The Confederacy's collapse ended the wartime blockade, but seizures and claims involving neutral shipping remained matters for legal and diplomatic handling. The fleet also moved into postwar responsibilities as the government reduced its wartime forces and reassessed its naval requirements.

British officials prepared for the possibility of war even as messages crossed the Atlantic. President Lincoln's administration had to consider the international law of neutral ships, the Union's own insistence on maritime rights, and the danger of adding Britain to an already costly civil war. Secretary of State William Seward replied to the British demand. The United States released the envoys, who continued their journey, and the immediate crisis subsided. Release did not mean Britain recognized the Confederacy; nor did it settle all the disputes that would arise over Confederate activity in British territory. Surviving dispatches and official decisions allow the order of events to be followed, though they do not make every public reaction or internal calculation identical on both sides of the Atlantic. The envoys' release was a deliberate response to British protest, not an admission that every British complaint about Union wartime conduct had been resolved. The crisis occurred while both sides were making decisions about Confederate diplomacy, neutral shipping, and the possibility of wider war. Avoiding that war mattered to the Union's ability to continue its own conflict. The incident began with a commander at sea but ended through decisions made by civilian governments. The prisoners were released after Washington accepted the need to correct the seizure. They proceeded to Europe, where their diplomatic work continued without obtaining recognition for Confederate independence. British and American relations remained strained over other incidents, including the construction and operation of Confederate raiders. Those issues later entered the Alabama claims dispute. The immediate release resolved the Trent confrontation without requiring either government to fight the other or settle every question arising from the Civil War at once.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H32-L1 | XIANG-L-32-02

187爻 Historical event The Alabama Claims arbitration. During the American Civil War, Confederate commerce raiders built or outfitted with help from British ports attacked Union shipping. The Alabama became the most famous, capturing or destroying many vessels before it was sunk in 1864. The United States argued that Britain had failed to exercise the neutral duties it owed when such ships escaped into Confederate service. Britain disputed the extent of its responsibility. The war ended in 1865, but the claims did not disappear. Years of diplomatic disagreement followed as both governments sought a means to settle them without turning the quarrel into another crisis. The Treaty of Washington in 1871 established rules and submitted the Alabama claims to an international tribunal meeting at Geneva. In 1872, the tribunal awarded compensation to the United States, which Britain paid. The decision did not reverse the wartime losses of particular owners or crews, but it gave the governments a formal result to implement. The claims had to be defined with evidence about vessels, ports, and official conduct. The tribunal relied on standards of neutral duty agreed in the Treaty of Washington, giving the parties a common basis for judgment. Evidence about the construction and departure of particular vessels could then be examined rather than replaced by broad accusation. The governments treated the award as a payable obligation. The Treaty of Washington in 1871 set out the arbitration arrangements. The tribunal met at Geneva and considered the parties' submissions under agreed standards of neutral responsibility. Its 1872 award required Britain to pay $15.5 million in compensation for the accepted claims. Britain subsequently made the payment under the settlement agreed by the two governments. The payment concluded the specific claims submitted to that process. Other Anglo-American questions were addressed through their own negotiated arrangements, and the governments continued developing diplomatic cooperation after the wartime grievances had been formally settled.

Line-specific comparison Seeking deep permanence at the beginning can create harm. The Alabama claims took years to resolve. The line invites patience with the gradual construction of arbitration rather than demanding immediate trust between governments still divided by wartime grievances. 193爻 Historical event Union victory and postwar diplomacy. In April 1865, Union armies forced the surrender of major Confederate forces, including Robert E. Lee's army at Appomattox. The Union government had preserved the United States, and emancipation had destroyed the legal foundation of slavery in the rebellious states. Victory, however, did not determine how former Confederate states would be governed, what rights formerly enslaved people would exercise, or how wartime debts and property would be handled. President Lincoln was assassinated soon after Appomattox, leaving Andrew Johnson to take office. The federal government demobilized large forces while political arguments over Reconstruction intensified. European governments that had remained outside formal recognition of the Confederacy dealt with a United States whose survival was now clear. The war's end affected American standing abroad, but diplomacy still had to address claims arising from the conflict, including disputes with Britain over Confederate raiders. Retreat from wartime emergency measures did not mean retreat from questions of citizenship and security. Some problems that commanders could not settle on the battlefield became central to legislation and local administration. Federal troops remained in parts of the South during Reconstruction. That transition put civilian rights and governance at the center of federal policy. With the Civil War over, the United States increased pressure against the French-supported empire in Mexico. American forces were deployed along the Texas border, while Mexican republicans continued fighting Maximilian's government. France withdrew its troops, and Maximilian's regime collapsed in 1867. In British North America, concern about American power and cross-border raids formed part of the setting for confederation. Canada was established in 1867. At home, Reconstruction continued amid disputes over citizenship, federal authority, violence, and the readmission of former Confederate states. Military victory had been followed by different political changes on both sides of the country's borders.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H34-L1 | XIANG-L-34-02

199爻 Historical event Mahan's sea power argument. In 1890, Alfred Thayer Mahan published The Influence of Sea Power upon History, a study of naval power and state competition in earlier centuries. He argued that trade routes, fleets, bases, and national policy were closely connected. The book appeared as industrial powers were debating shipbuilding and overseas interests. American officers and policymakers read and discussed his arguments; foreign naval circles did as well. But his writing gave participants in the debate a vocabulary for asking what a navy would protect and what kind of infrastructure it would need. During the 1890s, the United States continued expanding its modern fleet, while leaders argued over commerce, coaling stations, and its position beyond the continent. The Spanish–American War in 1898 brought naval operations in both the Caribbean and the Pacific, yet the war had its own causes and choices. The book's influence is documented through reception and discussion, not through a simple claim that each later ship or campaign fulfilled Mahan's instructions. A text can shape the way people talk about power while the actual decision to build, deploy, or fight remains with institutions and individuals confronting their own strategic setting. Mahan drew on earlier naval history rather than issuing a formal government plan. Mahan's first major study appeared in 1890, followed by a volume addressing the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic periods. His work developed from teaching at the U.S. Naval War College, where officers studied earlier campaigns alongside questions about the role of fleets in national policy. His books circulated among American and European naval officers and political figures. American debates over overseas commerce, bases, and a canal continued alongside shipbuilding decisions. Congress and successive administrations approved particular projects through their own procedures. By the end of the decade, the Spanish–American War had brought new territorial and naval responsibilities, while disputes over the country's overseas role continued in public life.

205爻 Historical event Venezuela boundary dispute. In the nineteenth century, Britain and Venezuela disputed the boundary of British Guiana. Venezuela sought outside support, and the United States became increasingly involved during the 1890s. In 1895, Secretary of State Richard Olney sent a forceful message asserting an American interest. Britain initially resisted the broad American interpretation of the doctrine, and President Cleveland then asked Congress for a commission to examine the boundary. The tone of the dispute raised fears of a confrontation between the United States and Britain. Both governments nevertheless moved toward a negotiated procedure. Britain and Venezuela agreed to arbitration under a treaty arranged in 1897, with the United States acting in support of the Venezuelan case. An international tribunal issued an award in 1899. Venezuela did not receive everything it had claimed, and later questions about the award persisted. Arbitration did not require the United States and Britain to agree about every interpretation of the Monroe Doctrine. It moved the immediate question from diplomatic confrontation toward a tribunal using maps and claims. The British government ultimately accepted arbitration of the boundary with Venezuela, but that willingness did not amount to accepting every U.S. claim about hemispheric authority. The tribunal's decision was a product of the legal process agreed afterward. The border itself still had to be defined through a procedure involving the governments that claimed the territory. Britain and Venezuela agreed to arbitration under arrangements negotiated after the 1895 crisis. The tribunal issued its award in 1899, assigning most of the disputed territory to British Guiana. Officials then worked on identifying the boundary on the ground. Venezuela did not cease to question the settlement permanently; the controversy reappeared in later diplomacy. British and American relations improved during the period surrounding arbitration, while the territory and the people living there remained the subject of claims made by the neighboring governments.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H36-L1 | XIANG-L-36-02

211爻 Historical event Spanish–American War. In 1898, an uprising against Spanish rule in Cuba had already drawn public attention and political pressure in the United States. The explosion of the U.S. battleship Maine in Havana harbor intensified the crisis, though its cause remained disputed. Congress and President McKinley moved toward intervention, and the United States declared war on Spain in April. American forces fought in the Caribbean, while a naval squadron defeated the Spanish fleet at Manila Bay in the Philippines. Land campaigns in Cuba and naval fighting near Santiago followed. Spain sought peace, and an armistice was agreed before the formal Treaty of Paris was signed in December 1898. The treaty ended Spanish rule in Cuba and transferred Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States. In the Philippines, disagreement over U.S. rule led to another war. In the United States, people debated whether acquiring overseas territories fit the republic's principles. A battlefield victory did not decide the political future of everyone affected. The United States declared that it would not annex Cuba, yet the settlement and subsequent occupation still gave Washington substantial influence over the island's future. In the Philippines, armed resistance against U.S. authority began after the war with Spain. The Treaty of Paris was signed in December 1898, and the United States debated its ratification and the acquisition of overseas territories. The treaty provided for an American payment of $20 million to Spain in connection with the Philippines. American rule in the Philippines met armed opposition, leading to a further war. Cuba remained under American military occupation until a republic was established in 1902, with restrictions affecting its relationship with the United States. Puerto Rico and Guam came under American authority through other arrangements. Spain's defeat therefore produced different political outcomes in each place, while debate continued in America over annexation and empire.

President Woodrow Wilson protested attacks on neutral rights while American opinion remained divided about joining the fighting. Germany's renewed unrestricted submarine warfare in 1917 brought fresh sinkings. Publication of the Zimmermann Telegram, in which Germany proposed an alliance with Mexico if the United States entered the war, added to the crisis. Wilson asked Congress for a declaration, and the United States entered the war against Germany in April 1917. Joining did not instantly place a large American army in France. The government raised forces, trained soldiers, organized shipping, and worked with Britain and France on loans, supplies, and operations. American troops reached Europe in growing numbers during 1918 and took part in major fighting before the armistice in November. At home, mobilization changed industry, public debate, and the powers exercised by government. The war's end created a new problem: how the United States would take part in making and enforcing a peace. The entry in April was a political turning point, but the military and civic consequences unfolded over many months and did not end with the first troops' arrival. The government used conscription and coordinated industrial production to enlarge its military effort. Thousands of families confronted the departure of soldiers and the pressures of wartime policy. These domestic changes occurred while the United States was negotiating how its troops would cooperate with existing Allied commands on the European front. After combat ended, demobilization brought soldiers and resources back to a country still disputing the peace. The United States declared war on Germany on April 6, 1917, and later on Austria-Hungary. Congress adopted conscription, and the government organized finance and industrial production for the expanding forces. After the armistice, Wilson participated in the Paris negotiations. The Senate did not consent to the Treaty of Versailles, and the United States made separate peace arrangements in 1921. Returning soldiers and the reduction of wartime activity accompanied continuing domestic argument about the obligations that should follow American participation in the conflict.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H38-L1 | XIANG-L-38-02

223爻 Historical event Wilson's Fourteen Points. As the First World War continued, President Woodrow Wilson sought to describe principles for a future peace. In January 1918 he presented the Fourteen Points to Congress. The address called for more open diplomacy, adjustments in trade and arms, arrangements for specific territorial questions, and a general association of nations. Its proposals reflected the United States' position as a belligerent and Wilson's effort to shape the settlement before fighting ended. The Allied governments did not share every point or interpret each one alike. National movements in Europe and beyond also pursued aims that could not be fitted into one American speech. When Germany sought an armistice later in 1918, Wilson's principles became part of the diplomatic exchange, but the final peace talks brought many other demands to the table. At Paris in 1919, Wilson worked for a League of Nations while negotiators argued about boundaries, reparations, security, and the future of defeated empires. The resulting treaties did not reproduce the Fourteen Points line by line. Back in the United States, the Senate refused to approve the Versailles Treaty and League membership. The address had real political consequences, but a statement of principles could not command agreement from every government or make each promised form of self-determination available to all peoples. Wilson's reference to self-determination carried different implications for different peoples. At Paris, some groups obtained new states or altered borders, while others remained under mandates or imperial control. Germany sought an armistice in the autumn of 1918 through exchanges that referred to Wilson's program. The fighting ended in November, and negotiations moved to the peace conference. The resulting treaties included a League of Nations but also reflected territorial and security demands not contained in the original speech. The U.S. Senate's refusal to approve Versailles left the United States outside the League. Governments and political movements continued invoking the published principles while pursuing different claims about national borders and representation.

Line-specific comparison Meeting an unwelcome person can avoid blame. Wilson's peace program had to engage governments with different priorities. Line 1 | TW-PM-H39-L1 | XIANG-L-39-02

229爻 Historical event Paris Peace Conference. The Paris Peace Conference opened in 1919 after an armistice had stopped major fighting in the First World War. The victorious powers faced urgent and competing questions: how to treat defeated Germany, redraw borders, address the collapsed empires, and build a mechanism to prevent another war. Delegations arrived with different instructions, while many affected communities sought recognition or influence without equal standing at the central table. U.S. President Wilson pressed for a League of Nations. British Prime Minister Lloyd George and French Prime Minister Clemenceau brought their own security and domestic concerns. Committees worked through territorial and financial questions as leaders negotiated larger compromises. The Treaty of Versailles was signed in June 1919, but it did not settle all postwar relations by itself. Separate treaties followed for other defeated powers. The United States Senate later rejected American participation in the Versailles settlement, leaving the country outside the League Wilson had championed. New borders and mandates generated further disputes, and the burdens of war and reconstruction continued. The conference had to make decisions before every demand could be reconciled. The central difficulty was to turn battlefield outcome into political rules accepted, resisted, or revised by people who would live with them. The victorious powers did not negotiate with Germany as an equal participant when the Versailles terms were set. German representatives received the treaty and objected to provisions before signing. Meanwhile other settlements and mandates affected people whose own representatives often lacked decisive power. Those differences in standing shaped the implementation problems that followed. Signature and enforcement then moved the settlement from conference rooms into the lives of affected communities. The German delegation signed the Treaty of Versailles in June 1919 after receiving the terms from the victors. Other treaties addressed Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria, and the Ottoman Empire through separate negotiations. Ratification and implementation proceeded differently among participating states. The U.S. Senate rejected the Versailles treaty, and the United States later negotiated a separate peace with Germany. European governments then dealt with reparations, boundaries, minority questions, and security arrangements established or left unresolved by the settlements.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H40-L1 | XIANG-L-40-02

235爻 Historical event League of Nations covenant. During the Paris peace negotiations, President Wilson and other leaders proposed a League of Nations to provide a standing forum for collective security and diplomacy. The Covenant became part of the Treaty of Versailles and described an assembly, a council, procedures for disputes, and duties accepted by members. The proposal followed a war in which bilateral commitments and military escalation had contributed to catastrophe, though the new institution was also shaped by the interests of victorious states. Negotiators approved the Covenant at the conference, and the League began work in 1920. The United States, whose president had strongly advocated it, did not join. American senators disagreed about whether membership would constrain Congress's authority and draw the country into future conflicts. Wilson rejected some proposed reservations, and the Senate failed to consent to the Versailles Treaty. Other states nevertheless used the League's forums, agencies, and procedures. The organization handled some disputes and humanitarian tasks but could not reliably prevent aggression by major powers in the decades before the Second World War. It starts with a proposal amid peace negotiations, passes through the Covenant's adoption and a major domestic rejection, and continues through years of practical work under limits that varied by issue and by member. The League created channels for cooperation while lacking the support of the government that had done much to promote its design. The Senate's opposition included concerns about the Covenant's collective security provisions and Congress's power over war. Other senators supported membership with reservations, but the administration and its opponents did not find a formula that won consent. League membership remained a domestic constitutional issue in the United States after the conference concluded. The League began work in 1920 from its headquarters in Geneva. Member states participated in its assembly and council, and its secretariat supported continuing administration. The United States cooperated in some international activities but remained outside membership. The organization addressed various disputes and humanitarian matters during the interwar years. Later aggression exposed serious limits in its collective-security arrangements. During the Second World War, governments designed a new organization, and the League was dissolved in 1946 as the United Nations assumed its place.

Line-specific comparison Meeting between firmness and flexibility can be without blame. The League's design sought cooperation among sovereign states. This line asks how different forms of authority can meet in a usable arrangement without requiring that every participant become identical. Line 1 | TW-PM-H41-L1 | XIANG-L-41-02

241爻 Historical event Washington Naval Conference. After the First World War, several naval powers faced high costs and growing competition in capital ships. The United States invited major governments to a conference in Washington in 1921. Britain, Japan, France, and Italy joined discussions over fleets; other agreements addressed questions concerning the Pacific and China. Delegates debated what each state could build and retain. The Five-Power Treaty of 1922 established limits on capital ships and specified tonnage ratios among the principal signatories. Older vessels were to be scrapped or converted under agreed rules, while the treaty also dealt with naval bases in parts of the Pacific. Other agreements in the conference package sought to manage regional relations and affirm principles concerning China. The treaties did not abolish navies or resolve every political rivalry. Limits applied to defined classes of vessels, and later developments in other ship types created new concerns. Governments had to implement the schedules, monitor construction, and revisit restrictions as technology and international politics changed. Each state accepted constraints in exchange for a broader arrangement it considered preferable to unregulated competition. The agreements were significant, yet their effect depended on continued observance and on whether changing security circumstances still made the bargain acceptable to the signatories. The ratios were controversial because they made the hierarchy of capital fleets explicit. Japan accepted a lower ratio than the United States and Britain while seeking safeguards for its regional position. Signatories also had to decide which existing ships would be removed from service. The conference agreements entered into force through national approval and subsequent compliance with building restrictions. The principal naval agreement specified limits for the United States, Britain, Japan, France, and Italy. Governments dealt with the disposal of designated ships and restrictions on construction. Other conference agreements addressed Pacific relationships and principles concerning China. Naval diplomacy continued through further meetings during the interwar period, including the London conference in 1930. Later disagreements and withdrawals weakened the limitation system.

Line 1 | TW-PM-H42-L1 | XIANG-L-42-02

247爻 Historical event Kellogg–Briand Pact. In 1928, French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand and U.S. Secretary of State Frank Kellogg helped bring about a pact in which states renounced war as an instrument of national policy. The agreement was signed in Paris by an initial group and attracted additional adherents. Governments publicly committed themselves to resolving disputes by peaceful means. The text gave the declaration broad symbolic reach, but it did not create a standing military force or an effective automatic procedure to stop a government that broke its promise. States continued to interpret questions of self-defense and other obligations in their own ways. In the following decade, armed aggression showed how far the written pledge was from reliable enforcement. The pact did not prevent the Second World War. It nevertheless remained part of later legal arguments about the use of force, including postwar prosecutions. The record contains the pact's words and the actions that followed; it does not support the claim that renunciation alone settled the security problems the signatories faced. The pact's signatories could still claim self-defense when they believed force was justified. Without a shared enforcement mechanism, the pledge depended heavily on each government's later choices and on political reaction by other states. It became one piece of the developing law concerning aggressive war, although that legal legacy did not save its first generation from renewed conflict. Many signatories still maintained forces and pursued security interests of their own. The pact entered into force in 1929 after national approval procedures. Governments continued maintaining armed forces and defining exceptions concerning self-defense. Aggression in the following decade brought new disputes over responses that the signatories would make. War expanded in Europe in 1939 despite the renunciation. After the Axis defeat, the prosecution of aggressive war became part of the charges before the international tribunal at Nuremberg. The pact remained a legal reference even though it had not prevented the renewed fighting.

Line-specific comparison A major undertaking needs support from above rather than an excessive burden below. Renouncing war through the Kellogg–Briand Pact involved responsibilities for governments. The line asks who supplies the means for the ambitious promise and who would bear failure. Line 1 | TW-PM-H43-L1 | XIANG-L-43-02

253爻 Historical event U.S. Neutrality Acts. As the 1930s brought war and aggression abroad, many Americans feared that arms sales, loans, and shipping might again draw the United States into a European conflict. Congress enacted a series of Neutrality Acts beginning in 1935. The laws restricted arms exports to belligerents and, in later versions, addressed travel, loans, and trade. They were designed to reduce connections through which a distant war could become an American war. The restrictions also limited the administration's room to distinguish an aggressor from a country resisting attack. After war began in Europe in 1939, Congress revised the rules to permit certain sales on a cash-and-carry basis. Further measures in 1941, including Lend-Lease, moved American policy toward active support for states fighting the Axis while the United States was not yet formally at war. Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor brought a declaration of war in December 1941. Neutrality laws expressed the country's anxieties about earlier entanglement, but events required legislators to reconsider the costs of preventing some forms of aid. The statutes' legal categories could affect very different conflicts in similar ways. Some restrictions were designed to apply to all belligerents alike, even when Americans saw a difference between aggressor and victim. That design limited presidential discretion and became increasingly contentious as the European crisis grew and the costs of withholding supplies changed. Public debate about intervention therefore continued alongside each statutory change. The 1937 law restricted travel on belligerent ships and included a temporary cash-and-carry arrangement for goods other than arms. In November 1939, Congress permitted arms sales under cash-and-carry conditions while retaining other limits. After Lend-Lease began, lawmakers also removed restrictions on arming American merchant vessels and entering designated war zones. Naval attacks and mounting assistance to the Allies continued during those changes. Formal declarations in December 1941 placed the United States in the war and displaced the earlier neutrality framework.

Line-specific comparison Advancing without the strength to prevail creates blame. Neutrality policy raised a question about legal declarations and practical consequences. The line asks whether a government can sustain the position it announces when war abroad changes the conditions. Line 1 | TW-PM-H44-L1 | XIANG-L-44-02

259爻 Historical event Pearl Harbor and the U.S. response. On December 7, 1941, Japanese aircraft attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet and military facilities at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The strike killed service members and civilians and damaged ships and aircraft. It followed months of worsening relations between Japan and the United States over war in Asia, economic sanctions, and negotiations that had not produced agreement. News of the attack reached Washington, where President Franklin Roosevelt addressed Congress the next day. Congress declared war on Japan. Germany and Italy then declared war on the United States, and Congress responded with declarations against them. The United States began a vast mobilization of armed forces, industry, and supplies for campaigns in the Pacific and in cooperation with European allies. Pearl Harbor was not a battle in Europe, but it changed American participation in the European war. The damaged fleet was repaired and rebuilt over time; immediate losses could not be undone by the rapid political decision to fight. Wartime policies at home also affected civilians, including the unjust incarceration of Japanese Americans. Political leaders then chose formal declarations and a program of mobilization that linked American factories and troops to existing Allied operations. The Pacific war expanded beyond the Hawaiian attack as Japanese forces struck other American, British, and Allied positions. The U.S. government organized additional forces and worked with Britain on strategy against Germany as well as Japan. Ship repair and new construction restored and enlarged American naval strength over time. The battleship Arizona remained a wreck at Pearl Harbor, while several other damaged ships returned to service after salvage and repairs. Campaigns continued for several years across the Pacific and Europe. Germany surrendered in May 1945, and Japan's surrender followed in August, with formal surrender documents signed in September. Service members and civilians then faced demobilization, occupation, and recovery after the fighting ended.

Line-specific comparison A firm restraint checks an emerging attachment. Relations with Japan had already become dangerous before Pearl Harbor. This line invites a question about early control of an escalating process, without suggesting a simple measure could certainly have prevented the attack. Pearl Harbor was not a battle in Europe, but it changed American participation in the European war. The damaged fleet was repaired and rebuilt over time; immediate losses could not be undone by the rapid political decision to fight. Wartime policies at home also affected civilians, including the unjust incarceration of Japanese Americans. Political leaders then chose formal declarations and a program of mobilization that linked American factories and troops to existing Allied operations. The Pacific war expanded beyond the Hawaiian attack as Japanese forces struck other American, British, and Allied positions. The U.S. government organized additional forces and worked with Britain on strategy against Germany as well as Japan. Ship repair and new construction restored and enlarged American naval strength over time. The battleship Arizona remained a wreck at Pearl Harbor, while several other damaged ships returned to service after salvage and repairs. Campaigns continued for several years across the Pacific and Europe. Germany surrendered in May 1945, and Japan's surrender followed in August, with formal surrender documents signed in September. Service members and civilians then faced demobilization, occupation, and recovery after the fighting ended.
